docs.title: About this book
docs.text: A complete first course in Spanish for English speakers, from the sounds and letters of the language to talking about what you did yesterday. Each of the sixteen lessons opens with a short dialogue, gives the vocabulary in a table, explains one or two points of grammar step by step, and ends with a cultural note on Spain and Latin America, a summary, exercises with answers and a quiz. Every Spanish word and sentence can be heard aloud. The course covers the A1 level of the Common European Framework and the first steps of A2.

docs.title: About this book
docs.text:
¡Bienvenidos!

This is a first course in Spanish for English speakers. It starts from nothing, not even the alphabet, and takes you in sixteen lessons to the point where you can introduce yourself, talk about your family, your town and your day, order a meal, ask the way, go shopping, make plans and tell a friend what you did on holiday. In the terms of the Common European Framework of Reference for Languages, it covers level A1 completely and the first part of A2. Spanish is spoken as a first language by several hundred million people in more than twenty countries, and it is one of the most rewarding languages an English speaker can learn: much of its vocabulary is related to English, its spelling is regular, and its grammar, though different from English, is logical and learnable.

docs.title: Who this book is for
docs.text:
The book is written for adult and teenage learners whose first or strongest language is English and who have studied little or no Spanish. You may be learning for travel, for work, for a first university course, to talk with family or friends, or simply for pleasure. No knowledge of grammar is assumed: every term is explained when it first appears, and the Glossary at the end collects them all. If you studied Spanish at school long ago, the first lessons will come back quickly, and the later ones will give you the structures most people never got to.

You can work through the book alone, with a teacher, or with a partner. Everything you need is on the page: dialogues you can hear, explanations, practice, and answers.

docs.text:

Part Lessons What you learn I · First steps 1 to 4 Sounds, spelling and stress; greetings and introductions; numbers, dates and time; nouns, gender and articles II · The present 5 to 8 Ser and estar; regular verbs in the present; family and describing people; food and the café III · Everyday life 9 to 12 The city and directions; the key irregular verbs; daily routine and reflexive verbs; likes with gustar IV · Plans and memories 13 to 16 Shopping and clothes; travel plans with ir a; the preterite; a final review

Table 1. The plan of the course.

At the end of the book are the Verb Tables, with every verb pattern of the course; a Glossary of grammar terms and troublesome words; and a short list of Further Reading.

docs.title: How to use a lesson
docs.text:
Every lesson has the same nine parts, so you always know where you are.

  1. Learning outcomes. What you will be able to do at the end. Read them first, and come back to them at the end.
  2. Dialogue. A short scene in Spanish, with an English translation, that uses the language of the lesson. Listen to it, read it, and read it aloud. Several characters appear again and again: Daniel, an English student on a course in Salamanca; Lucía, his Mexican classmate; their teacher, Señora Ruiz; and their friends.
  3. Vocabulary. The new words and phrases, in tables, with a sound guide for each.
  4. Grammar. Usually two sections, each explaining one point step by step, from the idea to the forms, with examples and a worked example.
  5. Practice. Tables to fill in from memory, sentences to say aloud, and a speaking task.
  6. Culture. A note on life and language in Spain and Latin America.
  7. Summary. The essentials of the lesson in a few lines. Reread it before you start the next lesson.
  8. Exercises. Questions with answers folded underneath. Try each one before you open the answer.
  9. Quiz. A set of questions of different kinds to check what you have learnt.

Aim to spend several sessions on each lesson rather than one long one. Short, regular practice works far better than long, occasional sessions: twenty minutes a day will take you further than three hours on a Sunday. Say everything aloud, even when you are alone. Go back to earlier lessons often; each review makes the language more automatic.

Learn phrases, not only words

Learn whole phrases such as ¿Me pone un café, por favor? or Me gustaría ir as they are, before you understand every part of them. The grammar sections explain the parts later, and by then you will already be using them.

docs.title: Hearing and practising
docs.text:
This book is meant to be heard as well as read. Every Spanish word, phrase and sentence has a listen button beside it: press it to hear the phrase, and press again to hear it slowly. A dialogue or a list of phrases also has a Play all button that reads it from start to finish.

  • Sound guides. New words have an approximate pronunciation in square brackets, using English spelling, with the stressed syllable in capitals: gracias [GRAH-syahs]. Lesson 1 explains how to read them. They help, but the recordings are the real model.
  • Practice tables. A table with a Practice switch hides its key forms and turns them into boxes for you to fill in; Check marks your answers.
  • Typed answers. Many exercises have a box in which to type your answer and check it before you open the model answer. Accents are checked too, but an answer typed without them is accepted with a reminder.
  • Quizzes. Each lesson ends with a quiz: multiple choice, gaps to fill, matching, words to put in order, a wrong word to find, sentences to listen to and write down, and phrases to say aloud. Your answers and best score are kept in your browser, so you can come back to a quiz later.
  • Speaking tasks. Boxes titled "Say it" ask you to speak. Where your browser can recognise speech, a microphone button lets you check your pronunciation.

docs.title: Which Spanish?
docs.text:
Spanish is one language with many accents, like English. This book teaches a neutral Spanish that is understood everywhere, and points out the main differences between Spain and Latin America as they come up: in pronunciation (Lesson 1), in the words for "you" (Lesson 2), in everyday vocabulary (in the culture notes of every lesson), and in the use of the past tenses (Lesson 15).

Two choices are worth knowing from the start:

  • Vosotros. Spain has a plural informal "you", vosotros, with its own verb forms. Latin America uses ustedes instead. The book shows the vosotros forms in every table so that you can understand Spaniards, but if your Spanish is for Latin America you may simply learn to recognise them.
  • The sound of z and c. Most speakers in Spain say gracias and cinco with a th sound; Latin Americans say them with an s. Both are correct. The sound guides show the Latin American [s] and mention the Spanish [th] where it helps.

Whichever variety you choose, keep to it, and enjoy hearing the others. ¡Vamos a empezar! Let's begin.

docs.title: Lesson 11: Daily Routine and Reflexive Verbs
docs.text:
La rutina diaria y los verbos reflexivos

What time do you get up? Do you shower in the morning or at night? When do you go to bed? Talking about your day is one of the first real conversations you have in a new language, and in Spanish it needs one new piece of grammar: the reflexive verb. In English we say "I get up", "I get dressed", "I go to bed". In Spanish these are actions you do to yourself: me levanto, "I raise myself", me visto, "I dress myself", me acuesto, "I lay myself down". You already know one reflexive verb, llamarse, from Lesson 2. This lesson gives you the whole pattern, the verbs of a normal day, and the words that put a routine in order.

Learning outcomes

By the end of this lesson you will be able to:

  • describe your daily routine from morning to night;
  • conjugate reflexive verbs in the present, including the stem-changing ones (despertarse, acostarse, vestirse);
  • put the reflexive pronoun in the right place, before the verb or attached to an infinitive;
  • tell the difference between lavar and lavarse, acostar and acostarse;
  • order events with primero, luego, después, por último, and say how often you do things.

masculinefeminineplural

docs.title: 11.1 Dialogue: early birds and night owls
docs.text:
Marta and Tomás share a flat in Madrid. It is Sunday evening, and they are planning who uses the bathroom first on Monday morning.

  • Tomás: Marta, ¿a qué hora te levantas mañana? — Marta, what time are you getting up tomorrow?
  • Marta: Entre semana me levanto siempre a las siete. — On weekdays I always get up at seven.
  • Tomás: ¡Qué temprano! ¿Y qué haces primero? — How early! And what do you do first?
  • Marta: Primero me ducho, luego me visto y después desayuno un café con tostadas. — First I shower, then I get dressed and after that I have coffee and toast for breakfast.
  • Tomás: Yo me despierto a las siete, pero no me levanto hasta las siete y media. — I wake up at seven, but I don't get up until half past seven.
  • Marta: ¿Y no llegas tarde al trabajo? — And aren't you late for work?
  • Tomás: No, porque me ducho muy rápido y no desayuno en casa. Tomo un café en la oficina. — No, because I shower very quickly and I don't have breakfast at home. I have a coffee at the office.
  • Marta: Entonces el baño es para mí de siete a siete y media. ¿Y por la noche? — So the bathroom is mine from seven to half past seven. And at night?
  • Tomás: Por la noche ceno a las nueve y media y me acuesto a las doce. — At night I have dinner at half past nine and go to bed at twelve.
  • Marta: ¿A las doce? Yo me acuesto a las once. Nunca me duermo tarde entre semana. — At twelve? I go to bed at eleven. I never fall asleep late on weekdays.
  • Tomás: ¿Y los sábados? — And on Saturdays?
  • Marta: Los sábados es diferente: me levanto a las diez y me relajo todo el día. — Saturdays are different: I get up at ten and relax all day.

Notice:

  1. Every verb about the body and the day comes with a small pronoun in front: me levanto, te levantas, me ducho, me acuesto. These are reflexive verbs.
  2. Some verbs change their stem: despertarse gives me despierto, acostarse gives me acuesto, vestirse gives me visto. You know the first two patterns from Lesson 10.
  3. desayunar ("to have breakfast") and cenar ("to have dinner") are ordinary verbs, not reflexive: desayuno, ceno.

docs.title: 11.2 Vocabulary: a day from morning to night
The verbs of the routine

Table 11.1. Reflexive verbs of the daily routine. The infinitive ends in -se; the yo form starts with me.

Spanish English Yo form desayunar to have breakfast desayuno comer to eat; to have lunch como cenar to have dinner ceno trabajar to work trabajo estudiar to study estudio salir de casa to leave home salgo de casa (irregular yo form) volver a casa (o→ue) to come back home vuelvo a casa dormir (o→ue) to sleep duermo

Table 11.2. Non-reflexive verbs of the routine. Comer is "to eat" in general and also "to have lunch", the main meal of the day in Spain and Mexico.

docs.title: Things you need
docs.text:
Spanish English el despertador the alarm clock el baño the bathroom la ducha the shower el jabón the soap el champú the shampoo el cepillo de dientes the toothbrush la toalla the towel la cara the face las manos the hands (la mano is feminine) el pelo the hair los dientes the teeth la ropa clothes (singular in Spanish)

Table 11.3. Things and body parts. Note la mano, a feminine noun ending in -o, and la ropa, a singular word for "clothes".

docs.title: Time phrases
docs.text:
Spanish English por la mañana in the morning por la tarde in the afternoon, in the early evening por la noche at night, in the evening a las siete at seven a las siete de la mañana at seven in the morning a mediodía at midday temprano / tarde early / late entre semana on weekdays de lunes a viernes from Monday to Friday los fines de semana at weekends

Table 11.4. When things happen. With a clock time, use de la mañana; without one, use por la mañana.

Common mistake: por la mañana or de la mañana?

Say Me levanto temprano por la mañana ("in the morning") but Me levanto a las seis de la mañana ("at six in the morning"). De goes with a clock time; por goes on its own. In parts of Latin America you will also hear en la mañana, which is correct there.

docs.title: 11.3 Grammar: reflexive verbs and their pronouns
What "reflexive" means
docs.text:
A reflexive verb describes an action that the subject does to itself. Compare:

  • Lavo el coche. — I wash the car. (the car gets washed)
  • Me lavo. — I wash (myself). (I get washed)

The infinitive of a reflexive verb has -se attached: lavarse, levantarse. When you conjugate it, the -se becomes a pronoun that matches the subject, and moves in front of the verb. The verb itself is conjugated exactly like any regular verb of Lesson 6.

docs.title: The reflexive pronouns
docs.text:
Subject Reflexive pronoun English yo me myself tú te yourself él, ella, usted se himself, herself, yourself nosotros, nosotras nos ourselves vosotros, vosotras os yourselves (Spain) ellos, ellas, ustedes se themselves, yourselves

Table 11.5. The reflexive pronouns. Se serves three persons: él, usted and ellos.

docs.title: Two regular reflexive verbs
docs.text:
Person levantarse (to get up) ducharse (to shower) yo me levanto me ducho tú te levantas te duchas él, ella, usted se levanta se ducha nosotros, nosotras nos levantamos nos duchamos vosotros, vosotras os levantáis os ducháis ellos, ellas, ustedes se levantan se duchan

Table 11.6. Two regular -ar reflexive verbs. Practice hides the pronoun and the ending.

  • ¿A qué hora te levantas? — What time do you get up?
  • Mi hermano se ducha por la noche. — My brother showers at night.
  • Nos levantamos a las ocho los domingos. — We get up at eight on Sundays.
  • ¿Usted se afeita todos los días? — Do you shave every day?

docs.title: Where the pronoun goes
docs.text:
The rule is simple, and it is the same for every pronoun you will learn in this book:

  1. Before a conjugated verb, as a separate word: Me levanto.
  2. In a negative sentence, after no and before the verb: No me levanto temprano. Never Me no levanto.
  3. With an infinitive (the -ar, -er, -ir form) the pronoun can be attached to the end of the infinitive, or placed before the conjugated verb in front of it. Both mean exactly the same:
Pronoun attached Pronoun in front English Voy a levantarme a las seis. Me voy a levantar a las seis. I'm going to get up at six. Tengo que ducharme. Me tengo que duchar. I have to have a shower. ¿Quieres acostarte? ¿Te quieres acostar? Do you want to go to bed? No podemos dormirnos. No nos podemos dormir. We can't get to sleep.

Table 11.7. Two positions with an infinitive. The pronoun must still match the subject: tengo que ducharme, not tengo que ducharse.

Common mistake: keeping -se

The -se of the dictionary form is only for the infinitive in the dictionary. In a sentence it changes with the person: Voy a ducharme (I), ¿Vas a ducharte? (you), Vamos a ducharnos (we). Saying Voy a ducharse is a very common beginner's error.

docs.title: Reflexive or not?
docs.text:
Many verbs exist in both forms. Without the pronoun, you do the action to someone or something else; with it, you do it to yourself.

Not reflexive Reflexive Lavo los platos. — I wash the dishes. Me lavo las manos. — I wash my hands. Despierto a mi hijo. — I wake my son. Me despierto. — I wake up. Acuesto a los niños. — I put the children to bed. Me acuesto. — I go to bed. Visto al bebé. — I dress the baby. Me visto. — I get dressed. Llamo a Ana. — I call Ana. Me llamo Ana. — My name is Ana.

Table 11.8. The same verb with and without the reflexive pronoun. The a before a person (a mi hijo, a los niños) is the "personal a".

My hands or the hands?

With parts of the body and clothes, Spanish uses the article, not the possessive, because the reflexive pronoun already shows whose hands they are: Me lavo las manos ("I wash my hands"), Me pongo la chaqueta ("I put on my jacket"), Se cepilla los dientes ("she brushes her teeth"). Me lavo mis manos is understood but sounds foreign.

docs.title: 11.4 Grammar: stem changes, and telling a routine in order
Reflexive verbs that change their stem
docs.text:
Reflexive verbs follow the same stem changes as other verbs. In Lesson 10 you met e→ie (querer → quiero) and o→ue (poder → puedo). Here is a third pattern, e→i, which only happens in -ir verbs such as vestirse. As always, the stem changes in every form except nosotros and vosotros, the "boot" shape.

Person despertarse (e→ie) acostarse (o→ue) vestirse (e→i) yo me despierto me acuesto me visto tú te despiertas te acuestas te vistes él, ella, usted se despierta se acuesta se viste nosotros, nosotras nos despertamos nos acostamos nos vestimos vosotros, vosotras os despertáis os acostáis os vestís ellos, ellas, ustedes se despiertan se acuestan se visten

Table 11.9. Three stem-changing reflexive verbs. The nosotros and vosotros forms keep the original vowel.

Other verbs of the day that change their stem: dormirse (o→ue: me duermo), volver (o→ue: vuelvo), and sentarse (e→ie: me siento, "I sit down").

Common mistake: changing the nosotros form

The stem change never reaches nosotros and vosotros: nos acostamos, not nos acuestamos; nos despertamos, not nos despiertamos. If the stress does not fall on the stem, the stem does not change.

docs.title: Dormir and dormirse
docs.text:
dormir means "to sleep"; dormirse means "to fall asleep". In the same way, ir is "to go" and irse is "to leave, to go away".

  • Duermo ocho horas. — I sleep for eight hours.
  • Me duermo en el sofá. — I fall asleep on the sofa.
  • Me voy. ¡Hasta mañana! — I'm off. See you tomorrow!

docs.title: Putting events in order
docs.text:
Sequence words make a list of actions into a story. They usually go at the start of the clause.

Spanish English primero first luego then después afterwards, after that más tarde later antes de + infinitive before (doing) después de + infinitive after (doing) por último / finalmente lastly, finally

Table 11.10. Sequence words.

After antes de and después de, Spanish uses the infinitive, where English uses "-ing". The reflexive pronoun is attached and matches the subject:

  • Desayuno después de ducharme. — I have breakfast after showering.
  • Antes de acostarse, mi padre lee el periódico. — Before going to bed, my father reads the newspaper.

docs.title: How often?
docs.text:
Spanish English siempre always todos los días / cada día every day normalmente normally, usually a menudo often a veces sometimes casi nunca hardly ever nunca never

Table 11.11. Frequency words.

  • Siempre me levanto a las siete. — I always get up at seven.
  • A veces me ducho por la noche. — Sometimes I shower at night.
  • Nunca me acuesto antes de las once. — I never go to bed before eleven.
  • No me acuesto nunca antes de las once. — The same: if nunca comes after the verb, put no in front.

Double negatives are correct in Spanish

nunca can go before the verb on its own, or after the verb with no in front: Nunca desayuno = No desayuno nunca. Unlike in standard English, the "double negative" is normal and correct.

Figure 11.1 A day in Spain. A typical weekday in Madrid, from waking up at seven to going to bed at midnight, with lunch at two and dinner at half past nine.

Worked example: describing a day

Turn these notes about Lucía into sentences: 7.00 wake up — shower — dress — 8.00 leave — 18.00 home — 22.30 bed.

  1. Wake up: Lucía se despierta a las siete. (despertarse, e→ie, third person)
  2. Shower and dress, in order: Primero se ducha y luego se viste. (vestirse, e→i)
  3. Leave: Sale de casa a las ocho.
  4. Come home: Vuelve a casa a las seis de la tarde. (de with a clock time)
  5. Bed: Por último, se acuesta a las diez y media. (acostarse, o→ue)

docs.title: Me, te, se …
docs.text:
Fill each gap aloud with the right pronoun, then listen.

  • Yo me levanto a las ocho. — I get up at eight.
  • ¿Tú te duchas por la mañana? — Do you shower in the morning?
  • Mi abuela se acuesta muy temprano. — My grandmother goes to bed very early.
  • Nosotros nos vestimos rápido. — We get dressed quickly.
  • ¿Vosotros os despertáis tarde? — Do you all wake up late?
  • Los niños se cepillan los dientes. — The children brush their teeth.

docs.title: A routine to complete
docs.text:
Time Activity Spanish 6.45 I wake up me despierto 7.00 I get up me levanto 7.10 I have a shower me ducho 7.30 I get dressed me visto 7.45 I have breakfast desayuno 23.00 I go to bed me acuesto

Table 11.12. Switch on Practice and write each yo form from memory.

Say it

Describe your own weekday in five or six sentences, with at least three sequence words and two frequency words. For example:

Normalmente me despierto a las siete. Primero me ducho y luego me visto. Después desayuno un café. A veces voy al trabajo en bicicleta. Por la noche ceno a las ocho y me acuesto a las once.

Then ask a partner: ¿A qué hora te levantas? ¿Te duchas por la mañana o por la noche? ¿A qué hora te acuestas?

docs.title: 11.6 Culture: the Spanish day and the Latin American day
docs.text:
Late meals in Spain. The Spanish timetable surprises most visitors. Breakfast is light, often just coffee and toast or a pastry. Many people have a small snack in the middle of the morning. Lunch, la comida, is the main meal and is usually eaten between two and three in the afternoon, and dinner, la cena, often not before nine or ten at night. In the afternoon, children and many adults have la merienda, a snack such as a sandwich or fruit. Restaurants follow the same hours, so a restaurant in Spain may be empty at seven in the evening and full at ten.

The split day. Many Spanish shops and offices traditionally work a jornada partida, a "split day": open in the morning, closed for two or three hours at lunchtime, open again until eight or nine. Others have a jornada continua, a continuous day that finishes in the mid-afternoon, which is common in summer. Large stores in cities stay open all day.

The siesta. The siesta, a short sleep after lunch, is famous, but in modern cities most people with a full-time job do not have time for one on weekdays. It is more a habit for weekends, holidays, hot summer afternoons, and for people who go home for lunch.

Latin America. Timetables vary from country to country, but in general meals are earlier than in Spain. In Mexico, la comida is also the big midday meal, eaten in the early or mid-afternoon, and la cena is lighter. In much of South America the midday meal is called el almuerzo. In Chile, an evening snack of tea, bread and something savoury is called la once, and in Argentina and Uruguay the afternoon merienda often comes with mate, a herbal drink shared from a gourd.

Words that change. In much of Latin America, especially Mexico, bañarse is the everyday word for having a shower, not only a bath: Me baño por la mañana usually means "I shower in the morning". In Spain, ducharse is the shower and bañarse the bath or a swim.

Getting up early. Spanish has a single verb for getting up early: madrugar. A well-known proverb says A quien madruga, Dios le ayuda, "God helps the one who gets up early", the Spanish cousin of "the early bird catches the worm". In Latin America you will often hear it as Al que madruga, Dios lo ayuda.

docs.title: 11.7 Summary
docs.text:
Summary

  • A reflexive verb is an action you do to yourself. Its infinitive ends in -se: levantarse, ducharse, acostarse.
  • The reflexive pronouns are me, te, se, nos, os, se. The verb itself is conjugated normally: me levanto, te levantas, se levanta, nos levantamos, os levantáis, se levantan.
  • Position: before the conjugated verb (no me levanto), or attached to an infinitive (voy a levantarme = me voy a levantar). The pronoun always matches the subject.
  • Stem changes work as usual, except in nosotros and vosotros: me despierto (e→ie), me acuesto (o→ue), me visto (e→i).
  • With and without -se: lavo el coche / me lavo; acuesto a los niños / me acuesto. Use the article with body parts: me lavo las manos.
  • Order and frequency: primero, luego, después, más tarde, por último; siempre, normalmente, a menudo, a veces, nunca. De la mañana with a clock time, por la mañana without.

docs.title: 11.8 Exercises
docs.text:
Exercise 1

Give the yo form of levantarse.

Answer

me levanto. me levanto

Exercise 2

Complete: Mis hijos ___ duchan por la noche.

Answer

se. Mis hijos se duchan por la noche. Ellos takes se.

Exercise 3

Give the tú form of acostarse.

Answer

te acuestas. te acuestas. The stem changes o→ue.

Exercise 4

Give the nosotros form of despertarse.

Answer

nos despertamos. nos despertamos. No stem change in the nosotros form.

Exercise 5

How do you say "she gets dressed"?

Answer

se viste. Se viste. Vestirse changes e→i.

Exercise 6

Rewrite with the pronoun attached to the infinitive: Me tengo que levantar temprano.

Answer

Tengo que levantarme temprano. Tengo que levantarme temprano.

Exercise 7

Reflexive or not? Choose lavo or me lavo: (a) ___ el pelo; (b) ___ la ropa; (c) ___ la cara; (d) ___ el coche.

Answer

(a) Me lavo el pelo. (b) Lavo la ropa. (c) Me lavo la cara. (d) Lavo el coche. Your own body: reflexive; something else: not reflexive.

Exercise 8

Correct the mistake: Voy a ducharse ahora.

Answer

Voy a ducharme ahora. Voy a ducharme ahora. The pronoun matches the subject, yo.

Exercise 9

Say "I never have breakfast" in two ways.

Answer

Nunca desayuno / No desayuno nunca. Nunca desayuno. No desayuno nunca.

Exercise 10

Write four sentences about Javier's Saturday, in order, using primero, luego, después and por último: he gets up at ten, has a bath, has breakfast in a café, and in the evening goes to bed late.

Answer

Primero, Javier se levanta a las diez. Luego se baña. Después desayuna en un café. Por último, por la noche, se acuesta tarde. Other orders of the sequence words are possible, as long as primero comes first and por último last.

docs.title: 11.9 Quiz
docs.text:
Quiz: daily routine and reflexive verbs

Exercise 11

Nosotros ___ a las siete.

  1. nos levantamos
  2. se levantan
  3. me levanto
  4. nos levantan
Answer

nos levantamos

Nosotros takes nos and the -amos ending.

Exercise 12

Which sentence means "I put the children to bed"?

  1. Me acuesto a los niños.
  2. Acuesto a los niños.
  3. Se acuestan los niños.
  4. Me acuesto.
Answer

Acuesto a los niños.

You do the action to someone else, so the verb is not reflexive.

Exercise 13

Mi madre se ___ a las seis. (despertarse)

Hint: e→ie in the third person

Answer

despierta

despertarse changes e→ie in every form except nosotros and vosotros.

Exercise 14

¿A qué hora ___ acuestas?

Answer

te

The tú form takes the pronoun te.

Exercise 15

Say "I get dressed" in Spanish.

Answer

me visto / yo me visto

Exercise 16

Match the Spanish to the English.

ABa menudonevera vecesfinallynuncaoftenpor últimosometimes Answer

a menudo — often; a veces — sometimes; nunca — never; por último — finally

Exercise 17

Put the words in order: "I'm going to get up early."

Words: a / temprano. / levantarme / Voy

Answer

Voy a levantarme temprano.

Exercise 18

Tap the wrong word.

Nosotros nos acuestamos a las once.

Answer

Wrong word: acuestamos.

Corrected: Nosotros nos acostamos a las once.

The stem does not change in the nosotros form.

Exercise 19

Write what you hear.

Dictation. Have someone read the sentence aloud, then write it down.

Primero me ducho y luego desayuno.

Answer

Primero me ducho y luego desayuno.

Exercise 20

Say it aloud.

Normalmente me levanto a las siete de la mañana.

Answer

Say: Normalmente me levanto a las siete de la mañana.

docs.title: Lesson 7: Family and Describing People
docs.text:
La familia y las descripciones

Sooner or later every conversation in Spanish turns to the family. People ask whether you have brothers and sisters, how old your children are, what your partner is like, and they show you photos on their phones with real enthusiasm. In this lesson you learn the words for the members of a family, the possessive words my, your, his, our, and how to describe what people look like and what they are like as people. Along the way you will meet the most important rule of Spanish adjectives: they agree with the noun they describe, in gender and in number.

Learning outcomes

By the end of this lesson you will be able to:

  • name the members of your family and talk about them;
  • use the possessive adjectives mi, tu, su, nuestro, vuestro and make them agree;
  • make any adjective agree with its noun and put it in the right place;
  • describe people's appearance with ser, tener and llevar, and their character with ser;
  • soften or strengthen a description with muy, bastante, un poco and nada.

masculinefeminineplural

docs.title: 7.1 Dialogue: photos of the family
docs.text:
After class, Lucía shows Daniel some photos of her family on her phone.

  • Daniel: ¿Quién es este señor? — Who is this man?
  • Lucía: Es mi padre, Luis. Es médico. — That's my father, Luis. He's a doctor.
  • Daniel: Es muy alto. ¿Y la mujer rubia? — He's very tall. And the blonde woman?
  • Lucía: Es mi madre, Elena. Es simpática y muy divertida. — That's my mother, Elena. She's nice and really funny.
  • Daniel: ¿Tienes hermanos? — Do you have any brothers or sisters?
  • Lucía: Sí, tengo un hermano. Se llama Diego y tiene diecisiete años. — Yes, I have a brother. His name is Diego and he's seventeen.
  • Daniel: ¿Es el chico de pelo largo? — Is he the boy with the long hair?
  • Lucía: Sí, es él. Es un poco tímido, pero es muy inteligente. — Yes, that's him. He's a bit shy, but he's very clever.
  • Daniel: ¿Y estos señores mayores? — And this older couple?
  • Lucía: Son mis abuelos, Antonio y Carmen. Viven con nosotros. — They're my grandparents, Antonio and Carmen. They live with us.
  • Daniel: ¡Qué familia tan grande! Yo soy hijo único. — What a big family! I'm an only child.
  • Lucía: ¿Y cómo son tus padres? — And what are your parents like?
  • Daniel: Mi madre es baja y morena, y lleva gafas. Mi padre es bastante serio, pero es un buen hombre. — My mother is short and dark-haired, and she wears glasses. My father is quite serious, but he's a good man.

Notice:

  1. hermanos in Daniel's question means "brothers and sisters", not only "brothers". A masculine plural covers a mixed group, just as nosotros does (Lesson 2).
  2. The adjectives change with the person: mi padre es alto but mi madre es baja; simpática and divertida end in -a because they describe a woman.
  3. Age uses tener: tiene diecisiete años, literally "he has seventeen years" (Lesson 3).
  4. un buen hombre: the adjective bueno comes before the noun here and loses its final -o. Section 7.4 explains why.

docs.title: 7.2 Vocabulary: the family and describing people
The family
docs.text:
Figure 7.1 Lucía's family. Lucía's family tree: her grandparents Antonio and Carmen; their children Luis (her father) and Rosa (her aunt); Luis's wife Elena (her mother); Rosa's husband Javier (her uncle); Lucía, her brother Diego, and her cousin Marta. Masculine Feminine Plural (mixed group) English el padre la madre los padres father, mother, parents el hijo la hija los hijos son, daughter, children el hermano la hermana los hermanos brother, sister, siblings el abuelo la abuela los abuelos grandfather, grandmother, grandparents el nieto la nieta los nietos grandson, granddaughter, grandchildren el tío la tía los tíos uncle, aunt, uncles and aunts el primo la prima los primos cousin (male, female), cousins el sobrino la sobrina los sobrinos nephew, niece, nephews and nieces el marido, el esposo la mujer, la esposa los esposos husband, wife, husband and wife el novio la novia los novios boyfriend, girlfriend; also groom, bride el suegro la suegra los suegros father-in-law, mother-in-law el cuñado la cuñada los cuñados brother-in-law, sister-in-law

Table 7.1. Family words. Almost all of them follow the pattern -o for a man, -a for a woman.

A few more useful words and phrases:

Spanish Sounds like English la familia [fah-MEE-lyah] the family papá, mamá [pah-PAH, mah-MAH] dad, mum el bebé [beh-BEH] the baby (for boys and girls alike) hijo único, hija única [EE-hoh OO-nee-koh] only child (boy, girl) mayor [mah-YOR] older; elderly (polite) menor [meh-NOR] younger mi hermano mayor my older brother mi hermana menor my younger sister casado, casada [kah-SAH-doh] married soltero, soltera [sohl-TEH-roh] single divorciado, divorciada [dee-bor-SYAH-doh] divorced la pareja [pah-REH-hah] partner, couple

Table 7.2. More family vocabulary. The j of hijo and pareja is the throaty sound of Lesson 1.

Common mistake: parents are not relatives

los padres means "the parents". The word for "relatives" is los parientes or los familiares. So Tengo muchos parientes en Chile means "I have a lot of relatives in Chile".

docs.title: What people look like
docs.text:
Spanish Sounds like English alto / alta [AHL-toh] tall bajo / baja [BAH-hoh] short delgado / delgada [dehl-GAH-doh] slim fuerte [FWEHR-teh] strong, well-built guapo / guapa [GWAH-poh] good-looking joven [HOH-behn] young mayor [mah-YOR] old, elderly (polite) rubio / rubia [RROO-byoh] blond, fair-haired moreno / morena [moh-REH-noh] dark-haired; also dark-skinned or tanned pelirrojo / pelirroja [peh-lee-RROH-hoh] red-haired el pelo largo / corto [PEH-loh LAR-goh / KOR-toh] long / short hair el pelo rizado / liso [rree-SAH-doh / LEE-soh] curly / straight hair los ojos azules / verdes / marrones [OH-hohs ah-SOO-lehs] blue / green / brown eyes la barba, el bigote [BAR-bah, bee-GOH-teh] beard, moustache las gafas [GAH-fahs] glasses (Spain) los lentes, los anteojos [LEHN-tehs, ahn-teh-OH-hohs] glasses (Latin America)

Table 7.3. Appearance.

docs.title: What people are like
docs.text:
Spanish English Spanish English simpático nice, friendly antipático unfriendly divertido fun, funny aburrido boring trabajador hard-working perezoso lazy abierto open, outgoing tímido shy alegre cheerful serio serious generoso generous tacaño mean, stingy tranquilo calm nervioso nervous, restless amable kind inteligente intelligent

Table 7.4. Character, in pairs of opposites. They are given in the masculine singular, the form found in a dictionary.

False friend: sensible

sensible means "sensitive", not "sensible". A sensible person is sensato or razonable. Likewise, simpático means "nice, likeable", not "sympathetic".

docs.title: 7.3 Grammar: possessive adjectives
docs.text:
The possessive adjectives are the words for my, your, his, her, our, their. They go before the noun, and in Spanish they agree with the thing possessed, not with the owner.

Owner with a singular noun with a plural noun English yo mi hermano mis hermanos my tú tu hermano tus hermanos your (tú) él, ella, usted su hermano sus hermanos his, her, its, your (usted) nosotros nuestro hermano, nuestra hermana nuestros hermanos, nuestras hermanas our vosotros vuestro hermano, vuestra hermana vuestros hermanos, vuestras hermanas your (vosotros, Spain) ellos, ellas, ustedes su hermano sus hermanos their, your (ustedes)

Table 7.5. Possessive adjectives. Practice hides the possessives.

Three things to notice:

  • Only nuestro and vuestro have a feminine. mi, tu and su have just a singular and a plural: mi padre, mi madre, mis padres.
  • Agreement is with the noun. nuestra casa ("our house") is feminine because casa is feminine, even if the owners are all men. mis libros is plural because there are several books, even though there is only one owner.
  • No written accent on tu. tu without an accent is "your"; tú with one is "you" (Lesson 2): Tú tienes tu libro. — You have your book.

docs.title: The many meanings of su
docs.text:
su can mean his, her, its, your (usted), their or your (ustedes). Usually the context makes it clear. When it does not, Spanish replaces it with the article + noun + de + the owner:

Ambiguous Clear English su coche el coche de él his car su coche el coche de ella her car su coche el coche de usted your car (usted) su coche el coche de ellos their car

Table 7.6. Making su clear. In Latin America the word for car is usually el carro or el auto.

docs.title: There is no 's in Spanish
docs.text:
English says "Ana's mother". Spanish has no apostrophe s: it says "the mother of Ana".

  • la madre de Ana — Ana's mother
  • el marido de mi hermana — my sister's husband
  • los hijos de mis tíos — my aunt and uncle's children (my cousins)
  • la casa del profesor — the teacher's house (de + el = del, Lesson 4)

Worked example: whose is it?

Say "Our grandmother is Pedro's mother's mother."

  1. "Our grandmother": abuela is feminine singular, so nuestra abuela.
  2. "Pedro's mother" becomes "the mother of Pedro": la madre de Pedro.
  3. "the mother of Pedro's mother": la madre de la madre de Pedro.

Result: Nuestra abuela es la madre de la madre de Pedro. A natural speaker would of course simply say Es la abuela de Pedro.

docs.title: Agreement: one adjective, up to four forms
docs.text:
An adjective takes the gender and the number of the noun it describes. How many forms it has depends on its ending.

Type Masc. singular Fem. singular Masc. plural Fem. plural ends in -o alto alta altos altas ends in -e alegre alegre alegres alegres most consonants azul azul azules azules -dor, nationality trabajador trabajadora trabajadores trabajadoras

Table 7.7. The forms of adjectives. Practice hides the endings.

The plural follows the rules for nouns that you met in Lesson 4: add -s after a vowel, -es after a consonant. Watch the spelling changes:

  • z becomes c before -es: feliz → felices ("happy").
  • A written accent appears or disappears to keep the stress where it was: joven → jóvenes, but inglés → ingleses (Lesson 1 explains why).

A mixed group takes the masculine plural: Mi hermano y mi hermana son altos. — My brother and sister are tall.

docs.title: Position: usually after the noun
docs.text:
Most descriptive adjectives come after the noun, the opposite of English:

  • un chico alto — a tall boy
  • una mujer simpática — a nice woman
  • unos ojos verdes — green eyes
  • las casas blancas — the white houses

Words of quantity and number come before the noun, as in English: dos hermanos, muchos primos, pocos amigos.

docs.title: Bueno, malo, grande: the short forms
docs.text:
Three very common adjectives often go before the noun, and then they lose letters:

Adjective Before a masc. singular noun Before a fem. singular noun Example bueno buen buena un buen amigo, una buena amiga malo mal mala un mal día, una mala idea grande gran gran un gran hombre, una gran ciudad

Table 7.8. Short forms before the noun. In the plural there are no short forms: buenos amigos, grandes ciudades.

bueno and malo mean the same before or after the noun (un buen libro and un libro bueno are both "a good book"; before the noun is more common). With grande the meaning changes:

  • un hombre grande — a big man (size)
  • un gran hombre — a great man (importance)

docs.title: Describing people: ser, tener, llevar
docs.text:
Spanish uses three verbs where English mostly uses "be" and "have".

Verb For Examples ser build, looks and character: what someone is Es alta y delgada. Es muy simpático. tener hair, eyes, a beard, age: what someone has Tiene el pelo rizado. Tiene los ojos azules. llevar glasses, clothes, sometimes a beard: what someone wears Lleva gafas. Lleva barba.

Table 7.9. Three verbs for describing.

You know the forms of ser (Lesson 5) and of the regular verb llevar (Lesson 6). tener is irregular and is taught fully in Lesson 10; for now, use these three forms as phrases: tengo (I have), tienes (you have), tiene (he, she has; you have, usted).

Spanish uses the definite article with hair and eyes: tiene el pelo largo, literally "she has the hair long". The adjective agrees with pelo (masculine singular) or ojos (masculine plural), not with the person: a woman tiene el pelo rubio, but she es rubia.

To ask for a description, use ¿Cómo es? ("What is he or she like?"). Remember from Lesson 5 that ¿Cómo está? asks how someone is feeling at the moment.

  • ¿Cómo es tu novio? — Es alto, tiene el pelo corto y es muy divertido. — What's your boyfriend like? — He's tall, has short hair and is great fun.
  • ¿Cómo está tu abuela? — Está un poco cansada. — How is your grandmother? — She's a bit tired.

docs.title: Muy, bastante, un poco, nada
docs.text:
Spanish English Example muy very Es muy alto. bastante quite, rather Es bastante serio. un poco a little, a bit Es un poco tímida. no … nada not at all No es nada aburrido. demasiado too Es demasiado joven.

Table 7.10. Words that make an adjective stronger or weaker. They never change their form before an adjective.

Un poco is for the negative side

As in English, un poco sounds natural with qualities that are not entirely positive: un poco tímido, un poco nervioso. To praise, use muy or bastante. For a strong compliment, Spanish speakers love the ending -ísimo: guapísimo ("really good-looking"), simpatiquísima ("so nice").

Common mistake: gordo and viejo

gordo ("fat") and viejo ("old") are correct words but blunt when said about a person. Say un poco grande or fuerte, and mayor for an older person: mi abuelo es mayor.

docs.title: Make it agree
docs.text:
Read each phrase aloud, then change it to the feminine and to the plural.

Masculine singular Feminine singular Masculine plural un primo simpático una prima simpática unos primos simpáticos mi tío alegre mi tía alegre mis tíos alegres el abuelo trabajador la abuela trabajadora los abuelos trabajadores nuestro hijo joven nuestra hija joven nuestros hijos jóvenes un buen amigo una buena amiga unos buenos amigos un niño feliz una niña feliz unos niños felices

Table 7.11. Agreement drill.

docs.title: Who is it?
docs.text:
Listen to each description and point to the person in Figure 7.1.

  • Es el padre de Lucía y el marido de Elena. — (Luis)
  • Es la hija de Rosa y Javier. — (Marta)
  • Son los padres de Luis y de Rosa. — (Antonio and Carmen)
  • Es el hermano de Lucía y el primo de Marta. — (Diego)
  • Es la tía de Diego. — (Rosa)

Say it

Describe someone in your family in four sentences: who they are, what they look like, one thing they have or wear, and what they are like. For example:

Mi hermana se llama Emma. Es alta y rubia. Tiene los ojos verdes y lleva gafas. Es muy divertida, pero un poco perezosa.

docs.title: 7.6 Culture: the family in Spain and Latin America
docs.text:
Close and extended. In Spanish-speaking countries the family usually plays a larger part in daily life than in much of the English-speaking world. Grandparents often help to bring up the grandchildren, and a long Sunday lunch with parents, grandparents, aunts, uncles and cousins is a weekly custom in many families. It is common for young adults to live with their parents until they are well into their twenties, or until they marry, both because housing is expensive and because it is considered normal.

Godparents. The padrino (godfather) and madrina (godmother) often remain important figures throughout a child's life. In Mexico and other parts of Latin America the parents and godparents of a child call each other compadre and comadre, a relationship close to family.

Affectionate words. Diminutives with -ito, -ita express affection: abuelito, abuelita, hermanito. They are used everywhere but especially often in Latin America. In Mexico you will hear mija and mijo (from mi hija, mi hijo) as terms of endearment, even for people who are not one's children.

Regional words for describing people.

Meaning Spain Latin America glasses las gafas los lentes, los anteojos brown (eyes) marrones marrones; in Mexico and Central America cafés cute, pretty mono, mona lindo, linda fair-haired, light-skinned rubio rubio; in Mexico güero husband, wife marido, mujer esposo, esposa (more common)

Table 7.12. Some regional differences.

Moreno. moreno can mean "dark-haired", "dark-skinned" or simply "tanned" (estás muy moreno, "you've got a good tan"). It is a neutral, everyday word in Spain; in some parts of Latin America other words are preferred for skin colour, and it is best to describe hair and eyes rather than skin.

docs.title: 7.7 Summary
docs.text:
Summary

  • Family: padre, madre, hijo, hija, hermano, hermana, abuelo, abuela, tío, tía, primo, prima. A masculine plural covers a mixed group: los padres = parents, los hermanos = brothers and sisters.
  • Possessives agree with the thing possessed: mi, mis; tu, tus; su, sus; nuestro, nuestra, nuestros, nuestras; vuestro … When su is unclear, say el coche de ella. There is no 's: la madre de Ana.
  • Adjectives agree in gender and number (alto, alta, altos, altas); those in -e and most consonants have no feminine. They normally follow the noun.
  • bueno → buen, malo → mal before a masculine singular noun; grande → gran before any singular noun, meaning "great".
  • Describing: ser for build and character, tener for hair, eyes and age, llevar for glasses. ¿Cómo es? asks for a description.
  • Degree: muy, bastante, un poco, no … nada, demasiado.

docs.title: 7.8 Exercises
docs.text:
Exercise 1

Your mother's sister is your …?

Answer

tía. Es mi tía.

Exercise 2

Give the Spanish for "my parents".

Answer

mis padres. mis padres. Plural noun, so plural possessive.

Exercise 3

Give the Spanish for "our grandmother".

Answer

nuestra abuela. nuestra abuela. abuela is feminine, so nuestra.

Exercise 4

Give the feminine of trabajador.

Answer

trabajadora. trabajadora. Adjectives in -dor add -a.

Exercise 5

Give the plural of joven.

Answer

jóvenes. jóvenes. The written accent keeps the stress on the same syllable.

Exercise 6

Translate "a good friend" (a man).

Answer

un buen amigo. un buen amigo. Before a masculine singular noun, bueno becomes buen.

Exercise 7

Complete with the right verb: Mi hermana ___ los ojos verdes.

Answer

tiene. Mi hermana tiene los ojos verdes. Eyes and hair go with tener.

Exercise 8

Marta está con Pablo. Su coche es rojo. Rewrite the second sentence so that it clearly means "Her car is red."

Answer

El coche de ella es rojo. El coche de ella es rojo.

Exercise 9

Correct the mistakes: Mi hermanas son muy altos y simpático.

Answer

Mis hermanas son muy altas y simpáticas. The possessive and both adjectives must be feminine plural to agree with hermanas.

Exercise 10

Describe this person in Spanish: Carlos, your cousin, is tall and slim, has short curly hair, wears glasses and is quite shy but very kind.

Answer

Mi primo Carlos es alto y delgado. Tiene el pelo corto y rizado y lleva gafas. Es bastante tímido, pero muy amable. In Latin America: lleva lentes or usa lentes.

docs.title: 7.9 Quiz
docs.text:
Quiz: family and describing people

Exercise 11

The son of your uncle is your:

  1. sobrino
  2. primo
  3. nieto
  4. hermano
Answer

primo

Your uncle's son is your cousin, el primo.

Exercise 12

___ abuelos viven en Lima. (our)

  1. Nuestro
  2. Nuestra
  3. Nuestros
  4. Nuestras
Answer

Nuestros

abuelos is masculine plural, so nuestros.

Exercise 13

Es un ___ hombre. (great: grande)

Answer

gran

Before a singular noun grande becomes gran and means great.

Exercise 14

Mi madre ___ el pelo rizado y ___ gafas.

Answer

tiene · lleva

Hair goes with tener, glasses with llevar.

Exercise 15

Say "Ana's brother" in Spanish.

Answer

el hermano de Ana

Exercise 16

Match the opposites.

ABaltoperezososimpáticoaburridotrabajadorbajodivertidoantipático Answer

alto — bajo; simpático — antipático; trabajador — perezoso; divertido — aburrido

Exercise 17

Tap the wrong word.

Mis primas son muy simpáticos.

Answer

Wrong word: simpáticos.

Corrected: Mis primas son muy simpáticas.

primas is feminine plural, so the adjective is simpáticas.

Exercise 18

Put the words in order.

Words: dos / mayores / hermanos / Tengo

Answer

Tengo dos hermanos mayores

Exercise 19

Write what you hear.

Dictation. Have someone read the sentence aloud, then write it down.

Mi padre es alto y tiene los ojos azules.

Answer

Mi padre es alto y tiene los ojos azules.

Exercise 20

Say it aloud.

Mi abuela es muy simpática y un poco tímida.

Answer

Say: Mi abuela es muy simpática y un poco tímida.

docs.title: Lesson 8: Food and Ordering in a Café
docs.text:
La comida y el café

Food is one of the great pleasures of the Spanish-speaking world, and the café or bar is where you will practise your Spanish most. The language you need there is small and very repetitive: a handful of phrases for asking, a few dozen words for things to eat and drink, and the courage to call the waiter. In this lesson you learn to read a simple menu, order food and drink politely, ask what a dish contains, ask for the bill, and say what you like and do not like. You also learn when Spaniards, Mexicans and Argentinians actually eat, which may surprise you.

Learning outcomes

By the end of this lesson you will be able to:

  • name common foods, drinks and meals;
  • order in a café or restaurant with quiero, quisiera, ¿me pone …? and ¿me trae …?;
  • ask what a dish contains, how much it costs, and for the bill;
  • use nouns without an article for "some" (quiero agua) and with de, con and sin;
  • say what you like and dislike with me gusta and no me gusta.

masculinefeminineplural

docs.title: 8.1 Dialogue: in a café in Salamanca
docs.text:
Lucía and Daniel go to a café on the main square after class. The waiter comes to their table.

  • Camarero: Buenas tardes. ¿Qué les pongo? — Good afternoon. What can I get you?
  • Lucía: Para mí, un café con leche, por favor. — For me, a white coffee, please.
  • Daniel: Yo quiero un zumo de naranja. — I'd like an orange juice.
  • Camarero: Muy bien. ¿Algo para comer? — Fine. Anything to eat?
  • Daniel: Sí. ¿Qué lleva el bocadillo vegetal? — Yes. What's in the vegetable sandwich?
  • Camarero: Lleva lechuga, tomate, huevo y mayonesa. — It has lettuce, tomato, egg and mayonnaise.
  • Daniel: Vale, quisiera un bocadillo vegetal, pero sin mayonesa. — OK, I'd like a vegetable sandwich, but without mayonnaise.
  • Lucía: ¿Me pone también una ración de patatas bravas? — Could I also have a portion of patatas bravas?
  • Camarero: Por supuesto. ¿Algo más? — Of course. Anything else?
  • Lucía: Nada más, gracias. — Nothing else, thanks.
  • Daniel: Mmm, me gustan mucho las patatas bravas. ¡Pican un poco! — Mmm, I really like patatas bravas. They're a bit spicy!
  • Lucía: ¡Perdone! ¿Nos trae la cuenta, por favor? — Excuse me! Could you bring us the bill, please?
  • Camarero: Sí, ahora mismo. Son doce euros con cuarenta. — Yes, right away. That's twelve euros forty.
  • Daniel: Hoy invito yo. — It's on me today.
  • Lucía: ¡Gracias, Daniel! La próxima vez, invito yo. — Thanks, Daniel! Next time it's on me.

Notice:

  1. Nobody says "can I have". Spanish orders are direct: para mí, un café, quiero un zumo, ¿me pone …? Politeness comes from por favor, gracias and a friendly tone.
  2. ¿Qué lleva?, literally "What does it carry?", is how you ask what is in a dish.
  3. un zumo de naranja, un café con leche, sin mayonesa: three small prepositions do most of the work on a menu.
  4. me gustan las patatas: with a plural thing, gusta becomes gustan.

docs.title: Drinks
docs.text:
Spanish Sounds like English el café solo [kah-FEH SOH-loh] black coffee (an espresso) el café con leche [kah-FEH kohn LEH-cheh] white coffee (half milk) el cortado [kor-TAH-doh] espresso with a dash of milk el té [TEH] tea el agua (con gas / sin gas) [AH-gwah] water (sparkling / still) el zumo de naranja [THOO-moh deh nah-RAHN-hah] orange juice (Spain) el jugo de naranja [HOO-goh] orange juice (Latin America) la leche [LEH-cheh] milk el refresco [rreh-FREHS-koh] soft drink la cerveza [sehr-BEH-sah] beer el vino tinto / blanco [BEE-noh TEEN-toh] red / white wine el chocolate caliente [choh-koh-LAH-teh kah-LYEHN-teh] hot chocolate

Table 8.1. Drinks. In Spain, the z of zumo and cerveza has the th sound (Lesson 1).

El agua is feminine

agua is a feminine noun, but because it begins with a stressed a, it takes el in the singular, to avoid the clash la agua. Adjectives stay feminine: el agua fría ("cold water"), and the plural is las aguas. The same happens with el hambre ("hunger") and el aula ("classroom").

docs.title: Food
docs.text:
Spanish English Spanish English el pan bread la tostada toast el bocadillo filled roll (Spain) el sándwich sandwich (sliced bread) el queso cheese el jamón ham el huevo egg la tortilla omelette (Spain); flatbread (Mexico) la ensalada salad la sopa soup el pollo chicken la carne meat el pescado fish (to eat) el arroz rice las patatas potatoes (Spain) las papas potatoes (Latin America, Canaries) las patatas fritas chips, crisps las verduras vegetables la lechuga lettuce el tomate tomato la fruta fruit la manzana apple el plátano banana la naranja orange el postre dessert el helado ice cream la tarta cake, tart el azúcar sugar la sal salt el aceite de oliva olive oil

Table 8.2. Food. pescado is fish on the plate; a live fish in the water is un pez.

docs.title: Meals and verbs
docs.text:
Meal Verb When (roughly, in Spain) el desayuno — breakfast desayunar 7 to 9 a.m., light: coffee and toast el almuerzo — mid-morning snack (Spain); lunch (Latin America) almorzar about 11 a.m. in Spain la comida — lunch, the main meal comer 2 to 3.30 p.m. la merienda — afternoon snack merendar 5 to 7 p.m. la cena — dinner, supper cenar 9 to 11 p.m.

Table 8.3. The meals. comida also means "food" in general, and comer means both "to eat" and "to have lunch".

Use tomar ("to take") for "have" with food and drink: ¿Qué vas a tomar? — What are you having?; Tomo un té. — I'll have a tea.

docs.title: In the café or restaurant
docs.text:
Spanish English el camarero, la camarera waiter, waitress (Spain) el mesero, la mesera waiter, waitress (Mexico, Central America) la carta, el menú the menu el menú del día the set lunch menu de primero, de segundo, de postre for the first course, for the main course, for dessert la tapa, la ración, media ración a small bite, a portion to share, a half portion la cuenta the bill, the check la propina the tip rico, delicioso tasty, delicious picante spicy, hot soy vegetariano, soy vegetariana I'm a vegetarian (man, woman) soy alérgico a …, soy alérgica a … I'm allergic to …

Table 8.4. Café and restaurant words.

docs.title: What the waiter says
docs.text:
You will hear one of these when the waiter arrives. All of them mean "What would you like?"

  • ¿Qué le pongo? / ¿Qué les pongo? — What can I get you? (to one person / to several; Spain)
  • ¿Qué desea? — What would you like? (formal)
  • ¿Qué van a tomar? — What are you going to have?
  • ¿Ya saben qué van a pedir? — Do you know what you'd like to order?
  • ¿Y para beber? — And to drink?
  • ¿Algo más? — Anything else?

docs.title: How to order
docs.text:
From the most direct to the most polite. All are correct and normal; choose by how formal the place is.

Phrase Literally Use Un café, por favor. A coffee, please. always fine Para mí, un té. For me, a tea. when several people order Quiero una cerveza. I want a beer. normal in Spanish, not rude ¿Me pone un café? Will you put me a coffee? Spain, at the bar ¿Me da un agua? Will you give me a water? everywhere, especially Latin America ¿Me trae la carta? Will you bring me the menu? asking for something to be brought Quisiera la sopa. I would like the soup. polite, a little formal Me gustaría probar el pescado. I would like to try the fish. polite

Table 8.5. Ordering. quisiera and me gustaría are fixed polite forms; learn them as phrases.

Common mistake: can I have

Do not translate "Can I have a coffee?" as ¿Puedo tener un café? It sounds as if you are asking permission to own a coffee. Say ¿Me pone un café?, ¿Me da un café? or simply Un café, por favor.

docs.title: Asking questions about food and paying
docs.text:
• ¿Qué lleva la ensalada? — What's in the salad?
  • ¿Tiene carne? — Does it have meat in it?
  • ¿Qué me recomienda? — What do you recommend?
  • ¿Cuál es el menú del día? — What is today's set menu?
  • ¿Cuánto es? / ¿Cuánto cuesta? — How much is it?
  • La cuenta, por favor. — The bill, please.
  • ¿Me cobra, por favor? — Can I pay, please? (Spain, literally "will you charge me?")
  • ¿Puedo pagar con tarjeta? — Can I pay by card?

Prices are written with a comma for the decimal point: 2,50 €. Say dos euros con cincuenta or simply dos cincuenta. The numbers are in Lesson 3.

Figure 8.1 A café menu. The menu of Café La Plaza, in four parts: breakfasts (toast with tomato and oil, croissant, churros with chocolate), filled rolls (cured ham, cheese, potato omelette), portions to share (patatas bravas, garlic prawns, mixed salad) and drinks (black coffee, white coffee, fresh orange juice, mineral water, soft drink), with prices in euros.

Worked example: ordering from the menu

You want breakfast at Café La Plaza (Figure 8.1): toast with tomato and a white coffee. Your friend wants churros with chocolate and nothing to drink.

  1. Get attention: ¡Perdone!
  2. Order for yourself: Para mí, una tostada con tomate y un café con leche.
  3. Order for your friend: Y para ella, churros con chocolate.
  4. Pay: ¿Cuánto es? The waiter adds 2,50 + 1,70 + 3,90 = 8,10 and answers: Son ocho euros con diez.

docs.title: 8.4 Grammar: some, of, with and without; me gusta
No article for "some"
docs.text:
English often uses "some" or nothing at all for an unspecified amount: "I want water", "Have you got any bread?" Spanish uses no article in these cases.

  • Quiero agua. — I want (some) water.
  • ¿Tienen pan sin gluten? — Do you have (any) gluten-free bread?
  • No como carne. — I don't eat meat.
  • No hay leche. — There's no milk.

With a countable item, un or una means one portion, glass or cup: un café, una cerveza, un agua ("a bottle of water"). unos and unas mean "some, a few": unas aceitunas ("some olives").

But when you talk about a food in general, especially to say you like it, Spanish uses the definite article, where English uses none:

English Spanish I want coffee. (some coffee, now) Quiero café. I like coffee. (coffee in general) Me gusta el café. Fish is healthy. El pescado es sano. Children love ice cream. A los niños les encanta el helado.

Table 8.6. Some (no article) and in general (the article).

docs.title: De, con, sin
docs.text:
Preposition Use Examples de what it is made of, its flavour un bocadillo de queso, un helado de fresa, zumo de manzana con with, added café con leche, té con limón, agua con gas sin without sin azúcar, sin hielo, sin cebolla a la / al cooked in the style of pollo al ajillo (with garlic), pescado a la plancha (grilled)

Table 8.7. Small words of the menu. Unlike English, the main word comes first: a cheese sandwich is a sandwich of cheese.

docs.title: Me gusta and me gustan
docs.text:
Lesson 12 explains gustar fully. For now, learn four phrases:

with one thing (or a verb) with several things I like me gusta el té me gustan las fresas I don't like no me gusta el té no me gustan las fresas do you like? (tú) ¿te gusta el té? ¿te gustan las fresas? do you like? (usted) ¿le gusta el té? ¿le gustan las fresas?

Table 8.8. gusta with a singular thing, gustan with a plural one.

me gusta literally means "it pleases me", so the verb agrees with the thing liked, not with you. Add mucho for "a lot" and nada for "at all": Me gusta mucho el chocolate. No me gusta nada el café. Me encanta means "I love" (food, places, activities): ¡Me encanta la paella!

Common mistake: me gusto

Me gusto el café is wrong: it would mean "I like myself". The verb agrees with the coffee: me gusta el café. And remember the article: not me gusta café but me gusta el café.

docs.title: Build the order
docs.text:
Read each order aloud. Then make your own orders by changing the food and drink.

  • Para mí, un café solo y una tostada con tomate. — For me, a black coffee and toast with tomato.
  • ¿Me pone una cerveza y una ración de calamares? — Could I have a beer and a portion of squid?
  • Quisiera un agua sin gas, por favor. — I'd like a still water, please.
  • ¿Me trae otro café con leche, por favor? — Could you bring me another white coffee, please?
  • De primero, sopa; de segundo, pollo asado, y de postre, fruta. — Soup to start, then roast chicken, and fruit for dessert.

docs.title: Like or don't like?
docs.text:
Food I like it I don't like it el pescado me gusta el pescado no me gusta el pescado las aceitunas me gustan las aceitunas no me gustan las aceitunas el queso me gusta el queso no me gusta el queso los tomates me gustan los tomates no me gustan los tomates la comida picante me gusta la comida picante no me gusta la comida picante

Table 8.9. Practise gusta and gustan.

Say it

You are at the bar of a café in Madrid. Greet the waiter, order a drink and something to eat, ask what one dish contains, and ask for the bill. For example:

Buenos días. ¿Me pone un cortado y un cruasán? ¿Qué lleva el bocadillo de la casa? Gracias. ¿Me cobra, por favor?

docs.title: 8.6 Culture: eating in Spain and Latin America
docs.text:
Late meals in Spain. The Spanish day runs late. Lunch, the main meal, is eaten between two and half past three, and dinner rarely before nine; in summer, ten or later is normal. Restaurants may not serve dinner before eight or half past eight. In Latin America meals are generally earlier and closer to North American and British habits, although lunch is still often the main meal of the day in Mexico, where it is called la comida and is eaten from about two o'clock.

Tapas. A tapa is a small portion of food served with a drink in a bar. In some cities, such as Granada, a tapa traditionally comes free with each drink. Going from bar to bar for a drink and a tapa in each is called ir de tapas or tapear. A ración is a larger plate meant for sharing.

The menú del día. On weekdays most Spanish restaurants offer a fixed-price lunch, the menú del día: a first course, a main course, dessert or coffee, bread and a drink. It is usually the best value of the day. Similar set lunches exist in Latin America: la comida corrida in Mexico, el menú ejecutivo in Argentina and elsewhere.

Tipping. In Spain tipping is modest: people leave small change or round up the bill, and a little more in a restaurant if the service was good. In Mexico and much of Latin America a tip of around ten per cent is customary in restaurants, and some places add a service charge to the bill (look for servicio incluido).

Calling the waiter, and paying. It is normal to call the waiter with ¡Perdone! or ¡Disculpe!; in a busy Spanish bar you will even hear ¡Oiga! ("Listen!"). The bill is not brought until you ask for it, because rushing customers is considered rude. Friends often take turns to pay for the whole group (invito yo, "it's on me") rather than splitting the bill exactly.

Sobremesa. La sobremesa is the time spent at the table after a meal, talking over coffee. A family Sunday lunch with its sobremesa can easily last three or four hours, and there is no single English word for it.

Same food, different words.

English Spain Latin America juice el zumo el jugo potato la patata la papa prawn, shrimp la gamba el camarón peach el melocotón el durazno beans las judías los frijoles (Mexico), los porotos (Argentina, Chile) avocado el aguacate el aguacate; la palta (Argentina, Chile, Peru) cake la tarta el pastel, la torta waiter el camarero el mesero (Mexico), el mozo (Argentina)

Table 8.10. Regional food words. Everyone understands the Spanish words, but use the local ones where you are.

A tortilla is the best example of a word that changes completely: in Spain, una tortilla de patatas is a thick omelette of eggs, potatoes and often onion; in Mexico, una tortilla is the thin maize or wheat flatbread used for tacos.

docs.title: 8.7 Summary
docs.text:
Summary

  • Meals: el desayuno, la comida (lunch), la merienda, la cena. Use tomar for "have" with food and drink.
  • Ordering: Un café, por favor. Para mí … Quiero … ¿Me pone …? (Spain) ¿Me da …? ¿Me trae …? Quisiera … Never ¿puedo tener?
  • Asking: ¿Qué lleva? ¿Qué me recomienda? ¿Cuánto es? La cuenta, por favor.
  • Some: no article (quiero agua); in general: definite article (me gusta el agua).
  • Menu words: de (made of), con (with), sin (without): un bocadillo de jamón, café con leche, sin azúcar.
  • Likes: me gusta + one thing, me gustan + several; no me gusta; me encanta = I love.

docs.title: 8.8 Exercises
docs.text:
Exercise 1

Give the Spanish for "the bill".

Answer

la cuenta. la cuenta

Exercise 2

Which meal is la cena?

Answer

dinner. The evening meal, usually eaten late in Spain.

Exercise 3

Ask what is in the paella.

Answer

¿Qué lleva la paella? ¿Qué lleva la paella?

Exercise 4

Order "a coffee without sugar" in three words.

Answer

un café sin azúcar. Un café sin azúcar, por favor.

Exercise 5

Complete: No me ___ las aceitunas.

Answer

gustan. No me gustan las aceitunas. aceitunas is plural.

Exercise 6

Translate "a ham sandwich" (Spanish style, a filled roll).

Answer

un bocadillo de jamón. un bocadillo de jamón. The main word comes first, then de and the filling.

Exercise 7

You are in Mexico City and want orange juice. What do you ask for?

Answer

un jugo de naranja. Un jugo de naranja, por favor. In Spain it would be un zumo de naranja.

Exercise 8

Correct the mistake: Me gusta café, pero no me gusta las patatas.

Answer

Me gusta el café, pero no me gustan las patatas. Things you like in general need the article, and a plural thing needs gustan.

Exercise 9

Your bill at Café La Plaza (Figure 8.1) is a bocadillo de queso and a zumo de naranja natural. How much is it? Write the total as you would say it.

Answer

siete euros con ochenta. 3,80 + 3,00 = 7,80 €: siete euros con ochenta, or siete ochenta.

Exercise 10

Write a short exchange: the waiter asks what you want; you order a still water and a mixed salad; he asks if you want anything else; you say no and ask for the bill.

Answer

— ¿Qué le pongo? — Un agua sin gas y una ensalada mixta, por favor. — ¿Algo más? — No, nada más, gracias. ¿Me trae la cuenta, por favor?

docs.title: 8.9 Quiz
docs.text:
Quiz: food and the café

Exercise 11

The most natural way to order a coffee in a Spanish bar:

  1. ¿Puedo tener un café?
  2. ¿Me pone un café?
  3. ¿Me gusta un café?
  4. ¿Tengo un café?
Answer

¿Me pone un café?

In Spain, ¿me pone …? is the usual way to order at the bar.

Exercise 12

In Spain, the main meal of the day, eaten at about 2 p.m., is:

  1. el desayuno
  2. la comida
  3. la merienda
  4. la cena
Answer

la comida

Exercise 13

Me ___ mucho las fresas.

Answer

gustan

fresas is plural, so gustan.

Exercise 14

Un café ___ leche y un té ___ azúcar. (with, without)

Answer

con · sin

Exercise 15

How do you ask "How much is it?" (three words, starting with ¿)

Answer

¿Cuánto es? / ¿Cuánto cuesta?

Exercise 16

Match the Spain word to the Latin American word.

ABzumocamarónpatataduraznogambajugomelocotónpapa Answer

zumo — jugo; patata — papa; gamba — camarón; melocotón — durazno

Exercise 17

Tap the wrong word.

La agua está muy fría.

Answer

Wrong word: La.

Corrected: El agua está muy fría.

agua starts with a stressed a, so it takes el in the singular.

Exercise 18

Put the words in order.

Words: ¿Nos / cuenta, / trae / la / favor? / por

Answer

¿Nos trae la cuenta, por favor?

Exercise 19

Write what you hear.

Dictation. Have someone read the sentence aloud, then write it down.

Para mí, un bocadillo de queso y un agua sin gas.

Answer

Para mí, un bocadillo de queso y un agua sin gas.

Exercise 20

Say it aloud.

Quisiera una tostada con tomate y un café con leche.

Answer

Say: Quisiera una tostada con tomate y un café con leche.

docs.title: Further Reading
docs.text:
Para seguir aprendiendo

These are standard, widely used works and official sources for the next stage of your Spanish. Most of the reference works of the Spanish academies and the Instituto Cervantes can be consulted free of charge online.

docs.title: Dictionaries and official reference works
docs.text:
• Real Academia Española and Asociación de Academias de la Lengua Española, Diccionario de la lengua española. The standard monolingual dictionary of Spanish, published in print and freely searchable online. Use it once you can read simple definitions in Spanish.
  • Real Academia Española and Asociación de Academias de la Lengua Española, Diccionario panhispánico de dudas (2005). Short, clear answers to the questions that native speakers and learners ask most: spelling, accents, plurals, agreement and usage in different countries.
  • Real Academia Española and Asociación de Academias de la Lengua Española, Ortografía de la lengua española (2010). The official rules of spelling and punctuation, including the alphabet and the written accent taught in Lesson 1.
  • Real Academia Española and Asociación de Academias de la Lengua Española, Nueva gramática de la lengua española (2009), with its shorter Manual (2010) and Nueva gramática básica de la lengua española (2011). The reference grammar of the whole Spanish-speaking world, describing the usage of every country.
  • A good bilingual dictionary, such as the Collins Spanish Dictionary or the Oxford Spanish Dictionary, both of which mark the words used in Spain and in particular Latin American countries.

docs.title: Grammars and practice books in English
docs.text:
• John Butt and Carmen Benjamin, A New Reference Grammar of Modern Spanish (Routledge, several editions). A detailed and readable grammar of Spanish for English speakers, with attention to the differences between Spain and Latin America. The book to consult when this course leaves a question unanswered.
  • Christopher Kendris and Theodore Kendris, 501 Spanish Verbs (Barron's, many editions). Full conjugation tables of the common verbs in every tense, a natural next step after the Verb Tables of this book.

docs.title: The levels, the exams and the Instituto Cervantes
docs.text:
• Council of Europe, Common European Framework of Reference for Languages: Learning, Teaching, Assessment (2001), and its Companion Volume (2020). The six levels, A1 to C2, used in this book and in most language courses and exams. The descriptors of what a learner "can do" at each level are freely available.
  • Instituto Cervantes, Plan curricular del Instituto Cervantes: Niveles de referencia para el español (2006). The detailed inventory of the grammar, vocabulary, functions and cultural knowledge expected at each level of Spanish, built on the Framework.
  • Instituto Cervantes, the DELE exams (Diplomas de Español como Lengua Extranjera). The official diplomas of Spanish as a foreign language, from A1 to C2. The Instituto Cervantes publishes the exam guides and sample papers.
  • The Centro Virtual Cervantes (cvc.cervantes.es), the online centre of the Instituto Cervantes, with materials for learners and teachers, reading texts and resources on the cultures of the Spanish-speaking world.

docs.title: Glossary
docs.text:
Glosario

The first part of this glossary explains the grammar terms used in the book, with a Spanish example of each and the lesson where it is taught. The second part lists words and phrases that often confuse English speakers.

docs.title: Grammar terms
docs.text: Accent (written) The mark ´ over a vowel (á, é, í, ó, ú). It shows a stressed syllable that does not follow the stress rules (café, música), or tells apart two words spelt alike (tú, you; tu, your). Spanish calls it la tilde. Lesson 1. Adjective A word that describes a noun: alto, rojo, simpático. In Spanish it usually comes after the noun and agrees with it. Lesson 7. Adverb A word that describes a verb, an adjective or another adverb: bien, muy, siempre, aquí. Adverbs do not change their form. Lessons 7 and 11. Agreement The matching of an article, adjective or possessive to the gender and number of its noun: la casa blanca, los coches blancos. Lessons 4 and 7. Article The words for the (definite: el, la, los, las) and a, some (indefinite: un, una, unos, unas). Lesson 4. Comparative The form used to compare: más caro que (more expensive than), menos alto que, tan grande como; irregular mejor, peor. Lesson 13. Conjugation The set of forms of a verb for the different persons and tenses (hablo, hablas, habla …); also each of the three verb groups, in -ar, -er and -ir. Lesson 6. Contraction Two words joined into one: a + el = al, de + el = del. Lesson 4. Demonstrative A word that points: este (this), ese (that), aquel (that, over there), with their feminine and plural forms, and the neuter esto, eso, aquello. Lesson 13. Digraph Two letters that spell one sound: ch, ll, rr, qu, gu. Lesson 1. Diminutive A form with a suffix such as -ito, -ita that adds the idea of smallness or affection: abuelita, un momentito. Lesson 7. Diphthong Two vowels said in one syllable, one of them i or u: bien, bueno, hoy. Lesson 1. Direct object The person or thing that receives the action of the verb directly: in compro la chaqueta, la chaqueta. Its pronouns are lo, la, los, las: la compro. Lesson 13. Ending The last part of a verb, which shows the person and the tense: habl-o, habl-amos, habl-é. Lesson 6. Feminine, masculine The two genders of Spanish nouns. Every noun is one or the other, and the articles and adjectives that go with it follow: el libro (masculine), la mesa (feminine). Lesson 4. Gender The grammatical class, masculine or feminine, to which every Spanish noun belongs. It is not always related to sex: la mano (hand) is feminine, el día (day) masculine. Lesson 4. Imperative The form of a verb used for instructions and commands: gira a la derecha (tú), siga todo recto (usted). In this book it is learnt as fixed phrases. Lesson 9. Imperfect A past tense for descriptions, background and habits in the past (vivía, hacía sol). It is beyond this course; Lesson 15 shows how to recognise it. Indirect object The person to whom or for whom something is done. Its pronouns are me, te, le, nos, os, les, and they are used with gustar: le gusta (it pleases him or her). Lesson 12. Infinitive The basic form of a verb, the one found in a dictionary, ending in -ar, -er or -ir: hablar, comer, vivir. Lesson 6. Intonation The rise and fall of the voice. A yes/no question differs from a statement only by its rising intonation: ¿Hablas español? Lessons 1 and 6. Irregular verb A verb whose forms do not follow the regular pattern: ser (soy), ir (voy), tener (tengo). Lessons 5, 10 and 15. Near future The construction ir + a + infinitive, for plans and predictions: voy a viajar, va a llover. Lesson 14. Noun A word for a person, place, thing or idea: la mujer, la ciudad, el libro, la libertad. Lesson 4. Number Singular (one) or plural (more than one). Nouns, articles, adjectives and verbs all show number. Lesson 4. Ordinal number A number that gives order: primero, segundo, tercero; before a masculine noun primer and tercer. Lesson 9. Personal a The word a placed before a direct object that is a person: Visito a mis abuelos. It has no English translation. Lessons 6 and 16. Plural The form for more than one: libros, ciudades, lápices. Lesson 4. Possessive A word that shows who owns something: mi, tu, su, nuestro, vuestro, su. Possessives agree with the thing owned, not with the owner. Lesson 7. Preposition A short word that links a noun to the rest of the sentence: a, de, en, con, para, por, cerca de, al lado de. Lesson 9. Present perfect The tense formed with haber and a participle: he comido (I have eaten). Spain uses it for events of today; Latin America mostly uses the preterite. Lesson 15, for recognition. Present tense The tense for what is true now, habits, and often the near future: trabajo en Madrid, mañana salgo a las ocho. Lesson 6. Preterite The past tense of completed actions: ayer comí paella, fuimos a Perú. Lesson 15. Pronoun A word that stands for a noun: subject pronouns (yo, tú, él), reflexive (me, te, se), object pronouns (lo, la, le) and pronouns after prepositions (mí, ti). Lessons 2, 11, 12 and 13. Reflexive verb A verb used with a pronoun that refers back to the subject: me levanto (I get up, literally "I raise myself"), te duchas. Its infinitive ends in -se: levantarse. Lesson 11. Seseo Pronouncing c (before e, i) and z as [s], as in all of Latin America, the Canary Islands and parts of southern Spain. Lesson 1. Stem The part of a verb left when the ending is removed: habl- in hablar. Lesson 6. Stem-changing verb A verb whose stem vowel changes when it is stressed: e → ie (quiero), o → ue (puedo), e → i (pido). Lesson 10. Stress The extra force on one syllable of a word. Spanish stress follows simple rules, and a written accent marks every exception. Lesson 1. Subject The person or thing that does the action of the verb. In Spanish it is often not stated, because the verb ending shows it: hablo = I speak. Lesson 2. Superlative The form for "the most" or "the least": el más caro, la menos cara; and the ending -ísimo for "very, extremely": carísimo. Lessons 7 and 13. Tú, usted The two words for "you" to one person: informal tú and formal usted, which takes the third-person form of the verb. Lesson 2. Voseo The use of vos instead of tú, with its own verb forms (vos sos, vos tenés), in Argentina, Uruguay, Paraguay and much of Central America. Lesson 2. Vosotros, ustedes The two plural words for "you": vosotros (informal, Spain only) and ustedes (formal in Spain; the only plural "you" in Latin America). Lesson 2. Yeísmo Pronouncing ll and y the same way, as most Spanish speakers do today: calle rhymes with valle and sounds like it is spelt with y. Lesson 1.

docs.title: Words that cause trouble
docs.text: Coger To take, to catch (coger el autobús) in Spain. In parts of Latin America it is a vulgar word, and tomar is used instead. Lessons 10 and 14. Embarazada Pregnant, not "embarrassed" (avergonzado, or in much of Latin America apenado). Lesson 16. Éxito Success, not "exit" (la salida). Lesson 16. Hace With a length of time, "ago": hace dos años, two years ago. With weather, "it is": hace calor. Lessons 10 and 15. Librería Bookshop, not "library" (la biblioteca). Lesson 16. Muy, mucho muy (very) goes with adjectives and adverbs: muy bueno. mucho (a lot, much, many) goes with verbs and nouns, and agrees with nouns: me gusta mucho, muchas gracias. Lesson 16. Pero, perro pero (but) has a single tapped r; perro (dog) a rolled rr. Lesson 1. Por qué, porque ¿por qué?, two words with an accent, asks "why?"; porque, one word without an accent, answers "because". Lesson 6. Saber, conocer Both mean "to know": saber for facts and skills (sé nadar, I can swim), conocer for people and places (conozco Madrid). Lesson 10 introduces saber; both are in the Verb Tables. Ser, estar Both mean "to be": ser for what something is (identity, origin, job, character, time), estar for where it is and how it is (location, feelings, temporary states). Lesson 5. Tener "To have", but also used where English says "to be": tengo veinte años (I am twenty), tengo hambre (I am hungry), tengo frío (I am cold). Lessons 3 and 10.

docs.title: Lesson 2: Greetings and Introductions
docs.text:
Saludos y presentaciones

The first Spanish most people ever use is a greeting, and it is worth getting right: a well-placed buenos días or mucho gusto opens doors in every one of the twenty-odd countries where Spanish is spoken.
