In this lesson you learn to say hello and goodbye at any time of day, to ask how someone is, to give your name and where you are from, and to choose between the two words for "you" that Spanish keeps apart: the friendly tú and the polite usted.

Learning outcomes

By the end of this lesson you will be able to:

  • greet people and say goodbye at any time of day, formally and informally;
  • ask how someone is and answer;
  • say your name, ask someone's name and react when you meet them;
  • say where you are from and give your nationality, in the masculine and feminine;
  • use the subject pronouns, and choose between tú, usted, vosotros and ustedes.

masculinefeminine

docs.title: 2.1 Dialogue: on the first day of class
docs.text:
It is the first morning of a Spanish course in Salamanca. Daniel, a student from Manchester, sits down next to Lucía, who is from Mexico. Then the teacher, Señora Ruiz, arrives. Listen to each line, then read it aloud yourself.

  • Daniel: ¡Hola! Buenos días. — Hi! Good morning.
  • Lucía: ¡Hola! ¿Qué tal? — Hi! How's it going?
  • Daniel: Bien, gracias. ¿Y tú? — Fine, thanks. And you?
  • Lucía: Muy bien. Me llamo Lucía. ¿Cómo te llamas? — Very well. My name is Lucía. What's your name?
  • Daniel: Me llamo Daniel. Encantado. — My name is Daniel. Pleased to meet you.
  • Lucía: Encantada. ¿De dónde eres, Daniel? — Pleased to meet you. Where are you from, Daniel?
  • Daniel: Soy inglés, de Mánchester. ¿Y tú? — I'm English, from Manchester. And you?
  • Lucía: Yo soy mexicana, de Guadalajara. — I'm Mexican, from Guadalajara.
  • Señora Ruiz: Buenos días a todos. Soy la profesora Ruiz. — Good morning, everyone. I'm Señora Ruiz, the teacher.
  • Daniel: Buenos días. ¿Cómo está usted? — Good morning. How are you?
  • Señora Ruiz: Muy bien, gracias. ¿Y usted? ¿Cómo se llama? — Very well, thank you. And you? What is your name?
  • Daniel: Me llamo Daniel Brown. Mucho gusto. — My name is Daniel Brown. Nice to meet you.
  • Señora Ruiz: Mucho gusto, Daniel. Bienvenido a Salamanca. — Nice to meet you, Daniel. Welcome to Salamanca.

Notice three things before we explain them:

  1. Daniel says ¿Y tú? to Lucía, a fellow student, but ¿Y usted? to the teacher. Spanish has a friendly "you" and a polite "you".
  2. Daniel says encantado, Lucía says encantada. The word changes with the speaker: -o for a man, -a for a woman. The same happens with mexicano and mexicana.
  3. Questions begin with an upside-down question mark ¿ and exclamations with ¡. They are part of the spelling, not decoration: they tell you, before you start reading aloud, that the sentence will rise or be exclaimed.

docs.title: 2.2 Vocabulary: hello, goodbye and how are you
Saying hello
docs.text:
Spanish Sounds like English When hola [OH-lah] hello, hi any time; friendly but never rude buenos días [BWEH-nohs DEE-ahs] good morning until lunch (in Spain, lunch is about 2 p.m.) buenas tardes [BWEH-nahs TAR-dehs] good afternoon, good evening from lunch until it gets dark buenas noches [BWEH-nahs NOH-chehs] good evening, good night after dark; also when you go to bed buenas [BWEH-nahs] hi (short for all three) very common in shops and bars bienvenido / bienvenida [byehn-beh-NEE-doh / -dah] welcome to a man / to a woman

Table 2.1. Greetings. The h of hola is silent.

docs.title: Asking how someone is
docs.text:
Spanish Sounds like English ¿Qué tal? [keh TAHL] How's it going? How are things? ¿Cómo estás? [KOH-moh ehs-TAHS] How are you? (to a friend: tú) ¿Cómo está usted? [KOH-moh ehs-TAH oos-TEHD] How are you? (polite: usted) ¿Y tú? / ¿Y usted? [ee TOO / ee oos-TEHD] And you? muy bien [mwee BYEHN] very well bien, gracias [byehn GRAH-syahs] fine, thanks regular [rreh-goo-LAR] so-so más o menos [MAHS oh MEH-nohs] more or less, so-so mal [MAHL] bad, not well cansado / cansada [kahn-SAH-doh / -dah] tired (man / woman)

Table 2.2. How are you? The th sound of Spain is explained in Lesson 1: in Spain gracias sounds like [GRAH-thyahs].

docs.title: Saying goodbye
docs.text:
Spanish Sounds like English adiós [ah-DYOHS] goodbye hasta luego [AHS-tah LWEH-goh] see you later (the everyday goodbye) hasta mañana [AHS-tah mah-NYAH-nah] see you tomorrow hasta pronto [AHS-tah PROHN-toh] see you soon nos vemos [nohs BEH-mohs] see you chao [CHAH-oh] bye (informal; written chau in Argentina and Uruguay) que tengas un buen día [keh TEHN-gahs oon bwehn DEE-ah] have a good day

Table 2.3. Goodbyes.

docs.title: Meeting people
docs.text:
Spanish English ¿Cómo te llamas? What's your name? (tú) ¿Cómo se llama usted? What's your name? (usted) Me llamo Ana. My name is Ana. (literally: I call myself Ana) Soy Ana. I'm Ana. Mucho gusto. Nice to meet you. (the same for everyone) Encantado. / Encantada. Delighted. (said by a man / by a woman) Igualmente. Likewise. ¿De dónde eres? Where are you from? (tú) ¿De dónde es usted? Where are you from? (usted) Soy de Londres. I'm from London. Te presento a mi amigo Pablo. Let me introduce my friend Pablo. Por favor. / Gracias. / De nada. Please. / Thank you. / You're welcome. Perdón. / Lo siento. Excuse me, sorry. / I'm sorry.

Table 2.4. Phrases for meeting people.

Hola is never rude

In English "hi" can sound too casual for a bank manager. In Spanish hola is fine with anyone. To be polite, add the time-of-day greeting: Hola, buenos días. That combination is what you will hear most at a shop counter.

docs.title: 2.3 Grammar: the subject pronouns, and four ways to say "you"
docs.text:
The subject pronouns are the words for I, you, he, she, we, they. Here they are, with the "you" forms highlighted.

Person Spanish English 1st singular yo I 2nd singular, informal tú you (one friend, a child, a relative) 2nd singular, formal usted you (one person, politely) 3rd singular él / ella he / she 1st plural nosotros / nosotras we (any group / an all-female group) 2nd plural, informal vosotros / vosotras you all (friends; Spain only) 2nd plural ustedes you all (formal in Spain; formal and informal in Latin America) 3rd plural ellos / ellas they (any group / an all-female group)

Table 2.5. The subject pronouns.

Four details matter:

  • Accents that change meaning. tú with an accent is "you"; tu without is "your". él with an accent is "he"; el without is "the". The written accent makes no difference to the sound here, only to the meaning.
  • Masculine wins in mixed groups. nosotros, vosotros and ellos are used for any group with at least one male in it. The forms in -as are only for groups made up entirely of women.
  • Usted is grammatically "he/she". Historically usted comes from vuestra merced, "your grace", so it takes the same verb form as él and ella: ¿Cómo está usted? has the same verb as ¿Cómo está él? In writing it is often shortened to Ud. or Vd., and ustedes to Uds. or Vds.
  • Pronouns are usually left out. Spanish verb endings already show who is speaking, so Soy inglés means "I'm English" without yo. You add the pronoun for emphasis or contrast, as Lucía does in the dialogue: Yo soy mexicana, "I'm Mexican (and you're English)".

docs.title: Tú or usted?
docs.text:
Informal Formal one person tú (vos in some countries) usted several people, Spain vosotros, vosotras ustedes several people, Latin America ustedes ustedes

Table 2.6. The four words for "you", and where they are used.

Use tú with friends, family, children, other students and people your own age in a relaxed setting. Use usted with older people you do not know, officials, and in formal situations: a job interview, a bank, a doctor's surgery. When a Spanish speaker says puedes tutearme ("you can call me tú") or simply starts using tú with you, you may switch.

Common mistake: mixing the two

Once you have chosen, keep the same "you" for the whole conversation. ¿Cómo está usted? ¿Y de dónde eres? mixes polite and friendly forms and sounds odd. Say either ¿Cómo está usted? ¿De dónde es? or ¿Cómo estás? ¿De dónde eres?

Vos

In Argentina, Uruguay, Paraguay and much of Central America, people say vos instead of tú, with verb forms of its own: vos sos ("you are") instead of tú eres, ¿Cómo te llamás? instead of ¿Cómo te llamas? You do not need to use vos yourself, and everybody understands tú, but you should recognise it when you hear it. This book teaches tú and notes vos where it matters.

docs.title: 2.4 Grammar: giving your name and where you are from
Me llamo …
docs.text:
The everyday way to give your name is me llamo, literally "I call myself". The verb is llamarse, "to be called". Its first three forms are all you need at this stage:

Person llamarse English yo me llamo my name is, I'm called tú te llamas your name is él, ella, usted se llama his / her / your name is nosotros, nosotras nos llamamos our names are vosotros, vosotras os llamáis your names are (Spain) ellos, ellas, ustedes se llaman their / your names are

Table 2.7. The verb llamarse. Switch on Practice and fill in the endings.

The small word in front (me, te, se) is a reflexive pronoun, "myself, yourself, himself". You will meet many verbs like this in Lesson 11; for now, learn the phrases whole.

  • ¿Cómo te llamas? — Me llamo Sofía. — What's your name? — I'm Sofía.
  • ¿Cómo se llama usted? — Me llamo Antonio García. — What's your name, sir? — Antonio García.
  • Mi amiga se llama Carmen. — My friend's name is Carmen.
  • Mis padres se llaman Luis y Elena. — My parents are called Luis and Elena.

Two other ways are also correct: Soy Sofía ("I'm Sofía"), which is short and friendly, and Mi nombre es Sofía ("My name is Sofía"), which is fine but more formal and more common in writing.

Common mistake

Do not translate "my name is" word for word into me llamo es. Either me llamo Sofía or mi nombre es Sofía, never both verbs at once. And "what is your name?" is ¿Cómo te llamas? (literally "how do you call yourself?"), not ¿Qué te llamas?

docs.title: Soy de … : where you are from
docs.text:
To say where you come from, use soy de + the place. The verb is ser, "to be", which Lesson 5 explains fully. Its first three forms are:

Person ser Example yo soy Soy de Toronto. — I'm from Toronto. tú eres ¿De dónde eres? — Where are you from? él, ella, usted es Marta es de Bogotá. — Marta is from Bogotá.

Table 2.8. Three forms of ser.

The question ¿De dónde eres? is literally "From where are you?" Spanish never ends a sentence with a preposition, so the de moves to the front.

docs.title: Nationalities: masculine and feminine
docs.text:
A nationality is an adjective, and Spanish adjectives change their ending to match the person (Lesson 7 has the full rules). There are three patterns:

Country Masculine Feminine English México mexicano mexicana Mexican Colombia colombiano colombiana Colombian Argentina argentino argentina Argentinian Australia australiano australiana Australian la India indio india Indian España español española Spanish Inglaterra inglés inglesa English Irlanda irlandés irlandesa Irish Escocia escocés escocesa Scottish Alemania alemán alemana German Estados Unidos estadounidense estadounidense American (of the USA) Canadá canadiense canadiense Canadian

Table 2.9. Nationalities. Practice hides the endings in bold.

The patterns:

  1. -o becomes -a: mexicano → mexicana.
  2. A consonant adds -a: español → española. If the masculine has a written accent on its last syllable, the accent disappears in the feminine, because the stress no longer needs marking: inglés → inglesa, alemán → alemana. (Lesson 1 explains why.)
  3. -e and most other endings do not change: canadiense, estadounidense.

No capital letters

In Spanish, nationalities and languages are written with a small letter: Soy inglés. Hablo español. Only the names of countries and cities take a capital: Inglaterra, Madrid.

Worked example: introducing a friend

Daniel introduces his friend Priya, an Indian woman who lives in Leeds, to Lucía.

  1. Introduce: Lucía, te presento a mi amiga Priya.
  2. Her name: Se llama Priya. (third person: se llama)
  3. Nationality, feminine: Es india. (indio → india)
  4. Where she lives now: Vive en Leeds. ("she lives in Leeds")

Lucía answers Encantada, Priya, and Priya answers Igualmente.

docs.title: Formal or informal?
docs.text:
For each situation, decide whether you would use tú or usted, then say the greeting aloud.

Situation You say a classmate of your age Hola, ¿qué tal? ¿Cómo estás? an elderly neighbour Buenos días, señora. ¿Cómo está usted? a hotel receptionist, at night Buenas noches. ¿Cómo está? your host family's ten-year-old ¡Hola! ¿Cómo te llamas? two friends together, in Madrid ¡Hola, chicos! ¿Qué tal estáis? two friends together, in Lima ¡Hola, chicos! ¿Qué tal están?

Table 2.10. Choosing the right "you". Señor, señora and señorita are Mr, Mrs and Miss; señorita is now used mostly for young women and in shops.

docs.title: A first conversation
docs.text:
Read each part of this conversation aloud. Then cover the Spanish and say it from the English.

  • Buenas tardes. ¿Cómo se llama usted? — Good afternoon. What is your name?
  • Me llamo Elena Torres. ¿Y usted? — My name is Elena Torres. And yours?
  • Me llamo Robert Kim. Soy canadiense, de Vancouver. — My name is Robert Kim. I'm Canadian, from Vancouver.
  • Mucho gusto, señor Kim. — Nice to meet you, Mr Kim.
  • Igualmente. Hasta luego. — Likewise. See you later.

Say it

Introduce yourself in three sentences: a greeting, your name, and where you are from. For example:

Hola, buenos días. Me llamo Sarah. Soy inglesa, de Bristol.

Then ask your partner the same things, once with tú and once with usted.

docs.title: 2.6 Culture: greetings in Spain and Latin America
docs.text:
Kisses and handshakes. In Spain, friends and people being introduced in a relaxed setting usually greet with dos besos, two light kisses, cheek to cheek, starting with the right cheek (so you lean to your left). This happens between women and between a man and a woman; two men usually shake hands or, if they are close, hug. In most of Latin America the custom is a single kiss on the right cheek. In business settings everywhere, a handshake is the safe choice. Do not worry about getting it perfect: follow the other person's lead.

Time of day. Spanish days are divided by meals, not by the clock. In Spain lunch is late (often between 2 and 3 p.m.), so buenos días is used until then, and buenas tardes can last until nine in the evening in summer, when it is still light. In much of Latin America the change to buenas tardes comes at noon.

Tú and usted around the world. Spain uses tú very widely, even with strangers of similar age, shop assistants and, increasingly, teachers. In much of Latin America usted is used more, and in parts of Colombia, Costa Rica and Central America some people use usted even with friends and family. When in doubt, start with usted: no one is offended by politeness, and the other person will tell you if you can switch.

Vosotros and ustedes. Only Spain uses vosotros for "you all" among friends. In the Canary Islands and all of Latin America, ustedes is the only plural "you". This book shows the vosotros forms so that you can understand Spaniards, but if you are learning for Latin America you may skip them in your own speech.

Names. Most Spanish speakers have two surnames: the father's first surname followed by the mother's first surname. In Gabriel García Márquez, García comes from his father and Márquez from his mother; he is "García" for short, not "Márquez". Women do not traditionally change their surnames when they marry.

Señor, señora, don, doña. Señor and señora go with surnames (señora Ruiz). Don and doña go with first names and show respect, often to older people: don Antonio, doña Carmen.

docs.title: 2.7 Summary
docs.text:
Summary

  • Greetings: hola (any time), buenos días (morning), buenas tardes (afternoon, early evening), buenas noches (night). Goodbyes: adiós, hasta luego, hasta mañana, nos vemos.
  • How are you? ¿Qué tal? ¿Cómo estás? (tú) ¿Cómo está usted? (usted). Answer muy bien, bien, regular, mal.
  • Names: ¿Cómo te llamas? — Me llamo … React with mucho gusto or encantado / encantada.
  • Origin: ¿De dónde eres? — Soy de … Nationalities agree with the person (inglés, inglesa) and take no capital letter.
  • Pronouns: yo, tú, usted, él, ella, nosotros, vosotros, ustedes, ellos, ellas. Usted takes the same verb form as él and ella. Pronouns are usually left out.
  • "You": tú (friendly), usted (polite); for several people vosotros (friendly, Spain only) and ustedes (everywhere else, and formal in Spain).

docs.title: 2.8 Exercises
docs.text:
Exercise 1

It is 10 a.m. You walk into a bakery. What do you say to greet the baker? Give the two words.

Answer

Buenos días. Buenos días is used until lunchtime. Hola, buenos días is also very natural.

Exercise 2

Give the Spanish for "See you tomorrow".

Answer

Hasta mañana. Hasta mañana.

Exercise 3

A friend asks ¿Qué tal?. Answer "Very well, thanks. And you?"

Answer

Muy bien, gracias. ¿Y tú? Muy bien, gracias. ¿Y tú? Since the question was informal, you answer with tú.

Exercise 4

Ask an older man you have just met, politely, what his name is.

Answer

¿Cómo se llama usted? ¿Cómo se llama usted? With usted the verb is the third person form, se llama.

Exercise 5

Give the feminine form of escocés.

Answer

escocesa. escocesa. A consonant adds -a, and the written accent disappears because the stress is now on the next-to-last syllable, where Spanish expects it.

Exercise 6

Which subject pronoun would you use for each? (a) your two brothers, talking about them; (b) your sister and her friend Ana; (c) yourself and your friend Marta (both women); (d) a group of friends you are speaking to, in Seville; (e) the same, in Buenos Aires.

Answer

(a) ellos; (b) ellas; (c) nosotras; (d) vosotros; (e) ustedes.

Exercise 7

Correct the mistake: Me llamo es Tom. Soy Inglés.

Answer

Me llamo Tom. Soy inglés. Do not add es after me llamo, and write nationalities with a small letter.

Exercise 8

Write a short introduction for Kenji, a Japanese man from Osaka. Use the third person. (Japanese: japonés.)

Answer

Se llama Kenji. Es japonés, de Osaka. For a woman it would be Es japonesa.

docs.title: 2.9 Quiz
docs.text:
Quiz: greetings and introductions

Exercise 9

It is 9 p.m. and you arrive at a hotel. You say:

  1. Buenos días.
  2. Buenas tardes.
  3. Buenas noches.
  4. Hasta luego.
Answer

Buenas noches.

After dark, buenas noches is both a greeting and a goodbye.

Exercise 10

A woman says she is pleased to meet you. She says:

  1. Encantado.
  2. Encantada.
  3. Encantados.
  4. Encantar.
Answer

Encantada.

The word agrees with the speaker; a woman says encantada.

Exercise 11

¿Cómo te ___? — Me llamo Pablo.

Hint: llamarse, tú form

Answer

llamas

te llamas is the tú form of llamarse.

Exercise 12

Say "I am from Chicago" in Spanish.

Answer

Soy de Chicago / Yo soy de Chicago

Exercise 13

Match each phrase to its meaning.

ABhasta luegolikewisemucho gustoyou're welcomeigualmentesee you laterde nadanice to meet you Answer

hasta luego — see you later; mucho gusto — nice to meet you; igualmente — likewise; de nada — you're welcome

Exercise 14

Put the words in order to ask "Where are you from?" (tú).

Words: dónde / ¿De / eres / tú?

Answer

¿De dónde eres tú?

Exercise 15

Tap the wrong word.

Soy inglesa y mi amigo es irlandesa.

Answer

Wrong word: irlandesa.

Corrected: Soy inglesa y mi amigo es irlandés.

amigo is a man, so the nationality is masculine, irlandés.

Exercise 16

Write what you hear.

Dictation. Have someone read the sentence aloud, then write it down.

Me llamo Carmen y soy de Sevilla.

Answer

Me llamo Carmen y soy de Sevilla.

Exercise 17

Say it aloud.

Buenos días, ¿cómo está usted?

Answer

Say: Buenos días, ¿cómo está usted?

docs.title: Lesson 10: Irregular Verbs: tener, ir, hacer, querer, poder
docs.text:
Los verbos irregulares

In Lesson 6 you learned the regular present tense: take the infinitive, remove -ar, -er or -ir, add the endings. Unfortunately, the verbs people use most often are exactly the ones that do not follow the rules. This lesson takes five of them, tener (to have), ir (to go), hacer (to do, to make), querer (to want) and poder (to be able to), and shows that their irregularity is not chaos. Most irregular verbs belong to a few families with predictable patterns, and once you know the patterns you know dozens of verbs. With these five you can make plans, talk about the weather, say what you have to do and what you can and cannot do.

Learning outcomes

By the end of this lesson you will be able to:

  • conjugate tener, ir, hacer, querer and poder in the present tense;
  • recognise the two main families of stem-changing verbs, e → ie and o → ue, and the "boot" pattern they share;
  • use tener in expressions of feeling and need (tengo hambre, tengo que estudiar);
  • say where you are going with ir a, and talk about the weather with hace;
  • make requests and offers with ¿puedo …?, ¿puedes …? and ¿quieres …?;
  • recognise the "yo-go" verbs: salgo, pongo, vengo, digo.

docs.title: 10.1 Dialogue: plans for the weekend
docs.text:
It is Friday. Lucía and Daniel are leaving class.

  • Lucía: ¿Qué haces este fin de semana? — What are you doing this weekend?
  • Daniel: No sé. El sábado por la mañana tengo que estudiar. Tenemos un examen el lunes. — I don't know. On Saturday morning I have to study. We have an exam on Monday.
  • Lucía: Sí, es verdad. ¿Y por la tarde? ¿Quieres ir al cine? — Yes, that's true. And in the afternoon? Do you want to go to the cinema?
  • Daniel: Por la tarde no puedo. Juego al fútbol con unos amigos. — I can't in the afternoon. I'm playing football with some friends.
  • Lucía: ¿Y el domingo? Mis primos y yo vamos a la sierra. Hacemos una ruta por la montaña. — And on Sunday? My cousins and I are going to the mountains. We're doing a walk in the hills.
  • Daniel: ¡Qué bien! ¿Puedo ir con vosotros? — Great! Can I come with you?
  • Lucía: ¡Claro que sí! Salimos a las ocho de la mañana. — Of course! We leave at eight in the morning.
  • Daniel: ¿A las ocho? ¡Qué temprano! Los domingos duermo hasta las diez. — At eight? That's early! On Sundays I sleep until ten.
  • Lucía: Es que en verano hace mucho calor a mediodía. Por la mañana hace fresco. — The thing is, in summer it's very hot at midday. In the morning it's cool.
  • Daniel: Vale. ¿Qué tengo que llevar? — OK. What do I have to bring?
  • Lucía: Agua, un bocadillo y una gorra. Y si quieres, puedes traer la cámara. — Water, a sandwich and a cap. And if you want, you can bring your camera.
  • Daniel: Perfecto. ¿Cuándo volvemos? — Perfect. When do we come back?
  • Lucía: Volvemos por la tarde, a las seis o así. — We come back in the afternoon, at about six.

Notice:

  1. Spanish often uses the present tense for arrangements in the near future: el sábado juego al fútbol, "on Saturday I'm playing football".
  2. tengo que estudiar: tener que + infinitive means "to have to".
  3. puedo, duermo, juego have ue where the infinitives poder, dormir, jugar have o or u. But volvemos, with nosotros, keeps the o of volver. This is the boot pattern of section 10.4.
  4. Weather uses hacer: hace calor, literally "it makes heat".

docs.title: 10.2 Vocabulary: feelings, weather and free time
Tener: what you feel and need
docs.text:
Spanish Literally English tener hambre to have hunger to be hungry tener sed to have thirst to be thirsty tener frío to have cold to be (feel) cold tener calor to have heat to be (feel) hot tener sueño to have sleep to be sleepy tener prisa to have hurry to be in a hurry tener miedo (de) to have fear to be afraid (of) tener razón to have reason to be right tener suerte to have luck to be lucky tener … años to have … years to be … years old tener que + infinitive to have that to have to, must tener ganas de + infinitive to have desires of to feel like (doing)

Table 10.1. Expressions with tener. Where English says "be", Spanish often says "have".

Since hambre, sed, frío and the rest are nouns, "very" is mucho or mucha, not muy: tengo mucha hambre (hambre is feminine), tengo mucho frío, tienes mucha razón.

docs.title: Hacer: the weather
docs.text:
Spanish Sounds like English ¿Qué tiempo hace? [keh TYEHM-poh AH-seh] What's the weather like? hace calor [AH-seh kah-LOR] it's hot hace frío [AH-seh FREE-oh] it's cold hace fresco [AH-seh FREHS-koh] it's cool, chilly hace sol [AH-seh SOHL] it's sunny hace viento [AH-seh BYEHN-toh] it's windy hace buen tiempo [AH-seh bwehn TYEHM-poh] the weather is good hace mal tiempo [AH-seh mahl TYEHM-poh] the weather is bad llueve [YWEH-beh] it's raining, it rains (llover) nieva [NYEH-bah] it's snowing, it snows (nevar) está nublado [ehs-TAH noo-BLAH-doh] it's cloudy hay niebla [ai NYEH-blah] it's foggy

Table 10.2. The weather. hace is the third person of hacer; llueve and nieva are verbs of their own.

docs.title: Free time: hacer and ir
docs.text:
Spanish English hacer deporte to do sport hacer los deberes (Spain), hacer la tarea (Latin America) to do homework hacer la compra (Spain), hacer las compras (Latin America) to do the food shopping hacer la cama to make the bed hacer una ruta, hacer senderismo to go for a walk, to go hiking hacer un viaje to take a trip hacer una foto (Spain), tomar una foto (Latin America) to take a photo ir de compras to go shopping (for pleasure) ir de vacaciones to go on holiday ir de excursión to go on an outing ir a la playa, ir a la montaña to go to the beach, to the mountains jugar al fútbol, jugar al tenis to play football, tennis el fin de semana the weekend

Table 10.3. Free-time activities. In much of Latin America people say jugar fútbol, without al.

docs.title: Tener: to have
docs.text:
Person tener English yo tengo I have tú tienes you have él, ella, usted tiene he, she has; you have nosotros, nosotras tenemos we have vosotros, vosotras tenéis you have (Spain) ellos, ellas, ustedes tienen they, you have

Table 10.4. tener. Two irregularities: a g in the yo form, and e → ie in the boot (section 10.4).

tener is used for possession (tengo un coche), family (tiene tres hijos), age (tenemos veinte años), the expressions of Table 10.1, and obligation:

  • Tengo que trabajar el sábado. — I have to work on Saturday.
  • ¿Tienes que irte ya? — Do you have to go already?
  • No tenemos que pagar. — We don't have to pay.
  • Tienen que coger el tren de las nueve. — They have to catch the nine o'clock train. (Latin America: tomar el tren)

Common mistake: I am hungry

Do not translate "I am hungry" as Estoy hambre or Soy hambre. Hunger is something you have: Tengo hambre. In the same way, "I am 25" is Tengo veinticinco años, and "I'm cold" is Tengo frío.

docs.title: Ir: to go
docs.text:
Person ir English yo voy I go, I'm going tú vas you go él, ella, usted va he, she goes; you go nosotros, nosotras vamos we go vosotros, vosotras vais you go (Spain) ellos, ellas, ustedes van they, you go

Table 10.5. ir. Completely irregular, but with the regular -ar endings after the v.

ir is followed by a before a destination, and a + el contracts to al (Lesson 4). Transport takes en (Lesson 9).

  • Voy al cine. — I'm going to the cinema.
  • ¿Vas a la playa en coche o en tren? — Are you going to the beach by car or by train?
  • Los niños van al colegio a pie. — The children walk to school.
  • ¿Adónde vais este verano? — Where are you going this summer?

To ask "where to?", use ¿adónde? (also written ¿a dónde?). ¿Dónde? alone asks where something is. ¡Vamos! on its own means "Let's go!", and ¡Vamos a la playa! "Let's go to the beach!"

Coming soon: ir a + infinitive

ir a followed by an infinitive, as in voy a estudiar ("I'm going to study"), is the everyday way to talk about the future. It is the subject of Lesson 14. In this lesson, ir a is always followed by a place.

docs.title: Hacer: to do, to make
docs.text:
Person hacer English yo hago I do, I make tú haces you do él, ella, usted hace he, she does; you do nosotros, nosotras hacemos we do vosotros, vosotras hacéis you do (Spain) ellos, ellas, ustedes hacen they, you do

Table 10.6. hacer. Only the yo form is irregular: hago.

hacer covers both English "do" and "make": hago la cena ("I make dinner"), hago ejercicio ("I do exercise"). It is also the verb of the weather (Table 10.2). The question ¿Qué haces? ("What are you doing? What do you do?") is usually answered with a different verb: ¿Qué haces los domingos? — Duermo mucho y leo.

Common mistake: muy calor

In weather expressions calor, frío and sol are nouns, so "very" is mucho: hace mucho calor, hace mucho frío. Never hace muy calor. And keep three ideas apart: hace calor (the weather is hot), tengo calor (I feel hot), la sopa está caliente (the soup is hot).

docs.title: 10.4 Grammar: stem-changing verbs, querer and poder
The boot pattern
docs.text:
Many verbs keep the regular endings of Lesson 6 but change a vowel in their stem, the part before the ending. The change happens only when that vowel is stressed, which is in four of the six forms: yo, tú, él and ellos. In nosotros and vosotros the stress moves to the ending, and the stem stays as it is in the infinitive. Drawn in a table, the four changed forms make the shape of a boot.

Figure 10.1 The boot. A conjugation table of poder in two columns, singular on the left and plural on the right. A boot shape encloses puedo, puedes, puede and pueden, which have the stem pued-; podemos and podéis, outside the boot, keep the stem pod-.

There are two big families:

  • e → ie: querer → quiero, pensar → pienso.
  • o → ue: poder → puedo, dormir → duermo.

Dictionaries and verb lists show the change in brackets: querer (ie), poder (ue). There is nothing in the infinitive itself that tells you whether a verb changes (comer does not, volver does), so learn the bracket with the verb.

docs.title: Querer (e → ie): to want, to love
docs.text:
Person querer pensar preferir yo quiero pienso prefiero tú quieres piensas prefieres él, ella, usted quiere piensa prefiere nosotros, nosotras queremos pensamos preferimos vosotros, vosotras queréis pensáis preferís ellos, ellas, ustedes quieren piensan prefieren

Table 10.7. e → ie verbs: one -er, one -ar and one -ir verb. The endings are regular.

Other common e → ie verbs: empezar (to begin: empiezo), cerrar (to close: cierro), entender (to understand: entiendo), and tener and venir, which add a g in the yo form as well.

querer is used with a noun or an infinitive:

  • Quiero un café. — I want a coffee.
  • ¿Quieres venir a la fiesta? — Do you want to come to the party? (an invitation)
  • No queremos salir esta noche. — We don't want to go out tonight.

With people, querer means "to love": Te quiero ("I love you") is said to partners, family and close friends. Te amo is stronger and more romantic, used more in Latin America and in songs.

docs.title: Poder (o → ue): can, to be able to
docs.text:
Person poder dormir volver yo puedo duermo vuelvo tú puedes duermes vuelves él, ella, usted puede duerme vuelve nosotros, nosotras podemos dormimos volvemos vosotros, vosotras podéis dormís volvéis ellos, ellas, ustedes pueden duermen vuelven

Table 10.8. o → ue verbs.

Other common o → ue verbs: costar (to cost: ¿Cuánto cuesta?, ¿Cuánto cuestan?), encontrar (to find: encuentro), recordar (to remember: recuerdo), almorzar (to have lunch: almuerzo). The verb jugar (to play) is the only verb with u → ue: juego, juegas, juega, jugamos, jugáis, juegan.

poder is followed by an infinitive. It expresses ability and permission, and it is the verb of polite requests:

Use Example English ability, possibility No puedo ir el sábado. I can't go on Saturday. asking permission ¿Puedo abrir la ventana? Can I open the window? asking a favour (tú) ¿Puedes ayudarme? Can you help me? asking a favour (usted) ¿Puede repetir, por favor? Could you repeat that, please? is it allowed? ¿Se puede pagar con tarjeta? Can one pay by card?

Table 10.9. Uses of poder.

Can and know how

For a skill you have learned, Spanish uses saber, not poder: Sé nadar ("I can swim, I know how to swim"). No puedo nadar means you are unable to at the moment: the pool is closed, or you have hurt your arm.

A third family: e → i

A smaller group of -ir verbs changes e → i in the boot: pedir (to ask for, to order: pido, pides, pide, pedimos, pedís, piden), repetir (to repeat), servir (to serve), seguir (to follow, to continue: sigo). You met siga and sigue in Lesson 9.

docs.title: The yo-go verbs
docs.text:
tengo and hago belong to a group of very common verbs whose yo form ends in -go. Learn to recognise them; the other forms are regular, or follow the stem changes you already know.

Infinitive yo tú English salir salgo sales to go out, to leave poner pongo pones to put traer traigo traes to bring venir vengo vienes to come (also e → ie) decir digo dices to say, to tell (also e → i) tener tengo tienes to have (also e → ie) hacer hago haces to do, to make

Table 10.10. The yo-go verbs. Full tables are in the Verb Tables at the end of the book.

Worked example: conjugating a new verb

You meet the verb encontrar (ue), "to find". Give the yo and nosotros forms.

  1. It is an -ar verb, so the endings are those of hablar: -o, -as, -a, -amos, -áis, -an.
  2. The bracket says o → ue in the boot. yo is inside the boot: encuentro.
  3. nosotros is outside the boot, so the stem is unchanged: encontramos.

Check: No encuentro mis llaves. — I can't find my keys. Siempre encontramos sitio. — We always find a place.

docs.title: Inside or outside the boot?
docs.text:
Infinitive yo nosotros ellos cerrar (ie) cierro cerramos cierran entender (ie) entiendo entendemos entienden empezar (ie) empiezo empezamos empiezan costar (ue) — — cuestan recordar (ue) recuerdo recordamos recuerdan jugar (ue) juego jugamos juegan venir (ie, -go) vengo venimos vienen

Table 10.11. Stem-change drill. costar is used almost only in the third person: el libro cuesta, los libros cuestan.

docs.title: What is the weather like?
docs.text:
Say what the weather is like, and what you feel, in each case.

  • En agosto, en Sevilla, hace mucho calor. Tengo calor y tengo sed. — In August, in Seville, it's very hot. I'm hot and thirsty.
  • En enero, en Madrid, hace frío y a veces nieva. — In January, in Madrid, it's cold and sometimes it snows.
  • En Londres llueve mucho y está nublado. — In London it rains a lot and it's cloudy.
  • Hoy hace sol, pero hace viento. — Today it's sunny, but it's windy.

docs.title: Requests and invitations
docs.text:
• ¿Puedes cerrar la puerta, por favor? — Can you close the door, please?
  • ¿Quieres un café? — Sí, gracias. — Would you like a coffee? — Yes, thanks.
  • ¿Quieres ir a la playa mañana? — No puedo, tengo que trabajar. — Do you want to go to the beach tomorrow? — I can't, I have to work.
  • ¿Puedo hacer una pregunta? — Can I ask a question?

Say it

Invite a friend to do something this weekend. Your friend says no, gives a reason with tener que, and suggests another day. For example:

— ¿Quieres ir al cine el sábado? — Lo siento, no puedo. Tengo que estudiar. ¿Puedes el domingo? — Sí, el domingo puedo.

docs.title: 10.6 Culture: weather and free time in Spain and Latin America
docs.text:
Opposite seasons. Spain and Mexico are in the northern hemisphere, so their summer is from June to September, as in Britain or the United States. Argentina, Chile, Uruguay and Paraguay are in the southern hemisphere: there, el verano is December to February, and Christmas is a summer holiday, often spent at the beach or with a barbecue (el asado).

Altitude, not season. In the countries near the equator, such as Colombia, Ecuador and Venezuela, temperatures change little through the year. What matters is height above sea level: Bogotá and Quito, high in the Andes, are cool all year round, while the coast is hot all year round. People there speak of la temporada de lluvias (the rainy season) and la temporada seca (the dry season) rather than four seasons.

The paseo. In Spain and much of Latin America, an evening stroll, el paseo or dar un paseo, is a social custom: families and friends walk slowly round the square or along the seafront, greet neighbours and stop for a drink. In hot weather, streets that are empty in the afternoon fill with people after eight in the evening.

The siesta. The afternoon nap is famous, but most people who work in cities do not have time for it on working days. What survives, especially in smaller Spanish towns, is the long midday break: many shops close from about two until five and stay open until eight or later in the evening.

Football. el fútbol is the most popular sport in almost every Spanish-speaking country, and a match between great rivals, such as Real Madrid and FC Barcelona in Spain, or Boca Juniors and River Plate in Argentina, can stop a whole country. Baseball (el béisbol) is the leading sport in Cuba, the Dominican Republic and Venezuela.

Regional verbs. Spaniards say coger el autobús for "to catch the bus"; in much of Latin America tomar el autobús is the normal expression, and you should use tomar there. tomar is understood everywhere, so it is the safe choice.

docs.title: 10.7 Summary
docs.text:
Summary

  • tener: tengo, tienes, tiene, tenemos, tenéis, tienen. Expressions: tener hambre, sed, frío, calor, sueño, prisa, razón, … años; tener que + infinitive = to have to.
  • ir: voy, vas, va, vamos, vais, van; ir a + place (voy al cine), ir en + transport.
  • hacer: hago, haces, hace, hacemos, hacéis, hacen; weather: hace calor, frío, sol, viento, buen tiempo, but llueve, nieva. "Very" with these nouns is mucho.
  • Stem changes happen in the boot (yo, tú, él, ellos), never in nosotros or vosotros: e → ie (querer: quiero; pensar, empezar, preferir, cerrar, entender) and o → ue (poder: puedo; dormir, volver, costar, encontrar; jugar: juego).
  • querer + noun or infinitive; te quiero = I love you. poder + infinitive: ¿Puedo …? ¿Puedes …? ¿Se puede …?
  • yo-go verbs: salgo, pongo, traigo, vengo, digo, tengo, hago.

docs.title: 10.8 Exercises
docs.text:
Exercise 1

Give the yo form of tener.

Answer

tengo. tengo

Exercise 2

Give the nosotros form of ir.

Answer

vamos. vamos

Exercise 3

Complete: Mis hermanos ___ al fútbol los sábados. (jugar)

Answer

juegan. Mis hermanos juegan al fútbol los sábados. ellos is inside the boot: u → ue.

Exercise 4

Complete: Nosotros no ___ venir mañana. (poder)

Answer

podemos. Nosotros no podemos venir mañana. nosotros is outside the boot, so there is no change.

Exercise 5

Say "I'm very thirsty."

Answer

Tengo mucha sed. Tengo mucha sed. sed is a feminine noun, so mucha.

Exercise 6

Say "It's very cold today."

Answer

Hoy hace mucho frío. Hoy hace mucho frío. Never muy frío in this expression.

Exercise 7

Say "I have to work." (two verbs and a small word)

Answer

Tengo que trabajar. Tengo que trabajar.

Exercise 8

Complete with the right form of ir and the right preposition: ¿Tú ___ ___ cine esta noche?

Answer

vas al. ¿Tú vas al cine esta noche? a + el = al.

Exercise 9

Correct the mistakes: Yo hace los deberes y después yo salo con mis amigos.

Answer

Yo hago los deberes y después salgo con mis amigos. hacer and salir are yo-go verbs; the second yo is not needed.

Exercise 10

Write three sentences about your weekend: one thing you have to do, one thing you want to do, and one thing you cannot do.

Answer

A model answer: El sábado tengo que hacer la compra. Quiero ir a la playa con mis amigos. No puedo salir el domingo por la noche porque el lunes trabajo.

docs.title: 10.9 Quiz
docs.text:
Quiz: irregular verbs

Exercise 11

Los domingos yo ___ hasta las diez. (dormir)

  1. dormo
  2. duermo
  3. dormimos
  4. duerme
Answer

duermo

dormir is o → ue, and yo is inside the boot.

Exercise 12

"I'm hungry" in Spanish:

  1. Estoy hambre.
  2. Soy hambre.
  3. Tengo hambre.
  4. Hago hambre.
Answer

Tengo hambre.

Hunger is something you have, tener hambre.

Exercise 13

¿___ (tú) venir a mi fiesta? (querer)

Answer

Quieres

querer is e → ie; tú is inside the boot.

Exercise 14

Hoy ___ sol, pero mañana ___. (hacer, llover)

Answer

hace · llueve

Exercise 15

Give the yo form of salir.

Answer

salgo

Exercise 16

Match each infinitive to its yo form.

ABponerdigoirpuedodecirpongopodervoy Answer

poner — pongo; ir — voy; decir — digo; poder — puedo

Exercise 17

Tap the wrong word.

Nosotros pueden jugar al tenis el lunes.

Answer

Wrong word: pueden.

Corrected: Nosotros podemos jugar al tenis el lunes.

With nosotros the form is podemos, outside the boot.

Exercise 18

Put the words in order.

Words: que / deberes / los / Tenemos / hacer

Answer

Tenemos que hacer los deberes

Exercise 19

Write what you hear.

Dictation. Have someone read the sentence aloud, then write it down.

Hace mucho calor y tengo mucha sed.

Answer

Hace mucho calor y tengo mucha sed.

Exercise 20

Say it aloud.

¿Puedes ayudarme, por favor?

Answer

Say: ¿Puedes ayudarme, por favor?

docs.title: Lesson 12: Likes and Dislikes with gustar
docs.text:
Gustos y aficiones

"I like football", "I love chocolate", "my head hurts": to say these things in Spanish you need a verb that works back to front. In English, I like the film. In Spanish, the film pleases me: me gusta la película. You met me gusta as a phrase in the café in Lesson 8. This lesson takes it apart, shows you how to say what other people like, how to agree and disagree, and introduces the family of verbs that work the same way: encantar, interesar, molestar and doler. Along the way you learn to talk about hobbies and free time.

Learning outcomes

By the end of this lesson you will be able to:

  • say what you like and dislike, and how much, with gustar and encantar;
  • choose between gusta and gustan;
  • use the indirect object pronouns me, te, le, nos, os, les, and make them clear with a mí, a ti, a él, a María;
  • agree and disagree with a mí también, a mí tampoco, a mí sí, a mí no;
  • talk about hobbies, and use interesar, molestar, doler and preferir.

masculinefeminineplural

docs.title: 12.1 Dialogue: a language exchange
docs.text:
Sergio, from Valencia, and Valentina, a Colombian student from Medellín who lives in Valencia, meet every Thursday for an intercambio: half an hour of Spanish, half an hour of English. Today they speak Spanish.

  • Valentina: Sergio, ¿qué te gusta hacer en tu tiempo libre? — Sergio, what do you like doing in your free time?
  • Sergio: Me gusta mucho leer y me encanta el cine. ¿Y a ti? — I really like reading and I love the cinema. And you?
  • Valentina: A mí también me gusta el cine, pero no me gusta mucho leer. Prefiero el deporte. — I like the cinema too, but I don't like reading much. I prefer sport.
  • Sergio: ¿Qué deportes te gustan? — What sports do you like?
  • Valentina: Me encanta el fútbol. Juego con unas amigas los sábados. — I love football. I play with some friends on Saturdays.
  • Sergio: A mí no me gustan los deportes de equipo, pero me encanta nadar. — I don't like team sports, but I love swimming.
  • Valentina: ¿Y te gustan las películas de terror? — And do you like horror films?
  • Sergio: No, no me gustan nada. Prefiero las comedias. — No, I don't like them at all. I prefer comedies.
  • Valentina: A mí tampoco. ¿Y qué música te gusta? — Me neither. And what music do you like?
  • Sergio: Me gustan el flamenco y el rock. Toco la guitarra. — I like flamenco and rock. I play the guitar.
  • Valentina: ¡Qué casualidad! A mi hermano le encanta el rock, y le interesa mucho la guitarra flamenca. — What a coincidence! My brother loves rock, and he's very interested in flamenco guitar.
  • Sergio: Pues hay un concierto el viernes. ¿Vamos los tres? — Well, there's a concert on Friday. Shall we all three go?
  • Valentina: ¡Me encantaría! — I'd love to!

Notice:

  1. me gusta with one thing or an activity (me gusta leer, me gusta el cine), but me gustan with several things (me gustan los deportes). The verb agrees with the thing liked, not with the person.
  2. To say what another person likes, the pronoun changes: le encanta el rock, "he loves rock".
  3. Agreeing uses a mí, not yo: A mí también, A mí tampoco.
  4. ¡Me encantaría! ("I would love to!") is a fixed phrase for accepting an invitation. You will meet its tense, the conditional, after this course.

docs.text:

Table 12.1. Free-time activities. In Spain you will also hear hacer fotos, and in much of Latin America tomar fotos.

docs.title: Things to like
docs.text:
Spanish English el cine the cinema la música music el deporte sport el fútbol / el baloncesto / el tenis football / basketball / tennis la naturaleza nature el arte art los libros books las películas (de acción, de terror) films (action, horror) las comedias comedies los animales animals el tiempo libre free time la afición / el pasatiempo hobby, pastime

Table 12.2. Nouns for likes and hobbies. In much of Latin America basketball is el básquetbol.

docs.title: Jugar and tocar: two ways to "play"
docs.text:
English "play" is two verbs in Spanish. You jugar a game or a sport, and you tocar ("touch") a musical instrument.

  • Juego al tenis. — I play tennis.
  • Toco el violín. — I play the violin.

jugar has a stem change of its own, u→ue, the only verb with this pattern. It behaves like the o→ue verbs of Lesson 10:

Person jugar (u→ue) yo juego tú juegas él, ella, usted juega nosotros, nosotras jugamos vosotros, vosotras jugáis ellos, ellas, ustedes juegan

Table 12.3. The verb jugar.

Jugar al fútbol or jugar fútbol?

In Spain you always say jugar al fútbol, jugar al tenis (a + el = al). In much of Latin America, including Mexico, people often leave out the article and preposition: jugar fútbol. Both are correct in their regions.

docs.title: Back to front
docs.text:
gustar means "to please" or "to be pleasing". So Me gusta el café is, word for word, "To me is pleasing the coffee". The thing you like is the grammatical subject, and the person who likes it is an indirect object ("to me").

Figure 12.1 English like and Spanish gustar. In English the person is the subject of like; in Spanish the thing liked is the subject of gustar, and the verb agrees with it.

This has two consequences:

  1. The verb agrees with the thing, not the person. In practice you need only two forms: gusta for one thing or for activities, gustan for several things.
  2. The person is shown by a pronoun before the verb: me, te, le and so on.

docs.title: Gusta or gustan?
docs.text:
You like … Form Example one thing (singular noun) gusta Me gusta el chocolate. — I like chocolate. several things (plural noun) gustan Me gustan los gatos. — I like cats. an activity (infinitive) gusta Me gusta bailar. — I like dancing. several activities gusta Me gusta cantar y bailar. — I like singing and dancing. two singular nouns gustan Me gustan el té y el café. — I like tea and coffee.

Table 12.4. Choosing gusta or gustan. Infinitives always take gusta, however many there are.

Common mistake: forgetting the article

With gustar, a noun almost always needs its article, because you are talking about the thing in general: Me gusta el café, Me gustan los perros. Me gusta café is wrong, though English says "I like coffee" without "the".

docs.title: The indirect object pronouns
docs.text:
The pronoun in front of gustar shows who likes the thing. These indirect object pronouns mean "to me, to you, to him …". Four of them are the same as the reflexive pronouns of Lesson 11; only the third person is different: le, les instead of se.

Who likes it Pronoun One thing Several things (a mí) me me gusta me gustan (a ti) te te gusta te gustan (a él, a ella, a usted) le le gusta le gustan (a nosotros, a nosotras) nos nos gusta nos gustan (a vosotros, a vosotras) os os gusta os gustan (a ellos, a ellas, a ustedes) les les gusta les gustan

Table 12.5. Gustar with the indirect object pronouns. Practice hides the pronoun.

  • ¿Te gusta la pizza? — Do you like pizza?
  • Nos gusta mucho viajar. — We love travelling. (We like travelling a lot.)
  • A mis padres les gustan las películas antiguas. — My parents like old films.
  • ¿Le gusta el vino tinto, señora? — Do you like red wine, madam?

docs.title: Negatives and questions
docs.text:
The word no goes before the pronoun, never between the pronoun and the verb:

  • No me gusta el fútbol. — I don't like football. (never Me no gusta)
  • ¿No te gustan las fresas? — Don't you like strawberries?

A question has the same words as a statement; only the intonation and the question marks change: ¿Te gusta el café? To ask what someone likes: ¿Qué te gusta hacer? or ¿Qué música te gusta?

docs.title: How much?
docs.text:
Spanish English Me encanta el chocolate. I love chocolate. Me gusta mucho el chocolate. I really like chocolate. Me gusta el chocolate. I like chocolate. Me gusta bastante el chocolate. I quite like chocolate. No me gusta mucho el chocolate. I don't like chocolate much. No me gusta nada el chocolate. I don't like chocolate at all. Odio el chocolate. I hate chocolate.

Table 12.6. A scale from love to hate. Odiar ("to hate") is an ordinary -ar verb: odio, odias, odia …

Common mistake: encantar mucho

encantar already means "to like a lot", so it is not used with mucho: say Me encanta el cine, not Me encanta mucho el cine. Like gustar, it agrees with the thing: Me encantan los gatos.

docs.title: 12.4 Grammar: a mí, agreeing, and other verbs like gustar
Making it clear: a mí, a ti, a él, a María
docs.text:
le gusta can mean "he likes", "she likes" or "you (usted) like". To make it clear, add a + the person:

  • A él le gusta el jazz. — He likes jazz.
  • A ella le gusta el rock. — She likes rock.
  • A usted le gusta la ópera. — You like opera.
  • A María le gustan las novelas. — María likes novels.
  • A mis amigos les gusta salir. — My friends like going out.

Notice that the pronoun le or les stays, even when the person is named. A María gustan las novelas is wrong; Spanish wants both a María and le.

With me, te, nos and os there is no confusion, so a mí, a ti, a nosotros, a vosotros are used only for emphasis or contrast:

  • A mí me gusta el té, pero a ti te gusta el café. — I like tea, but you like coffee.

Note the accent on mí ("me") to tell it from mi ("my"). ti never has an accent.

docs.title: Agreeing and disagreeing
docs.text:
Because the person in a gustar sentence is "to me", short answers use a mí, not yo. Be careful: when the first sentence is negative, the words change.

Someone says You agree You disagree Me gusta el teatro. A mí también. (me too) A mí no. (not me) No me gusta el teatro. A mí tampoco. (me neither) A mí sí. (I do) Juego al tenis. Yo también. Yo no. No juego al tenis. Yo tampoco. Yo sí.

Table 12.7. Short answers. Gustar-type verbs take a mí; ordinary verbs take yo.

You can do the same for other people: A mi hermana también ("my sister does too"), A nosotros tampoco ("we don't either").

Common mistake: yo también with gustar

After Me encanta la playa, answer A mí también, not Yo también. You will hear yo también from some native speakers in relaxed speech, but a mí también is the correct form and the one to learn.

docs.title: Other verbs that work like gustar
docs.text:
Verb Meaning Example encantar to love (things, activities) Me encanta la playa. — I love the beach. interesar to interest Nos interesa la historia. — We're interested in history. molestar to bother, annoy Me molesta el ruido. — Noise bothers me. importar to matter No me importa. — I don't mind. It doesn't matter to me. doler (o→ue) to hurt Me duele la cabeza. — My head hurts. I have a headache.

Table 12.8. Verbs of the gustar type. All of them agree with the thing, not with the person.

doler is very useful at the doctor's or the chemist's. Like other verbs of this type, it is used mostly in two forms, duele and duelen, and it takes the article with the body part:

  • Me duele el estómago. — I have a stomach ache.
  • Me duelen los pies. — My feet hurt.
  • ¿Te duele la espalda? — Does your back hurt?
  • A mi hijo le duele una muela. — My son has toothache. (una muela = a back tooth)

Gustar with people

Me gusta Ana usually means more than "I like Ana": it suggests you find her attractive. To say you like someone as a person, use caer bien, another verb of the gustar type: Ana me cae bien, "I like Ana, I get on with her"; Tu jefe me cae mal, "I don't like your boss".

docs.title: Preferir: a normal verb
docs.text:
preferir ("to prefer") is not a gustar-type verb: the person is the subject, as in English. It is an e→ie verb like querer.

Person preferir (e→ie) yo prefiero tú prefieres él, ella, usted prefiere nosotros, nosotras preferimos vosotros, vosotras preferís ellos, ellas, ustedes prefieren

Table 12.9. The verb preferir.

  • ¿Prefieres el té o el café? — Prefiero el café. — Do you prefer tea or coffee? — I prefer coffee.
  • Preferimos ir a la playa. — We'd rather go to the beach.

Worked example: a profile for a language exchange

Write three sentences about Ana for an exchange website: she loves dancing, she likes French films, and noise bothers her.

  1. Love + an activity → encanta: A Ana le encanta bailar.
  2. Like + a plural noun → gustan: Le gustan las películas francesas.
  3. Bother + a singular noun → molesta: Le molesta el ruido.

In each sentence, the verb agrees with what follows it, and the pronoun le shows that it is Ana who likes it.

docs.title: Gusta or gustan?
docs.text:
Read each sentence aloud and decide why the verb is singular or plural.

  • Me gusta la música clásica. — one thing
  • Me gustan las canciones de Shakira. — several things
  • Nos gusta correr por el parque. — an activity
  • ¿Os gustan los museos? — several things
  • A Pedro no le gusta cocinar. — an activity
  • Les encantan los animales. — several things

docs.title: Who likes what?
docs.text:
Person Likes Spanish I dogs Me gustan los perros. you (tú) the sea Te gusta el mar. my father reading A mi padre le gusta leer. we Mexican food Nos gusta la comida mexicana. my friends video games A mis amigos les gustan los videojuegos. you (usted) flowers A usted le gustan las flores.

Table 12.10. Switch on Practice and write the pronoun and the verb.

docs.title: Me too, me neither
docs.text:
Answer each statement as indicated, aloud, then listen.

  • Me encanta el verano. — A mí también. — I love summer. — Me too.
  • No me gustan las arañas. — A mí tampoco. — I don't like spiders. — Me neither.
  • Me gusta levantarme temprano. — Pues a mí no. — I like getting up early. — Well, I don't.
  • No me interesa la política. — A mí sí. — I'm not interested in politics. — I am.

Say it

Tell a partner about your free time: two things you love, two things you like, and one thing you do not like at all. For example:

Me encanta viajar y me encantan los museos. Me gusta cocinar y me gusta la música latina. No me gusta nada el fútbol.

Your partner answers each one with a mí también, a mí no, a mí tampoco or a mí sí.

docs.title: 12.6 Culture: free time in Spain and Latin America
docs.text:
Football everywhere. El fútbol is the most popular sport in Spain and in most of Latin America, and the rivalry between big clubs, and between national teams, is a constant topic of conversation. If you want small talk with almost anyone, ask ¿De qué equipo eres?, "Which team do you support?"

Baseball in the Caribbean. In Cuba, the Dominican Republic and Venezuela, and in parts of Mexico and Central America, the favourite sport is el béisbol, and many professional players in the United States come from these countries.

Music and dance. Every region has its own music. Flamenco, with its guitar, singing and dance, comes from Andalusia in southern Spain. Tango was born in the cities of the Río de la Plata, Buenos Aires and Montevideo. Salsa grew from Cuban rhythms, cumbia from Colombia, and reggaeton from Puerto Rico and Panama. In many places dancing is a normal part of a night out, and people of all ages dance at family parties.

Making plans. In Spain the verb for arranging to meet friends is quedar: ¿Quedamos el sábado?, "Shall we meet on Saturday?" In Latin America you are more likely to hear ¿Nos vemos el sábado? or, in Chile, juntarse. Social life happens outdoors and in public: on the main square, in bars and cafés, and on el paseo, the evening stroll through town.

Saying no politely. When someone invites you and you do not want to go, a direct "no" can sound abrupt. Spanish speakers soften it: Me encantaría, pero no puedo ("I'd love to, but I can't") or Gracias, pero no me gusta mucho el teatro.

docs.title: 12.7 Summary
docs.text:
Summary

  • gustar means "to please": the thing liked is the subject, the person is an indirect object. Me gusta el café = "coffee pleases me".
  • Use gusta with one thing or with activities (me gusta bailar), gustan with several things (me gustan los libros). Nouns take the article.
  • The indirect object pronouns are me, te, le, nos, os, les. No goes before them: no me gusta.
  • Add a él, a ella, a usted, a María to make le and les clear; add a mí, a ti for emphasis. The pronoun stays: A María le gusta.
  • Agree and disagree with a mí también / a mí no after a positive sentence, and a mí tampoco / a mí sí after a negative one.
  • encantar, interesar, molestar, importar, doler work like gustar: me duele la cabeza, me duelen los pies. preferir (e→ie) is a normal verb. jugar (u→ue) is for games and sports, tocar for instruments.

docs.title: 12.8 Exercises
docs.text:
Exercise 1

Complete with gusta or gustan: Me ___ los tomates.

Answer

gustan. Me gustan los tomates. Los tomates is plural.

Exercise 2

Complete with gusta or gustan: ¿Te ___ nadar y correr?

Answer

gusta. ¿Te gusta nadar y correr? Infinitives always take gusta.

Exercise 3

Say "We like the cinema."

Answer

Nos gusta el cine. Nos gusta el cine.

Exercise 4

Complete: A mis abuelos ___ gusta pasear.

Answer

les. A mis abuelos les gusta pasear. Several people: les.

Exercise 5

Your friend says No me gusta el café. You don't like it either. What do you say?

Answer

A mí tampoco. A mí tampoco.

Exercise 6

Your friend says Me encanta la playa. You don't like the beach. What do you say?

Answer

A mí no. A mí no.

Exercise 7

Say "My feet hurt."

Answer

Me duelen los pies. Me duelen los pies. Plural subject, so duelen.

Exercise 8

Correct the mistake: Yo gusto el chocolate.

Answer

Me gusta el chocolate. Me gusta el chocolate. The chocolate is the subject; the person is me.

Exercise 9

Jugar or tocar? (a) ___ el piano; (b) ___ al baloncesto; (c) ___ a las cartas; (d) ___ la batería (the drums). Use the yo form.

Answer

(a) toco el piano; (b) juego al baloncesto; (c) juego a las cartas; (d) toco la batería. Instruments: tocar; games and sports: jugar.

Exercise 10

Write two sentences about Luis: he is interested in art, and he prefers museums to the beach (use preferir … a …).

Answer

A Luis le interesa el arte. Prefiere los museos a la playa. Interesar works like gustar; preferir is a normal verb with Luis as subject.

docs.title: 12.9 Quiz
docs.text:
Quiz: likes and dislikes

Exercise 11

A mi hermana le ___ los perros.

  1. gusta
  2. gustan
  3. gusto
  4. gustas
Answer

gustan

Los perros is plural, so the verb is gustan.

Exercise 12

Someone says "No me gusta el frío." You agree. You say:

  1. A mí también.
  2. A mí tampoco.
  3. A mí sí.
  4. Yo también.
Answer

A mí tampoco.

After a negative sentence, agreement is a mí tampoco.

Exercise 13

¿___ gusta bailar, señor García?

Hint: usted

Answer

Le / le

Usted takes le.

Exercise 14

Me ___ la cabeza.

Hint: doler, o→ue

Answer

duele

La cabeza is singular, so duele.

Exercise 15

Say "I love music" in Spanish, with encantar.

Answer

Me encanta la música / A mí me encanta la música

Exercise 16

Match the Spanish to the English.

ABme interesaI don't mindme molestaI like him or herno me importaI'm interested inme cae bienit bothers me Answer

me interesa — I'm interested in; me molesta — it bothers me; no me importa — I don't mind; me cae bien — I like him or her

Exercise 17

Put the words in order: "My parents like travelling."

Words: A / gusta / mis / viajar. / padres / les

Answer

A mis padres les gusta viajar.

Exercise 18

Tap the wrong word.

A María gusta mucho el teatro.

Answer

Wrong word: gusta.

Corrected: A María le gusta mucho el teatro.

The pronoun le is needed even when the person is named.

Exercise 19

Write what you hear.

Dictation. Have someone read the sentence aloud, then write it down.

Nos encanta ir al cine los domingos.

Answer

Nos encanta ir al cine los domingos.

Exercise 20

Say it aloud.

Me gusta mucho leer, pero prefiero el deporte.

Answer

Say: Me gusta mucho leer, pero prefiero el deporte.

docs.title: Lesson 4: Nouns, Gender and Articles
docs.text:
Los sustantivos, el género y los artículos

Every Spanish noun is either masculine or feminine. A book is masculine, a table is feminine, a problem is masculine and a hand is feminine. This has nothing to do with the things themselves; it is a grammatical class, like the classes of nouns in many other languages, and it decides the form of the words around the noun: the word for "the", the word for "a", and the adjectives. The good news is that the ending of a noun tells you its gender most of the time. In this lesson you learn the rules, the common exceptions, how to make nouns plural, the articles, and the very useful word hay, "there is, there are".

Learning outcomes

By the end of this lesson you will be able to:

  • tell the gender of most nouns from their ending, and remember the common exceptions;
  • make nouns plural, including the spelling and accent changes;
  • use the definite articles el, la, los, las and the indefinite articles un, una, unos, unas;
  • use the contractions al and del, and the rule of el agua;
  • say what there is in a room with hay, and name everyday objects at home and in class.

masculinefeminineplural

docs.title: 4.1 Dialogue: a new flat
docs.text:
Daniel has just moved into a small flat in Salamanca. Lucía comes to see it.

  • Lucía: ¡Hola, Daniel! ¡Qué bonito es el piso! — Hi, Daniel! What a lovely flat!
  • Daniel: Gracias. Es pequeño, pero la cocina es grande. — Thanks. It's small, but the kitchen is big.
  • Lucía: ¿Cuántas habitaciones hay? — How many rooms are there?
  • Daniel: Hay dos habitaciones, un baño, una cocina y un salón. — There are two bedrooms, a bathroom, a kitchen and a living room.
  • Lucía: ¿Y esta es tu habitación? — And is this your room?
  • Daniel: Sí. Hay una cama, una mesa, una silla y unos libros. — Yes. There's a bed, a table, a chair and some books.
  • Lucía: ¡Y el mapa de España en la pared! ¿Y las fotos? — And the map of Spain on the wall! And the photos?
  • Daniel: Son las fotos de mi familia. Y esa es la guitarra de mi hermano. — They're photos of my family. And that's my brother's guitar.
  • Lucía: ¿Hay un sofá en el salón? — Is there a sofa in the living room?
  • Daniel: No, no hay sofá. Hay dos sillas y una lámpara. — No, there's no sofa. There are two chairs and a lamp.
  • Lucía: ¡Es un piso de estudiante! — It's a student flat!
  • Daniel: Sí, pero el problema es la ventana: no hay luz por la mañana. — Yes, but the problem is the window: there's no light in the morning.

Notice:

  1. The word for "the" changes: el piso, la cocina, las fotos. So does the word for "a": un baño, una cama.
  2. Most masculine nouns end in -o and most feminine nouns in -a, but not all: el mapa and el problema are masculine, la foto is feminine.
  3. hay means both "there is" and "there are", and it never changes.

docs.title: 4.2 Vocabulary: at home and in class
At home
docs.text:
Spanish Sounds like English la casa [lah KAH-sah] the house, home el piso [ehl PEE-soh] the flat, apartment (Spain); also the floor, storey la habitación [lah ah-bee-tah-SYOHN] the room; the bedroom la cocina [lah koh-SEE-nah] the kitchen; also the cooker el baño [ehl BAH-nyoh] the bathroom el salón [ehl sah-LOHN] the living room la cama [lah KAH-mah] the bed el sofá [ehl soh-FAH] the sofa la lámpara [lah LAHM-pah-rah] the lamp la puerta [lah PWEHR-tah] the door la ventana [lah behn-TAH-nah] the window la pared [lah pah-REHD] the wall (inside) el espejo [ehl ehs-PEH-hoh] the mirror la nevera [lah neh-BEH-rah] the fridge la llave [lah YAH-beh] the key la televisión [lah teh-leh-bee-SYOHN] the television (often la tele)

Table 4.1. At home. The words are given with their article: learn them that way.

docs.title: In class
docs.text:
Spanish English el libro the book el cuaderno the exercise book, notebook el bolígrafo the pen (often el boli in Spain) el lápiz the pencil la goma the rubber, eraser la mesa the table, desk la silla the chair la pizarra the board (el pizarrón in much of Latin America) la mochila the backpack, school bag el diccionario the dictionary el ordenador the computer (Spain) la computadora the computer (Latin America) el móvil the mobile phone (Spain) el celular the mobile phone (Latin America) el aula the classroom (feminine: see section 4.4)

Table 4.2. In class. Several everyday words differ between Spain and Latin America; both are understood everywhere.

Learn the noun with its article

Never learn mesa on its own: learn la mesa. Make flashcards with the article, or colour the masculine words blue and the feminine words pink, as this book does. The article carries the gender, and it will save you guessing later.

docs.title: The main rule
docs.text:
Nouns ending in -o are masculine; nouns ending in -a are feminine. This covers a large part of the dictionary:

  • masculine: el libro, el piso, el baño, el vaso, el perro
  • feminine: la casa, la mesa, la ventana, la playa, la ciudad

docs.title: Other endings that tell you the gender
docs.text:
Ending Gender Examples -ción, -sión feminine la canción, la estación, la televisión -dad, -tad, -tud feminine la ciudad, la universidad, la libertad, la juventud -umbre feminine la costumbre -or usually masculine el color, el ordenador, el amor (but la flor) -aje masculine el viaje, el garaje, el mensaje -ma (from Greek) masculine el problema, el idioma, el tema, el programa, el sistema, el clima

Table 4.3. Endings that show the gender.

Figure 4.1 Endings and gender. A chart in two columns. The masculine column lists the endings -o, -or, -aje and -ma (from Greek), with the examples el libro, el color, el viaje and el problema. The feminine column lists -a, -ción and -sión, -dad and -tad, -tud and -umbre, with the examples la casa, la canción, la ciudad and la costumbre. Below, a box lists the common exceptions: el día, el mapa, el sofá, el planeta; la mano, la foto, la moto, la radio, la flor.

The -ma rule needs care. Words that came into Spanish from Greek and end in -ma are masculine: el problema, el programa, el idioma ("the language"). Ordinary words ending in -ma are feminine as usual: la cama, la goma, la forma. You cannot always tell the origin, so learn the common -ma masculines as a list.

docs.title: The exceptions to learn now
docs.text:
A handful of very common words break the -o / -a rule:

Masculine, ending in -a Feminine, ending in -o el día — the day la mano — the hand el mapa — the map la foto — the photo (short for la fotografía) el sofá — the sofa la moto — the motorbike (short for la motocicleta) el planeta — the planet la radio — the radio

Table 4.4. Common exceptions. La foto and la moto are feminine because they are short for feminine words.

docs.title: Nouns ending in -e or a consonant
docs.text:
For nouns ending in -e or in most consonants, the ending gives no reliable clue. Learn each one with its article:

  • masculine: el coche, el café, el hotel, el reloj, el lápiz, el autobús, el pan
  • feminine: la noche, la clase, la calle, la llave, la luz, la pared, la sal

docs.title: Nouns for people
docs.text:
For people (and many animals), the gender follows the person:

  • -o / -a: el chico / la chica (boy / girl), el amigo / la amiga, el hermano / la hermana.
  • Consonant + a: el profesor / la profesora, el señor / la señora.
  • One form, two articles. Nouns in -ista, many in -e and -nte do not change; only the article shows the gender: el estudiante / la estudiante, el turista / la turista, el artista / la artista, el policía / la policía.
  • Different words: el padre / la madre, el hombre / la mujer, el rey / la reina.

Changing usage

Some job titles traditionally used one form for both sexes, and today a feminine form is normal: la presidenta, la jefa ("the boss"), la médica (alongside la médico). You will hear both; the forms in -a are now widely accepted.

docs.title: 4.4 Grammar: articles, plurals, al and del, and hay
The articles
docs.text:
Masculine Feminine English definite, singular el libro la mesa the definite, plural los libros las mesas the indefinite, singular un libro una mesa a, an indefinite, plural unos libros unas mesas some, a few

Table 4.5. The articles. Switch on Practice and fill them in.

Three differences from English:

  • "The" for things in general. Spanish uses the definite article for things in general, where English uses none: Me gusta el café ("I like coffee"), Los gatos son independientes ("Cats are independent").
  • No article with jobs after ser. Soy estudiante, "I am a student", without un (Lesson 5).
  • Unos, unas mean "some" or "a few", and often "about" with numbers: unos libros ("some books"), unos veinte euros ("about twenty euros"). Often the article is left out altogether: Hay libros en la mesa ("There are books on the table").

docs.title: Plurals
docs.text:
Rule Singular Plural vowel: add -s el libro, la casa, el café los libros, las casas, los cafés consonant: add -es el hotel, la ciudad, la flor los hoteles, las ciudades, las flores -z: change to -ces el lápiz, la luz, la vez los lápices, las luces, las veces accent dropped la canción, el autobús, el inglés las canciones, los autobuses, los ingleses accent added el joven, el examen los jóvenes, los exámenes unstressed -s: no change el lunes, la crisis los lunes, las crisis

Table 4.6. Making nouns plural.

The accent changes are not extra rules to memorise: they follow from the stress rules of Lesson 1. The stress of the word stays on the same syllable; adding a syllable moves that syllable to a different position, so the written accent may become unnecessary (can-CIÓN → can-CIO-nes) or necessary (JO-ven → JÓ-ve-nes).

A masculine plural can cover a mixed group: los padres is "the parents" (father and mother), los hermanos is "the brothers" or "the brothers and sisters", los chicos can be "the boys" or "the kids".

docs.title: El agua: feminine nouns that take el
docs.text:
Feminine nouns that begin with a stressed a- or ha- take el and un in the singular, simply because la agua would run the two a sounds together:

  • el agua (water), el aula (classroom), el hambre (hunger), el águila (eagle), un arma (a weapon).

The nouns are still feminine. Adjectives are feminine, and the plural goes back to las: el agua fría ("the cold water"), las aulas ("the classrooms"). When the first a is not stressed, the rule does not apply: la amiga, la habitación.

docs.title: Al and del
docs.text:
Two little words join with el:

  • a + el = al: Voy al cine. — I'm going to the cinema.
  • de + el = del: la puerta del baño — the bathroom door (the door of the bathroom)

They are compulsory: never write a el or de el before a noun. But nothing joins with la, los or las: a la playa, de los chicos. And there is no contraction with the pronoun él ("he") or with El in a proper name: el libro de él, Soy de El Salvador.

Spanish has no apostrophe s. "My brother's guitar" is la guitarra de mi hermano, "the guitar of my brother"; "the teacher's book" is el libro del profesor.

docs.title: Hay: there is, there are
docs.text:
hay [eye, like English I] means "there is" and "there are". It has one form only.

  • with a singular noun, use un or una: Hay una farmacia en la calle. — There's a chemist's in the street.
  • with a plural noun, usually no article: Hay libros en la mesa. — There are books on the table.
  • with a number or quantity word: Hay tres sillas. Hay muchos estudiantes.
  • with things you cannot count, no article: Hay agua en la nevera. — There's water in the fridge.
  • questions: ¿Hay un baño aquí? ¿Cuántas sillas hay?
  • negatives, usually without un or una: No hay sofá. No hay leche.

Common mistake: hay with el or la

hay introduces something new, so it does not go with el, la, los or las. "There's the book on the table" is not hay el libro. To say where a particular thing is, use está: El libro está en la mesa. Lesson 5 compares the two.

Worked example: describing a room

Describe a classroom with one board, twelve chairs, a big table and no computer.

  1. One board: la pizarra is feminine, so Hay una pizarra.
  2. Twelve chairs: number, no article: Hay doce sillas.
  3. A big table: Hay una mesa grande. (the adjective follows the noun)
  4. No computer: No hay ordenador. (or computadora in Latin America)

All together: En el aula hay una pizarra, doce sillas y una mesa grande, pero no hay ordenador.

docs.title: Gender
docs.text:
Say each noun with el or la, then check.

Noun With its article Why ventana la ventana -a problema el problema -ma from Greek canción la canción -ción mano la mano exception día el día exception ciudad la ciudad -dad viaje el viaje -aje agua el agua stressed a-: el, but feminine idioma el idioma -ma from Greek foto la foto short for la fotografía

Table 4.7. Practice: el or la?

docs.title: What is there in your room?
docs.text:
Read the description aloud, then describe your own room in the same way.

  • En mi habitación hay una cama, una mesa y dos sillas. — In my room there's a bed, a table and two chairs.
  • En la mesa hay un ordenador, unos libros y una lámpara. — On the table there's a computer, some books and a lamp.
  • En la pared hay un mapa y unas fotos. — On the wall there's a map and some photos.
  • No hay televisión. — There's no television.

Say it

Look around the room you are in and say five sentences with hay and one with no hay. For example:

Hay una puerta y dos ventanas. Hay un sofá. Hay unos libros en la mesa. No hay espejo.

docs.title: 4.6 Culture: one language, many words for home
docs.text:
Flats and rooms. The everyday word for a flat is el piso in Spain, el departamento in Mexico, Argentina, Chile and Peru, and el apartamento in Colombia, Venezuela and the Caribbean (it is also understood in Spain). A bedroom is la habitación or el dormitorio in Spain, el cuarto in much of Latin America, and la recámara in Mexico.

The fridge, the pen and the car. Everyday objects have the most regional names, because each country named them as they arrived. The fridge is la nevera or el frigorífico in Spain, el refrigerador in Mexico and la heladera in Argentina. A ballpoint pen is el bolígrafo in Spain, la pluma in Mexico and la birome in Argentina. A car is el coche in Spain, el carro in Mexico, Colombia and Central America, and el auto in Argentina and Chile. None of these differences stops people understanding each other: they are like flat and apartment, or lift and elevator, in English.

Floors. In Spain a block of flats starts at la planta baja (the ground floor); el primer piso is the floor above it, as in British English. An address such as Calle Mayor 5, 3.º B means number 5, third floor, door B. In much of Latin America, buildings are counted the American way, and the ground floor is el primer piso.

Welcome to my home. When you visit someone, you may hear Estás en tu casa ("You're in your own home") or, in Mexico, Mi casa es su casa ("My house is your house"). They are friendly formulas of welcome; the polite answer is simply Muchas gracias.

docs.title: 4.7 Summary
docs.text:
Summary

  • Gender: nouns in -o are usually masculine, nouns in -a usually feminine. Feminine: -ción, -sión, -dad, -tad, -tud. Masculine: -or, -aje, and Greek words in -ma (el problema, el idioma).
  • Exceptions: el día, el mapa, el sofá; la mano, la foto, la moto, la radio. Learn nouns in -e and consonants with their article.
  • People: el chico / la chica, el profesor / la profesora, el / la estudiante.
  • Articles: el, la, los, las (the); un, una, unos, unas (a, some).
  • Plurals: vowel + s; consonant + es; -z → -ces; accents follow the stress rules (canciones, jóvenes).
  • el agua: feminine nouns starting with stressed a- take el in the singular, but stay feminine.
  • al, del: a + el = al, de + el = del. Possession: el libro de Ana.
  • hay: "there is / there are", one form; with un/una, numbers or no article, never with el/la.

docs.title: 4.8 Exercises
docs.text:
Exercise 1

Give the definite article: ___ problema.

Answer

el. el problema. Greek words in -ma are masculine.

Exercise 2

Give the definite article: ___ mano.

Answer

la. la mano. A common exception: feminine, though it ends in -o.

Exercise 3

Give the plural of el lápiz.

Answer

los lápices. los lápices. Final -z becomes -c before -es.

Exercise 4

Give the plural of la estación.

Answer

las estaciones. las estaciones. The written accent is no longer needed.

Exercise 5

Give the plural of el joven.

Answer

los jóvenes. los jóvenes. The stress stays on the same syllable, which is now third from the end, so it needs an accent.

Exercise 6

Complete with al or del: la puerta ___ salón.

Answer

del. la puerta del salón. de + el = del.

Exercise 7

Translate: "There is cold water in the fridge." (cold: fría)

Answer

Hay agua fría en la nevera. Hay agua fría en la nevera. No article after hay with water, and the adjective is feminine.

Exercise 8

Put un or una before each noun: (a) ___ mapa; (b) ___ ciudad; (c) ___ hotel; (d) ___ foto; (e) ___ aula; (f) ___ estudiante (a woman).

Answer

(a) un mapa; (b) una ciudad; (c) un hotel; (d) una foto; (e) un aula (feminine, but un before stressed a-); (f) una estudiante.

Exercise 9

Correct the mistakes: Hay el libro en la mesa. Es el libro de el profesor.

Answer

El libro está en la mesa. Es el libro del profesor. (Or, for a book that is new to the conversation: Hay un libro en la mesa.) De + el must contract to del.

Exercise 10

Translate: "My sister's room has two windows and a big mirror." Use tiene ("has") and grande ("big").

Answer

La habitación de mi hermana tiene dos ventanas y un espejo grande.

docs.title: 4.9 Quiz
docs.text:
Quiz: nouns, gender and articles

Exercise 11

___ idioma

  1. el
  2. la
  3. los
  4. las
Answer

el

idioma is one of the masculine Greek words in -ma.

Exercise 12

Which noun is feminine?

  1. mapa
  2. día
  3. foto
  4. sofá
Answer

foto

la foto is short for la fotografía. The others are masculine.

Exercise 13

Hay tres ___ en la mesa. (lápiz)

Answer

lápices / lapices

-z becomes -ces in the plural.

Exercise 14

Voy ___ cine y después a ___ playa.

Answer

al · la

a + el = al; a + la does not contract.

Exercise 15

Give the plural, with its article: la canción.

Answer

las canciones

Exercise 16

Match each noun to the right article.

ABproblemalosciudadlasluneselaulasla Answer

problema — el; ciudad — la; lunes — los; aulas — las

Exercise 17

Tap the wrong word.

En mi salón hay el sofá y dos sillas.

Answer

Wrong word: el.

Corrected: En mi salón hay un sofá y dos sillas.

hay is not used with the definite article; use un.

Exercise 18

Put the words in order: "There is a map on the wall."

Words: Hay / en / un / mapa / pared. / la

Answer

Hay un mapa en la pared.

Exercise 19

Write what you hear.

Dictation. Have someone read the sentence aloud, then write it down.

En la cocina hay una mesa y cuatro sillas.

Answer

En la cocina hay una mesa y cuatro sillas.

docs.title: Lesson 3: Numbers, Days, Dates and Time
docs.text:
Los números, los días, las fechas y la hora
