Numbers are everywhere: prices in a shop, the platform of a train, a phone number, the time of a class, your age, your birthday. They are also one of the hardest things to catch when someone speaks quickly, so it pays to practise them until they come without thinking. In this lesson you learn to count from zero to a thousand, to give prices and phone numbers, to name the days and months, to say the date, and to tell the time in the way people do in Spain and in Latin America.

Learning outcomes

By the end of this lesson you will be able to:

  • count from 0 to 1,000 and use uno, un and una correctly;
  • ask and give prices, phone numbers and ages;
  • name the days of the week and the months of the year, and say the date;
  • ask and tell the time, and say at what time something happens;
  • read times written in the 24-hour clock, as in timetables.

masculinefeminineplural

docs.title: 3.1 Dialogue: signing up for a course
docs.text:
Daniel, from Lesson 2, wants to join an extra conversation class at his language school in Salamanca. He goes to the reception desk.

  • Recepcionista: Buenas tardes. ¿Qué desea? — Good afternoon. Can I help you?
  • Daniel: Buenas tardes. Quiero información sobre el curso de conversación. — Good afternoon. I'd like some information about the conversation course.
  • Recepcionista: Sí, claro. Hay clases los martes y los jueves. — Yes, of course. There are classes on Tuesdays and Thursdays.
  • Daniel: ¿A qué hora son las clases? — What time are the classes?
  • Recepcionista: De seis y media a ocho de la tarde. — From half past six to eight in the evening.
  • Daniel: Perfecto. ¿Cuánto cuesta? — Perfect. How much does it cost?
  • Recepcionista: Cuesta ochenta y cinco euros al mes. — It costs eighty-five euros a month.
  • Daniel: ¿Y cuándo empieza el curso? — And when does the course start?
  • Recepcionista: El martes cinco de marzo. ¿Cómo se llama usted? — On Tuesday the fifth of March. What is your name?
  • Daniel: Daniel Brown. Tengo veintiocho años. — Daniel Brown. I'm twenty-eight.
  • Recepcionista: ¿Y su número de teléfono, por favor? — And your phone number, please?
  • Daniel: Es el seis, cuatro, siete, veinte, noventa y uno, cincuenta y tres. — It's 647 20 91 53.
  • Recepcionista: Muy bien. Hasta el martes, Daniel. — Very good. See you on Tuesday, Daniel.
  • Daniel: ¡Hasta el martes! Gracias. — See you on Tuesday! Thanks.

Before the explanations, notice:

  1. "On Tuesday" has no word for "on". Spanish says el martes ("the Tuesday") for one Tuesday and los martes ("the Tuesdays") for every Tuesday.
  2. The date puts the day first: el cinco de marzo, "the five of March". Months and days are written with a small letter.
  3. Daniel "has" his age: tengo veintiocho años, literally "I have twenty-eight years". Spanish never says soy veintiocho.
  4. Two verbs in the dialogue, cuesta ("it costs") and empieza ("it begins"), belong to a family of verbs whose vowel changes. Learn them as phrases for now; Lesson 10 explains them.

docs.title: 0 to 30
docs.text:
Spanish Sounds like Spanish Sounds like 0 cero [SEH-roh] 16 dieciséis [dyeh-see-SAYS] 1 uno [OO-noh] 17 diecisiete [dyeh-see-SYEH-teh] 2 dos [dohs] 18 dieciocho [dyeh-SYOH-choh] 3 tres [trehs] 19 diecinueve [dyeh-see-NWEH-beh] 4 cuatro [KWAH-troh] 20 veinte [BAYN-teh] 5 cinco [SEEN-koh] 21 veintiuno [bayn-TYOO-noh] 6 seis [says] 22 veintidós [bayn-tee-DOHS] 7 siete [SYEH-teh] 23 veintitrés [bayn-tee-TREHS] 8 ocho [OH-choh] 24 veinticuatro [bayn-tee-KWAH-troh] 9 nueve [NWEH-beh] 25 veinticinco [bayn-tee-SEEN-koh] 10 diez [dyehs] 26 veintiséis [bayn-tee-SAYS] 11 once [OHN-seh] 27 veintisiete [bayn-tee-SYEH-teh] 12 doce [DOH-seh] 28 veintiocho [bayn-TYOH-choh] 13 trece [TREH-seh] 29 veintinueve [bayn-tee-NWEH-beh] 14 catorce [kah-TOR-seh] 30 treinta [TRAYN-tah] 15 quince [KEEN-seh]

Table 3.1. The numbers from 0 to 30. In Spain the c and z of cinco, once, diez are said like English th: [THEEN-koh], [OHN-theh], [dyehth].

Look at the patterns, which make the list much easier to learn:

  • 11 to 15 are single words to learn by heart: once, doce, trece, catorce, quince.
  • 16 to 19 are "ten and six", "ten and seven" squeezed into one word: dieci-séis, dieci-siete. The z of diez becomes c.
  • 21 to 29 are "twenty and one" squeezed the same way: veinti-uno, veinti-dós. Note the written accents on dieciséis, veintidós, veintitrés and veintiséis: they are needed because these words end in a stressed vowel or s.

docs.title: 30 to 100: the tens
docs.text:
Spanish Sounds like Example 30 treinta [TRAYN-tah] treinta y uno (31) 40 cuarenta [kwah-REHN-tah] cuarenta y dos (42) 50 cincuenta [seen-KWEHN-tah] cincuenta y tres (53) 60 sesenta [seh-SEHN-tah] sesenta y cuatro (64) 70 setenta [seh-TEHN-tah] setenta y cinco (75) 80 ochenta [oh-CHEHN-tah] ochenta y seis (86) 90 noventa [noh-BEHN-tah] noventa y nueve (99) 100 cien [syehn] cien euros (100 euros)

Table 3.2. The tens. From 31 onwards, the units are added with y, "and", as separate words.

Common mistake: sesenta and setenta

sesenta (60) and setenta (70) sound alike. Link them to the units: seis → sesenta, siete → setenta. In the same way, seis and siete are often confused at first.

docs.title: 100 to 1,000
docs.text:
Spanish Spanish 100 cien 500 quinientos 101 ciento uno 600 seiscientos 150 ciento cincuenta 700 setecientos 200 doscientos 800 ochocientos 300 trescientos 900 novecientos 400 cuatrocientos 1.000 mil

Table 3.3. The hundreds. Three are irregular: quinientos (not cincocientos), setecientos and novecientos.

Four rules for the big numbers:

  1. Cien or ciento? Exactly 100 is cien: cien personas, cien libros. Anything from 101 to 199 starts with ciento: ciento veinte. There is no y after the hundreds: 120 is ciento veinte, never ciento y veinte.
  2. The hundreds agree. From 200 to 900 the hundreds have a feminine form in -as before a feminine noun: doscientos euros but doscientas personas; quinientas páginas.
  3. Mil does not change. 2,000 is dos mil, not dos miles. Years are said like any other number: 2025 is dos mil veinticinco, 1998 is mil novecientos noventa y ocho.
  4. Point and comma. Spain writes 1.000 for a thousand and 3,50 € for three euros fifty. Mexico and several other countries write it the English way, 1,000 and 3.50.

docs.title: Uno, un, una
docs.text:
The number "one" changes with the noun that follows:

  • before a masculine noun it is un: un café, veintiún años (note the accent);
  • before a feminine noun it is una: una cerveza, veintiuna personas;
  • when counting, or with no noun after it, it is uno: uno, dos, tres; ¿Cuántos cafés? — Uno.

docs.title: 3.3 Grammar: prices, phone numbers and age
How much is it?
docs.text:
Spanish English ¿Cuánto cuesta? How much does it cost? (one thing) ¿Cuánto cuestan? How much do they cost? (several things) ¿Cuánto es? How much is it? (asking for the total) Cuesta tres euros. It costs three euros. Son doce euros con cincuenta. That's twelve euros fifty. Es muy caro. / Es barato. It's very expensive. / It's cheap.

Table 3.4. Asking about prices.

To say a price with cents, the euro and the cents are joined by con ("with"), or simply put side by side: 4,75 € is cuatro euros con setenta y cinco or cuatro setenta y cinco. The cents are céntimos in Spain and centavos in Latin America. Spain uses the euro; most Latin American countries have a currency of their own, often called the peso (Mexico, Argentina, Colombia, Chile and others). The word for money itself is dinero, and in much of Latin America also plata.

docs.title: Phone numbers
docs.text:
People read phone numbers in different ways: one digit at a time, or in pairs. A Spanish mobile number such as 647 20 91 53 can be read as seis, cuatro, siete, veinte, noventa y uno, cincuenta y tres. If you are not sure, ask for one digit at a time: Más despacio, por favor. Número por número. ("More slowly, please. Number by number.")

  • ¿Cuál es tu número de teléfono? — What's your phone number? (tú)
  • ¿Cuál es su número de teléfono? — What's your phone number? (usted)
  • Mi número es el cinco, cinco, cero, dos, ocho, uno, nueve. — My number is 550 2819.
  • ¿Me lo repites, por favor? — Can you repeat it for me, please?

docs.title: How old are you?
docs.text:
Age is something you "have" in Spanish, with the verb tener, "to have". Learn these forms as phrases now; Lesson 10 gives the whole verb.

Spanish English ¿Cuántos años tienes? How old are you? (tú) ¿Cuántos años tiene usted? How old are you? (usted) Tengo diecinueve años. I'm nineteen (years old). Mi hermana tiene treinta y un años. My sister is thirty-one. El bebé tiene seis meses. The baby is six months old.

Table 3.5. Talking about age.

Common mistake: age with ser

"I am twenty" is tengo veinte años, never soy veinte. And do not drop años in a full sentence: Tengo veinte años. (In a quick reply, Veinte. on its own is fine.) Note also treinta y un años: uno becomes un before the masculine noun años.

Año and ano

Pronounce the ñ carefully: años [AH-nyohs] means "years". Without the tilde, the word is a rude word for a part of the body. This is the classic beginner's slip, and the reason the tilde matters.

docs.title: 3.4 Grammar: days, months, dates and the time
Days of the week
docs.text:
Spanish English Sounds like lunes Monday [LOO-nehs] martes Tuesday [MAR-tehs] miércoles Wednesday [MYEHR-koh-lehs] jueves Thursday [HWEH-behs] viernes Friday [BYEHR-nehs] sábado Saturday [SAH-bah-doh] domingo Sunday [doh-MEEN-goh]

Table 3.6. The days of the week. The week starts on Monday.

The days are masculine and written with a small letter. Use the article to say "on":

  • El lunes tengo clase. — On Monday I have class. (this Monday)
  • Los lunes tengo clase. — On Mondays I have class. (every Monday)
  • el fin de semana — the weekend; de lunes a viernes — from Monday to Friday
  • hoy, mañana, ayer — today, tomorrow, yesterday
  • ¿Qué día es hoy? — Hoy es jueves. — What day is it today? — Today is Thursday.

The days ending in -s do not change in the plural: el martes, los martes. Only sábado and domingo add -s: los sábados, los domingos.

docs.title: Months of the year
docs.text:
Spanish English Spanish English enero January julio July febrero February agosto August marzo March septiembre September abril April octubre October mayo May noviembre November junio June diciembre December

Table 3.7. The months, written with a small letter. The spelling setiembre is also accepted, and is common in some countries.

docs.title: The date
docs.text:
The pattern is el + number + de + month (+ de + year):

  • el cinco de mayo — the fifth of May
  • el veinticuatro de diciembre de dos mil veinticuatro — 24 December 2024
  • ¿Qué fecha es hoy? — Es el doce de octubre. — What's the date today? — It's the twelfth of October.
  • ¿Cuándo es tu cumpleaños? — Es el treinta de junio. — When is your birthday? — It's the thirtieth of June.
  • en agosto, en dos mil diez — in August, in 2010

Spanish uses ordinary numbers for dates, not "first, second, third". The one exception is the first of the month: Spain usually says el uno de enero, while much of Latin America says el primero de enero. Both are correct. When the date is written in figures, the day always comes first: 5/3 is the fifth of March, not the third of May.

docs.title: What time is it?
docs.text:
To ask the time, say ¿Qué hora es? The answer uses the verb ser and the feminine article, because hora ("hour") is feminine:

  • one o'clock is singular: Es la una.
  • every other hour is plural: Son las dos. Son las diez.

Minutes past the hour are added with y ("and"); minutes to the next hour are taken away with menos ("minus"). Quarter is cuarto, half is media.

Figure 3.1 Telling the time. A clock face divided into two halves. On the right half, minutes are added to the hour with y: y cinco, y diez, y cuarto at the quarter past position, y veinte, y veinticinco, and y media at the bottom. On the left half, minutes are taken away from the next hour with menos: menos veinticinco, menos veinte, menos cuarto at the quarter to position, menos diez and menos cinco. At the top is en punto. Time Spanish Literally 1:00 Es la una en punto. It is the one exactly. 2:05 Son las dos y cinco. They are the two and five. 3:15 Son las tres y cuarto. three and a quarter 4:20 Son las cuatro y veinte. four and twenty 5:30 Son las cinco y media. five and a half 6:40 Son las siete menos veinte. seven minus twenty 7:45 Son las ocho menos cuarto. eight minus a quarter 12:55 Es la una menos cinco. one minus five 12:00 Es mediodía. / Es medianoche. It's midday. / It's midnight.

Table 3.8. Telling the time. With menos, think of the next hour: 6:40 is "seven minus twenty".

To show the part of the day, add:

  • de la mañana — in the morning (until midday)
  • de la tarde — in the afternoon and early evening (until about 8 or 9 p.m.)
  • de la noche — at night
  • de la madrugada — in the small hours, after midnight

So 4 p.m. is las cuatro de la tarde and 4 a.m. is las cuatro de la madrugada.

docs.title: At what time?
docs.text:
To ask when something happens, use ¿A qué hora …?; the answer starts with a:

  • ¿A qué hora es la clase? — A las nueve y media. — What time is the class? — At half past nine.
  • ¿A qué hora abre el banco? — A las ocho y media. — What time does the bank open? — At half past eight.
  • La película es a la una. — The film is at one.
  • La tienda abre de nueve a dos. — The shop is open from nine to two.

Common mistake: qué hora es vs a qué hora

¿Qué hora es? asks for the time now. ¿A qué hora …? asks when something happens. Answer the first with Son las … and the second with A las …

docs.title: The 24-hour clock
docs.text:
Timetables, tickets, cinema programmes and official notices use the 24-hour clock, and the times are read out as plain numbers, without y cuarto or menos:

Written Read aloud In everyday speech 08:10 las ocho diez las ocho y diez de la mañana 13:30 las trece treinta la una y media de la tarde 17:45 las diecisiete cuarenta y cinco las seis menos cuarto de la tarde 21:15 las veintiuna quince las nueve y cuarto de la noche

Table 3.9. The 24-hour clock. Note las veintiuna (feminine, agreeing with horas).

  • El tren a Madrid sale a las diecisiete cuarenta y cinco. — The train to Madrid leaves at 17:45.

Worked example: reading a timetable

A bus timetable says Salamanca – Ávila: 09:15, 14:30, 19:50. Your friend asks ¿A qué hora hay autobuses?

  1. Read the times as numbers: a las nueve quince, a las catorce treinta y a las diecinueve cincuenta.
  2. Or say them in everyday style: a las nueve y cuarto de la mañana, a las dos y media de la tarde y a las ocho menos diez de la tarde.

Both answers are correct. The first is what you hear at the station; the second is what you hear from friends.

docs.title: Counting aloud
docs.text:
Say each line aloud, then cover the Spanish and say it from the figures.

  • dos, cuatro, seis, ocho, diez, doce, catorce, dieciséis, dieciocho, veinte — 2, 4, 6 … 20
  • diez, veinte, treinta, cuarenta, cincuenta, sesenta, setenta, ochenta, noventa, cien — 10, 20 … 100
  • cien, doscientos, trescientos, cuatrocientos, quinientos, seiscientos, setecientos, ochocientos, novecientos, mil — 100, 200 … 1,000

docs.title: Practice table: the time
docs.text:
Clock Spanish 1:00 Es la una. 2:10 Son las dos y diez. 3:15 Son las tres y cuarto. 5:30 Son las cinco y media. 8:35 Son las nueve menos veinticinco. 10:45 Son las once menos cuarto. 12:50 Es la una menos diez.

Table 3.10. Switch on Practice and write each time in words.

docs.title: Practice table: the hundreds
docs.text:
Number Masculine Feminine 200 doscientos euros doscientas personas 300 trescientos libros trescientas casas 500 quinientos años quinientas páginas 700 setecientos kilómetros setecientas palabras 900 novecientos metros novecientas botellas

Table 3.11. The hundreds agree with the noun.

Say it

Answer aloud, in full sentences:

  • ¿Cuántos años tienes?
  • ¿Cuándo es tu cumpleaños?
  • ¿Qué hora es ahora?
  • ¿Qué días tienes clase?

For example: Tengo treinta y dos años. Mi cumpleaños es el nueve de abril. Son las cinco y cuarto. Tengo clase los lunes y los miércoles.

docs.title: 3.6 Culture: the Spanish day and the Latin American clock
docs.text:
A late timetable. Spain keeps a famously late timetable. Many people have a light breakfast, a mid-morning snack, lunch (la comida) between about 2 and 3 p.m., and dinner (la cena) at 9 p.m. or later. Shops in smaller towns often close for a few hours in the afternoon and open again until 8 or 8.30 p.m. That is why la tarde stretches so far into what English speakers call the evening, and why buenas tardes can be heard at eight o'clock. In most of Latin America the meal times are closer to those of the English-speaking world, though lunch is still often the main meal of the day.

Other ways to tell the time. In Latin America you will often hear minutes "for" the next hour instead of menos: Son veinte para las tres or Faltan veinte para las tres ("It's twenty to three"). Digital-style times such as las dos y quince or las dos y cuarenta y cinco are also common everywhere, especially among younger speakers.

Punctuality. Ideas about being on time vary. For work, classes, trains and appointments, be on time as you would at home. For a party at a friend's house, arriving a little after the stated time is normal in much of the Spanish-speaking world; your hosts will not be ready at the exact minute. If you want to stress that a time is exact, add en punto.

Dates to know. Some dates are so important that they are known simply by the day and month. In Mexico, el dieciséis de septiembre is Independence Day; el cinco de mayo commemorates the Battle of Puebla of 1862, and is more widely celebrated in the United States than in Mexico itself. In Spain, el seis de enero, the feast of the Three Kings (los Reyes Magos), is the traditional day for giving presents to children. In many countries, el doce de octubre is a public holiday, celebrated under different names.

Unlucky days. In English-speaking countries Friday the thirteenth is unlucky. In Spain and much of Latin America the unlucky day is Tuesday the thirteenth: martes y trece. A saying warns En martes, ni te cases ni te embarques: "On a Tuesday, neither marry nor set sail."

docs.title: 3.7 Summary
docs.text:
Summary

  • 0 to 30: learn 11 to 15 by heart; 16 to 19 are dieci- + unit; 21 to 29 are veinti- + unit, written as one word.
  • 31 to 99: tens + y + unit, as separate words: cuarenta y siete. 100 is cien, 101 to 199 ciento …; 200 to 900 agree (doscientas personas); mil never changes.
  • One: un before a masculine noun, una before a feminine noun, uno when counting.
  • Prices and age: ¿Cuánto cuesta? ¿Cuánto es? Age uses tener: Tengo veinte años.
  • Days and months are written with a small letter. el lunes = on Monday; los lunes = on Mondays. Dates: el cinco de mayo.
  • Time: ¿Qué hora es? — Es la una. Son las dos y cuarto. Son las tres menos cuarto. At what time: ¿A qué hora …? — A las ocho. Timetables use the 24-hour clock, read as plain numbers.

docs.title: 3.8 Exercises
docs.text:
Exercise 1

Write 15 in Spanish.

Answer

quince. quince

Exercise 2

Write 76 in Spanish.

Answer

setenta y seis. setenta y seis. From 31 onwards, the tens and units are separate words joined by y.

Exercise 3

Write 500 in Spanish.

Answer

quinientos. quinientos. It is irregular: not cincocientos.

Exercise 4

How do you say "two hundred houses"? (house: casa, feminine)

Answer

doscientas casas. doscientas casas. The hundreds agree with a feminine noun.

Exercise 5

Say "I'm twenty-one" in Spanish.

Answer

Tengo veintiún años. Tengo veintiún años. Age uses tener, and veintiuno becomes veintiún before the masculine noun años.

Exercise 6

Write the time 4:30 in words, in a full sentence.

Answer

Son las cuatro y media. Son las cuatro y media.

Exercise 7

Write the time 9:45 in words, using menos.

Answer

Son las diez menos cuarto. Son las diez menos cuarto. With menos, count back from the next hour.

Exercise 8

Give the date "the 3rd of February" in Spanish.

Answer

el tres de febrero. el tres de febrero. Ordinary number, de, and the month with a small letter.

Exercise 9

Translate: (a) On Saturdays I don't have class. (b) The film is at a quarter past ten at night. (c) The shop opens from nine to two. (Use no tengo clase, la película, la tienda abre.)

Answer

(a) Los sábados no tengo clase. (b) La película es a las diez y cuarto de la noche. (c) La tienda abre de nueve a dos.

Exercise 10

A train ticket says Salida 18:20. Say the time (a) as it is announced at the station, and (b) in everyday style.

Answer

(a) a las dieciocho veinte; (b) a las seis y veinte de la tarde.

docs.title: 3.9 Quiz
docs.text:
Quiz: numbers, days, dates and time

Exercise 11

Which number is setenta?

  1. 60
  2. 70
  3. 17
  4. 700
Answer

70

setenta is 70; sesenta is 60; setecientos is 700.

Exercise 12

It is 1:20. You say:

  1. Son la una y veinte.
  2. Es la una y veinte.
  3. Es las una y veinte.
  4. Son las uno y veinte.
Answer

Es la una y veinte.

One o'clock is singular, es la una; every other hour is plural, son las.

Exercise 13

Tengo ___ años. (31)

Hint: uno changes before a masculine noun.

Answer

treinta y un

treinta y uno becomes treinta y un before años.

Exercise 14

Write 100 euros in Spanish words.

Answer

cien euros

Exactly 100 is cien.

Exercise 15

Match each day to its English name.

ABmiércolesSaturdayjuevesSundaysábadoWednesdaydomingoThursday Answer

miércoles — Wednesday; jueves — Thursday; sábado — Saturday; domingo — Sunday

Exercise 16

Put the words in order: "My birthday is on the tenth of July."

Words: diez / de / el / julio. / Mi / cumpleaños / es

Answer

Mi cumpleaños es el diez de julio.

Exercise 17

Tap the wrong word.

La clase es el lunes, quince de Marzo.

Answer

Wrong word: Marzo.

Corrected: La clase es el lunes, quince de marzo.

Months are written with a small letter in Spanish.

Exercise 18

Write what you hear.

Dictation. Have someone read the sentence aloud, then write it down.

El tren sale a las ocho y cuarto.

Answer

El tren sale a las ocho y cuarto.

Exercise 19

Say it aloud.

Hoy es martes, doce de octubre.

Answer

Say: Hoy es martes, doce de octubre.

docs.title: Lesson 6: The Present Tense of Regular Verbs
docs.text:
El presente de los verbos regulares

Until now you have used verbs as fixed phrases: me llamo, soy de, tengo veinte años. In this lesson you learn the system behind them. Spanish verbs change their ending to show who is doing the action: hablo is "I speak", hablas "you speak", hablamos "we speak". Because the ending already tells you the person, the pronoun is usually left out. There are three families of verbs, ending in -ar, -er and -ir, and once you know the pattern of each you can use hundreds of verbs. You will also learn to make sentences negative, to ask questions, and to use the question words.

Learning outcomes

By the end of this lesson you will be able to:

  • conjugate regular -ar, -er and -ir verbs in the present tense;
  • use about forty common regular verbs to talk about your everyday life;
  • make a sentence negative with no;
  • ask yes/no questions and questions with qué, quién, dónde, cuándo, cómo, cuánto, cuál and por qué;
  • use the present for habits, for what is happening now and for the near future, and say how often you do things.

docs.title: 6.1 Dialogue: a language exchange
docs.text:
Daniel has found a partner for a language exchange (un intercambio): Javier, a student who wants to practise English. They meet in a café; the first half hour is in Spanish.

  • Javier: Hola, Daniel. ¿Hablamos en español primero? — Hi, Daniel. Shall we speak Spanish first?
  • Daniel: Sí, perfecto. Después hablamos en inglés. — Yes, perfect. Then we'll speak English.
  • Javier: ¿Dónde vives? — Where do you live?
  • Daniel: Vivo en un piso en el centro. ¿Y tú? — I live in a flat in the centre. And you?
  • Javier: Vivo con mis padres, cerca de la universidad. Estudio medicina. — I live with my parents, near the university. I study medicine.
  • Daniel: ¿Trabajas también? — Do you work as well?
  • Javier: Sí, trabajo los sábados en una librería. ¿Y tú? — Yes, I work on Saturdays in a bookshop. And you?
  • Daniel: No, no trabajo. Estudio español todas las mañanas. — No, I don't work. I study Spanish every morning.
  • Javier: ¿Y por la tarde? — And in the afternoon?
  • Daniel: Por la tarde leo, escribo correos y escucho música. A veces corro en el parque. — In the afternoon I read, write emails and listen to music. Sometimes I run in the park.
  • Javier: ¿Comes en casa? — Do you eat at home?
  • Daniel: Normalmente sí, pero los viernes como con mis compañeros en un restaurante. — Usually, yes, but on Fridays I eat with my classmates in a restaurant.
  • Javier: ¿Qué idiomas hablas? — What languages do you speak?
  • Daniel: Hablo inglés, claro, y un poco de francés. ¿Tú hablas francés? — English, of course, and a little French. Do you speak French?
  • Javier: No, no hablo francés. Pero aprendo inglés en una academia. — No, I don't speak French. But I'm learning English at a language school.
  • Daniel: ¿Comemos juntos el viernes? — Shall we have lunch together on Friday?
  • Javier: ¡Vale! El viernes comemos juntos. — OK! On Friday we'll have lunch together.

Notice:

  1. The endings change with the person: vivo (I) but vives (you); como (I) but comes (you); hablamos (we).
  2. There is no word for "do" in questions or negatives: "Do you work?" is just ¿Trabajas?, and "I don't work" is No trabajo.
  3. One Spanish present covers several English forms: aprendo inglés is "I learn English" or "I'm learning English", and el viernes comemos juntos is "on Friday we're having lunch together".

docs.title: -ar verbs (the largest family)
docs.text:
Spanish English Spanish English hablar to speak, talk escuchar to listen (to) trabajar to work mirar to look (at), watch estudiar to study tomar to take; to have (a drink) comprar to buy necesitar to need cocinar to cook llegar to arrive desayunar to have breakfast esperar to wait (for); to hope cenar to have dinner llamar to call, phone bailar to dance viajar to travel cantar to sing visitar to visit enseñar to teach; to show ayudar to help

Table 6.1. Regular -ar verbs.

docs.title: -er verbs
docs.text:
Spanish English Spanish English comer to eat; to have lunch aprender to learn beber to drink comprender to understand leer to read correr to run vender to sell creer to believe, think deber to have to, must; to owe responder to answer

Table 6.2. Regular -er verbs.

docs.title: -ir verbs
docs.text:
Spanish English Spanish English vivir to live recibir to receive, get escribir to write compartir to share abrir to open subir to go up, climb; to upload decidir to decide asistir a to attend

Table 6.3. Regular -ir verbs.

docs.title: Other useful words
docs.text:
Spanish English el idioma, la lengua language la librería bookshop (not library!) la biblioteca library el compañero, la compañera classmate, colleague, flatmate el correo email; post, mail un poco de a little (of) juntos, juntas together vale OK (Spain)

Table 6.4. Other words from the dialogue.

False friends

la librería is a bookshop; a library is la biblioteca. Other traps among the verbs: asistir a means "to attend", not "to assist" (that is ayudar), and realizar means "to carry out", not "to realise". Words that look alike in two languages but mean different things are called false friends.

docs.title: 6.3 Grammar: the three conjugations
docs.text:
Every verb has a stem and an ending. In the dictionary form, the infinitive, the ending is -ar, -er or -ir: habl-ar, com-er, viv-ir. To make the present tense, take off the -ar, -er or -ir and add the ending for the person.

Figure 6.1 The present tense endings. A diagram of the present tense endings. The stems habl-, com- and viv- are on the left. Three columns show the endings for each person. For -ar verbs: -o, -as, -a, -amos, -áis, -an. For -er verbs: -o, -es, -e, -emos, -éis, -en. For -ir verbs: -o, -es, -e, -imos, -ís, -en. The -er and -ir columns are the same except for the nosotros and vosotros forms, which are highlighted. Person hablar comer vivir yo hablo como vivo tú hablas comes vives él, ella, usted habla come vive nosotros, nosotras hablamos comemos vivimos vosotros, vosotras habláis coméis vivís ellos, ellas, ustedes hablan comen viven

Table 6.5. The present tense of regular verbs. Switch on Practice and fill in the endings.

  • Hablo, hablas, habla, hablamos, habláis, hablan.
  • Como, comes, come, comemos, coméis, comen.
  • Vivo, vives, vive, vivimos, vivís, viven.

Five things make the table easier than it looks:

  1. The yo form always ends in -o, for all three families.
  2. The vowel of the family appears in the endings: a for -ar verbs, e for -er verbs.
  3. -er and -ir verbs share four endings. They differ only in the nosotros form (comemos / vivimos) and the vosotros form (coméis / vivís), where the -ir verbs keep their i.
  4. Usted goes with the él form, ustedes with the ellos form: ¿Habla usted inglés? ¿Viven ustedes aquí?
  5. The stress falls on the stem in four forms (HA-blo, HA-blas, HA-bla, HA-blan) and on the ending in the nosotros and vosotros forms (ha-BLA-mos, ha-BLÁIS). Do not stress the ending of hablo: habló, with the stress on the end, is a different tense (Lesson 15).

Common mistake: keeping the infinitive

Beginners often say yo hablar or yo hablo where Spanish only needs hablo. Drop the -ar, -er or -ir, add the ending, and leave out the pronoun unless you need it for emphasis or contrast: Yo trabajo y tú estudias.

Worked example: conjugating a new verb

Conjugate aprender ("to learn") for nosotros and for ellos.

  1. Family: -er. Stem: aprend-.
  2. nosotros: -emos → aprendemos, "we learn".
  3. ellos: -en → aprenden, "they learn".

Now the same with escribir: stem escrib-, -ir family → escribimos, escriben.

docs.title: What the present tense means
docs.text:
The Spanish present covers more ground than the English present simple:

Use Example English habits and routines Trabajo los sábados. I work on Saturdays. facts Los españoles cenan tarde. Spaniards have dinner late. what is happening now ¿Qué lees? — Leo una novela. What are you reading? — I'm reading a novel. the near future, with a time word Mañana visito a mi abuela. Tomorrow I'm visiting my grandmother. suggestions, in questions ¿Tomamos un café? Shall we have a coffee?

Table 6.6. The uses of the present tense.

Personal a

When the object of a verb is a specific person, Spanish puts a before it: Visito a mi abuela ("I visit my grandmother"), Llamo a Javier, Ayudo a mis padres. It is not translated. With things there is no a: Visito el museo.

docs.title: 6.4 Grammar: negatives, questions and question words
Negatives
docs.text:
To make a sentence negative, put no directly before the verb:

  • Hablo francés. → No hablo francés. — I don't speak French.
  • Mis padres viven aquí. → Mis padres no viven aquí. — My parents don't live here.
  • ¿Trabajas? — No, no trabajo. — Do you work? — No, I don't. The first no answers the question; the second makes the verb negative.

Some negative words can come before the verb on their own, or after it with no in front. Unlike standard English, Spanish is happy with this double negative:

  • Nunca como carne. = No como carne nunca. — I never eat meat.
  • No bebo nada. — I don't drink anything. (literally "I don't drink nothing")

docs.title: Yes/no questions
docs.text:
A yes/no question has the same words as a statement; only the voice rises at the end, and the writing adds ¿ ?:

  • Hablas español. — You speak Spanish.
  • ¿Hablas español? — Do you speak Spanish?

The subject, if there is one, can stay before the verb or go after it: ¿Tu hermano vive en Madrid? and ¿Vive tu hermano en Madrid? both mean "Does your brother live in Madrid?" To check something, add ¿verdad? or, in Spain, ¿no?: Vives en el centro, ¿verdad? ("You live in the centre, don't you?")

docs.title: Question words
docs.text:
Spanish English Example ¿qué? what? which? ¿Qué estudias? — What do you study? ¿quién?, ¿quiénes? who? ¿Quién habla? — Who's speaking? ¿dónde? where? ¿Dónde vives? — Where do you live? ¿adónde? where to? ¿Adónde viajas? — Where are you travelling to? ¿de dónde? where from? ¿De dónde eres? — Where are you from? ¿cuándo? when? ¿Cuándo llegas? — When do you arrive? ¿cómo? how? what … like? ¿Cómo se llama? — What's his name? ¿cuánto?, ¿cuánta? how much? ¿Cuánto cuesta? — How much is it? ¿cuántos?, ¿cuántas? how many? ¿Cuántas lenguas hablas? — How many languages do you speak? ¿cuál?, ¿cuáles? which? what? ¿Cuál es tu número? — What's your number? ¿por qué? why? ¿Por qué estudias español? — Why are you studying Spanish?

Table 6.7. Question words. All of them carry a written accent.

Three points:

  • Accents. Every question word has a written accent, which distinguishes it from the same word used without a question: ¿Dónde vives? but la casa donde vivo ("the house where I live").
  • Cuánto agrees with the noun: ¿Cuántos libros?, ¿Cuántas personas?
  • Por qué and porque. "Why?" is two words with an accent, ¿por qué?; "because" is one word without, porque: ¿Por qué estudias español? — Porque viajo mucho a México.

Qué or cuál?

Before a noun, use qué: ¿Qué idiomas hablas? Before ser, "what is…?" asking for a piece of information is usually ¿Cuál es…?: ¿Cuál es tu dirección? ("What is your address?"). ¿Qué es…? asks for a definition: ¿Qué es una librería? ("What is a librería?").

docs.title: How often?
docs.text:
Spanish English siempre always normalmente usually a menudo often a veces sometimes casi nunca hardly ever nunca never todos los días every day una vez a la semana once a week dos veces al mes twice a month

Table 6.8. Saying how often.

These words usually go at the beginning or the end of the sentence: A veces cocino yo. Corro en el parque dos veces a la semana.

docs.title: A preview: verbs that change
docs.text: Not every verb is regular. You have already met a few that change their stem: cuesta (from costar), empieza (from empezar), tengo (from tener). Their endings are still the ones in this lesson; only the stem changes. Lesson 10 explains them. For now, if a verb in this book is not marked as irregular, it follows the patterns of Table 6.5.

docs.title: Conjugate
docs.text:
Person trabajar beber escribir yo trabajo bebo escribo tú trabajas bebes escribes él, ella, usted trabaja bebe escribe nosotros, nosotras trabajamos bebemos escribimos vosotros, vosotras trabajáis bebéis escribís ellos, ellas, ustedes trabajan beben escriben

Table 6.9. Practice: three more verbs.

docs.title: Questions and answers
docs.text:
Read each question and answer aloud. Then answer the questions about yourself.

  • ¿Dónde vives? — Vivo en Londres. — Where do you live? — I live in London.
  • ¿Qué idiomas hablas? — Hablo inglés y un poco de español. — What languages do you speak? — English and a little Spanish.
  • ¿Trabajas o estudias? — Trabajo en un banco. — Do you work or study? — I work in a bank.
  • ¿Cuándo estudias español? — Estudio por la noche. — When do you study Spanish? — I study at night.
  • ¿Por qué aprendes español? — Porque viajo mucho. — Why are you learning Spanish? — Because I travel a lot.
  • ¿Lees mucho? — Sí, leo todos los días. — Do you read a lot? — Yes, I read every day.

Say it

Describe a normal week in five sentences, using at least one -ar, one -er and one -ir verb, a negative, and a frequency word. For example:

Trabajo de lunes a viernes. Normalmente como en casa. Los sábados escribo correos y leo. A veces cocino para mis amigos. Nunca trabajo los domingos.

docs.title: 6.6 Culture: language exchanges and new verbs
docs.text:
Intercambios. In most Spanish-speaking cities you will find intercambios: meetings, in a bar or café or online, where people who want to practise each other's language talk for half the time in one language and half in the other. They are free, friendly and one of the best ways to use the Spanish of this book with real people. The usual first questions are exactly those of this lesson: ¿De dónde eres? ¿Dónde vives? ¿Trabajas o estudias? ¿Por qué aprendes español?

Saying OK. Spaniards say vale dozens of times a day; it is the Spanish "OK". In Mexico you will hear sale among friends, in Argentina and Uruguay dale, and almost everywhere bueno or de acuerdo, which is also the neutral choice. "OK" itself is widely used too.

New verbs are -ar verbs. When Spanish makes a new verb, almost always from English, it joins the -ar family and is perfectly regular: chatear ("to chat online"), tuitear, escanear, googlear. So once you know hablar, you can already conjugate verbs that did not exist a few decades ago: chateo, chateas, chatea…

Living at home. Javier, in the dialogue, lives with his parents while he studies. This is common in Spain and in much of Latin America, where many students attend a university in their own city and young people often live in the family home until they are working or married. Saying vivo con mis padres at twenty-five carries no embarrassment.

Formal questions. When you speak to someone as usted, the verb is the él form, so questions can be ambiguous: ¿Habla inglés? can mean "Does he speak English?" or "Do you speak English?" Spanish speakers add usted when they need to be clear, especially in shops and offices: ¿Habla usted inglés?

docs.title: 6.7 Summary
docs.text:
Summary

  • Regular present tense: stem + ending. -ar: -o, -as, -a, -amos, -áis, -an. -er: -o, -es, -e, -emos, -éis, -en. -ir: -o, -es, -e, -imos, -ís, -en.
  • Usted takes the él form; ustedes the ellos form. Pronouns are usually left out.
  • Uses: habits, facts, what is happening now, the near future with a time word, suggestions (¿Tomamos un café?).
  • Negatives: no before the verb. Double negatives are normal: No como carne nunca.
  • Questions: same word order, rising voice, ¿ ? in writing. Question words have accents: qué, quién, dónde, cuándo, cómo, cuánto, cuál, por qué. Because = porque.
  • Frequency: siempre, normalmente, a menudo, a veces, casi nunca, nunca, todos los días.

docs.title: 6.8 Exercises
docs.text:
Exercise 1

Conjugate estudiar for tú.

Answer

estudias. estudias

Exercise 2

Conjugate vivir for nosotros.

Answer

vivimos. vivimos. -ir verbs keep the i in the nosotros form.

Exercise 3

Conjugate leer for ellos.

Answer

leen. leen. The stem le- plus the ending -en.

Exercise 4

Complete: ¿Usted ___ (trabajar) aquí?

Answer

trabaja. ¿Usted trabaja aquí? Usted takes the él form.

Exercise 5

Make negative: Bebo café.

Answer

No bebo café. No bebo café.

Exercise 6

Choose the question word: ¿___ vives? — En Sevilla.

Answer

Dónde. ¿Dónde vives?

Exercise 7

Complete with por qué or porque: ¿___ estudias español? — ___ trabajo en México.

Answer

¿Por qué estudias español? — Porque trabajo en México. The question word is two words with an accent; "because" is one word.

Exercise 8

Translate: "We eat at home on Sundays."

Answer

Los domingos comemos en casa. Los domingos comemos en casa. (Or Comemos en casa los domingos.)

Exercise 9

Translate: (a) Do you (tú) speak English? (b) My parents don't live in Madrid. (c) I never drink coffee. (d) How many languages does Ana speak?

Answer

(a) ¿Hablas inglés? (b) Mis padres no viven en Madrid. (c) Nunca bebo café. or No bebo café nunca. (d) ¿Cuántos idiomas habla Ana? or ¿Cuántas lenguas habla Ana?

Exercise 10

Correct the mistakes: Yo vivir en Londres. ¿Tú trabajar en una biblioteca? Ella no lee nunca porqué no tiene tiempo.

Answer

Vivo en Londres. ¿Trabajas en una biblioteca? Ella no lee nunca porque no tiene tiempo. Conjugate the verbs, and write porque, "because", as one word without an accent.

docs.title: 6.9 Quiz
docs.text:
Quiz: the present tense of regular verbs

Exercise 11

Nosotros ___ en un piso pequeño.

  1. vivemos
  2. vivimos
  3. viven
  4. vivís
Answer

vivimos

-ir verbs have -imos in the nosotros form.

Exercise 12

¿___ usted inglés?

  1. Hablas
  2. Habla
  3. Hablo
  4. Hablan
Answer

Habla

Usted takes the él form of the verb.

Exercise 13

Mis amigos ___ (comer) en casa y yo ___ (comer) en un restaurante.

Answer

comen · como

Exercise 14

¿Vosotros ___ (aprender) inglés?

Answer

aprendéis / aprendeis

The vosotros ending of -er verbs is -éis.

Exercise 15

Translate: "I don't work on Saturdays."

Answer

No trabajo los sábados / Los sábados no trabajo / Yo no trabajo los sábados

Exercise 16

Match each question word to its meaning.

AB¿cuándo?how many?¿quién?why?¿cuántos?when?¿por qué?who? Answer

¿cuándo? — when?; ¿quién? — who?; ¿cuántos? — how many?; ¿por qué? — why?

Exercise 17

Put the words in order: "Where do your parents live?"

Words: viven / padres? / tus / ¿Dónde

Answer

¿Dónde viven tus padres?

Exercise 18

Tap the wrong word.

Estudio español porqué viajo mucho.

Answer

Wrong word: porqué.

Corrected: Estudio español porque viajo mucho.

"Because" is porque: one word, no accent.

Exercise 19

Write what you hear.

Dictation. Have someone read the sentence aloud, then write it down.

Normalmente leo y escucho música por la noche.

Answer

Normalmente leo y escucho música por la noche.

Exercise 20

Say it aloud.

Vivo en el centro y trabajo en una librería.

Answer

Say: Vivo en el centro y trabajo en una librería.

docs.title: Lesson 16: Review: Putting It All Together
docs.text:
Repaso: todo junto

You have reached the last lesson. In fifteen lessons you have learnt to pronounce and spell Spanish, to greet people and introduce yourself, to count and tell the time, to use nouns, articles and adjectives, to choose between ser, estar and hay, to talk about your family, your town, your food, your day and your tastes, to shop, to make plans and to tell what happened. This lesson brings it all together. It has no new grammar: instead, it shows how the pieces fit, collects the mistakes English speakers make most often, gives you model texts to imitate, and ends with a long mixed quiz. Use it to find your weak points, and go back to the lesson that covers each one.

Learning outcomes

By the end of this lesson you will be able to:

  • hold a simple conversation that moves between present, past and future;
  • choose the right verb form for what you want to say, using the overview of the verb system;
  • avoid the ten most common mistakes of English-speaking learners;
  • write a short text about yourself, your routine, your last holiday and your plans;
  • check your level against the A1 descriptors and decide what to study next.

masculinefeminineplural

docs.title: 16.1 Dialogue: a farewell party
docs.text:
It is the end of Daniel's course in Salamanca. His friends have organised a small party in a café on the main square. Señora Ruiz, his teacher, and Javier, his language exchange partner, are there too. Notice how the conversation moves from the present to the past and the future.

  • Lucía: Daniel, ¿cuándo te vas? — Daniel, when are you leaving?
  • Daniel: Me voy el domingo. Mi vuelo sale a las once de la mañana. — I'm leaving on Sunday. My flight leaves at eleven in the morning.
  • Señora Ruiz: ¿Y qué tal el curso? ¿Estás contento? — And how was the course? Are you pleased?
  • Daniel: Sí, muy contento. Aprendí muchísimo. Cuando llegué en septiembre, solo sabía decir hola y gracias. — Yes, very pleased. I learnt a huge amount. When I arrived in September, I could only say hello and thank you.
  • Javier: ¡Es verdad! El primer día hablamos casi todo el tiempo en inglés. — That's true! On the first day we spoke English almost the whole time.
  • Lucía: ¿Qué es lo que más te gustó de Salamanca? — What did you like most about Salamanca?
  • Daniel: Me encantó la Plaza Mayor por la noche. Y la gente es muy simpática. — I loved the Plaza Mayor at night. And the people are very friendly.
  • Señora Ruiz: ¿Y qué vas a hacer en Inglaterra? — And what are you going to do in England?
  • Daniel: Voy a buscar trabajo y voy a seguir estudiando español. Quiero hacer el examen DELE el año que viene. — I'm going to look for a job and I'm going to keep on studying Spanish. I want to take the DELE exam next year.
  • Lucía: Y en verano tienes que venir a México. Te voy a enseñar Guadalajara. — And in the summer you have to come to Mexico. I'm going to show you Guadalajara.
  • Daniel: ¡Me encantaría! ¿Cuánto cuesta un billete a México? — I'd love to! How much is a ticket to Mexico?
  • Lucía: Un boleto, Daniel, en México decimos boleto. — A "boleto", Daniel, in Mexico we say "boleto".
  • Javier: Bueno, ¡un brindis! Por Daniel y por su español. — Right, a toast! To Daniel and his Spanish.
  • Todos: ¡Salud! — Cheers!

Find in the dialogue an example of each of these. The answers follow.

  1. A reflexive verb in the present (Lesson 11).
  2. Estar for a feeling (Lesson 5).
  3. Two regular preterites (Lesson 15).
  4. A sentence with ir a + infinitive (Lesson 14).
  5. Gustar or encantar in the past (Lessons 12 and 15).
  6. Tener que + infinitive (Lesson 10).
Answers
  1. te vas, me voy (irse, to leave). 2. ¿Estás contento? 3. aprendí, llegué, hablamos. 4. Voy a buscar trabajo, Te voy a enseñar Guadalajara. 5. me encantó, te gustó. 6. tienes que venir.

Two forms are new: sabía (I knew, I could) is the imperfect tense, mentioned in Lesson 15; me encantaría (I would love to) is the conditional. Both are taught at the next level, but you can learn these two as phrases now.

docs.title: 16.2 Vocabulary: the words you use most
Twenty verbs to know perfectly
docs.text:
These verbs appear on almost every page of real Spanish. You have met all of them. Can you give the yo forms of the present and the preterite without looking? The full tables are in the Verb Tables at the end of the book.

Infinitive English Present (yo) Preterite (yo) ser to be (identity) soy fui estar to be (place, state) estoy estuve tener to have tengo tuve hacer to do, to make hago hice ir to go voy fui poder can, to be able puedo pude querer to want, to love quiero quise decir to say, to tell digo dije ver to see veo vi dar to give doy di saber to know (a fact) sé supe venir to come vengo vine salir to go out, to leave salgo salí poner to put pongo puse hablar to speak hablo hablé comer to eat como comí vivir to live vivo viví trabajar to work trabajo trabajé gustar to please (I like) me gusta me gustó levantarse to get up me levanto me levanté

Table 16.1. Twenty essential verbs. Switch on Practice to hide the forms.

docs.text:
Spanish English Example y (e before i-, hi-) and padres e hijos o (u before o-, ho-) or siete u ocho pero but Es caro, pero es bonito. porque because Estudio español porque me gusta. también / tampoco also / not either Yo también. Yo tampoco. entonces so, then Entonces, ¿vamos? cuando when (not a question) Cuando llego a casa, ceno. si if Si quieres, vamos al cine. muy / mucho very / a lot Es muy bueno. Me gusta mucho.

Table 16.3. Classroom and survival phrases. Spanish often uses the angled quotation marks « » in print.

docs.title: 16.3 Grammar review: the verb system at a glance
docs.text:
Most of what you want to say at this level can be said with five tools. The table shows which tool to pick.

You want to talk about Use Lesson Example what is true now, habits, routines the present 6, 10, 11 Trabajo en un banco. Me levanto a las siete. what someone or something is ser 5 Mi hermana es médica. Es alta. where something is, how someone feels estar 5 El banco está en la plaza. Estoy cansado. that something exists hay 4, 5 Hay un banco en la plaza. likes and dislikes gustar, encantar 12 Me gusta el cine. Me encantan los libros. obligation tener que + infinitive 10 Tengo que estudiar. ability, permission poder + infinitive 10 ¿Puedo pagar con tarjeta? wishes querer + infinitive 10 Quiero viajar a Perú. plans and predictions ir a + infinitive 14 Voy a viajar a Perú. Va a llover. completed past events the preterite 15 El año pasado viajé a Perú.

Table 16.4. Which form for which meaning.

docs.title: The present in four families
docs.text:
Person regular -ar e → ie o → ue reflexive yo hablo quiero puedo me levanto tú hablas quieres puedes te levantas él, ella, usted habla quiere puede se levanta nosotros hablamos queremos podemos nos levantamos vosotros habláis queréis podéis os levantáis ellos, ellas, ustedes hablan quieren pueden se levantan

Table 16.5. The four kinds of present tense you know. Note that the stem changes leave nosotros and vosotros alone.

docs.title: Present, past and future of one verb
docs.text:
The same verb, viajar (to travel), in the three time frames:

  • Normalmente viajo en tren. — I usually travel by train. (present: habit)
  • El mes pasado viajé en avión. — Last month I travelled by plane. (preterite: finished event)
  • El mes que viene voy a viajar en autobús. — Next month I'm going to travel by bus. (ir a: plan)

Worked example: choosing the form

How would you say "This weekend I'm going to visit my grandparents, because last weekend I couldn't"?

  1. "This weekend I'm going to visit": a plan, so ir a + infinitive: Este fin de semana voy a visitar a mis abuelos. Note the personal a before people.
  2. "because": porque, one word, no accent.
  3. "last weekend I couldn't": a finished event in the past, so the preterite of poder, which is irregular: el fin de semana pasado no pude.

Result: Este fin de semana voy a visitar a mis abuelos, porque el fin de semana pasado no pude.

docs.title: 16.4 Grammar review: nouns, adjectives, pronouns and ten classic mistakes
The noun group
docs.text:
Everything in the noun group agrees with the noun, in gender and number (Lessons 4, 7 and 13):

Masculine Feminine singular este coche rojo es mío esta casa roja es mía plural estos coches rojos son míos estas casas rojas son mías

Table 16.6. Agreement: the demonstrative, the adjective and the possessive all follow the noun. Mío, mía (mine) are the stressed possessives, which you may meet before you study them.

docs.title: The pronouns you know
docs.text:
Subject Reflexive With gustar (indirect object) Direct object (it, them, him, her) After a preposition yo me me me mí (conmigo) tú te te te ti (contigo) él, ella, usted se le lo, la él, ella, usted nosotros nos nos nos nosotros vosotros os os os vosotros ellos, ellas, ustedes se les los, las ellos, ellas, ustedes

Table 16.7. Pronouns. Object pronouns go before a conjugated verb (me lo llevo) or are attached to an infinitive (voy a llevármelo).

docs.title: Ten classic mistakes of English speakers
docs.text:
Ten classic mistakes

  1. Age with ser. Not soy veinte años but tengo veinte años (Lessons 3 and 10).
  2. Feelings with ser. Not soy cansado but estoy cansado (Lesson 5).
  3. Location with ser. Not Madrid es en España but Madrid está en España (Lesson 5). But events use ser: La fiesta es en mi casa.
  4. An article with jobs. Not soy un profesor but soy profesor (Lesson 5).
  5. Gustar like "like". Not yo gusto el café but me gusta el café; and me gustan for plural things (Lesson 12).
  6. Forgetting agreement. Not la casa blanco but la casa blanca; not mis amigos es but mis amigos son (Lessons 4 and 7).
  7. Missing the article in general statements. English says "I like coffee"; Spanish says me gusta el café, and "Children like sweets" is a los niños les gustan los dulces (Lessons 4 and 12).
  8. Hot and cold with ser or estar. For a person, tengo calor, tengo frío; for the weather, hace calor, hace frío (Lesson 10).
  9. Translating "to" before an infinitive after ir. Not voy estudiar but voy a estudiar (Lesson 14).
  10. Accents left out. esta and está, hablo and habló, tu and tú are different words (Lessons 1 and 15).

docs.title: False friends
docs.text:
Some Spanish words look like English words but mean something else. These are the ones that cause the most embarrassment:

Spanish means not embarazada pregnant embarrassed (avergonzado) librería bookshop library (biblioteca) éxito success exit (salida) constipado having a cold (Spain) constipated carpeta folder carpet (alfombra) actual current, present-day actual (real) sensible sensitive sensible (sensato) asistir to attend to assist (ayudar) largo long large (grande) recordar to remember, to remind to record (grabar)

Table 16.8. False friends.

docs.title: 16.5 Practice: writing and speaking about yourself
A model text
docs.text:
Read this text by Priya, a learner who has finished a first course. It uses the main tools of the book: the present, ser and estar, gustar, the preterite and ir a. Listen to it, then use it as a model for your own.

Me llamo Priya y soy india, de Bombay, pero vivo en Leeds, en Inglaterra. Tengo treinta y dos años y soy enfermera. Trabajo en un hospital grande. Normalmente me levanto a las seis y media, porque empiezo a trabajar a las ocho. Mi trabajo es difícil, pero me gusta mucho. Tengo un hermano, Arjun, que vive en Toronto. Es ingeniero y es muy divertido. En mi tiempo libre me encanta cocinar y leer novelas. No me gusta nada el fútbol. Empecé a estudiar español hace un año. El verano pasado fui a Barcelona con unas amigas. Visitamos la Sagrada Familia, comimos tapas y pasamos dos días en la playa. ¡Lo pasamos genial! El año que viene voy a ir a México, porque quiero practicar mi español y conocer la cultura mexicana. Estoy muy contenta con mis progresos.

My name is Priya and I'm Indian, from Mumbai, but I live in Leeds, in England. I'm thirty-two and I'm a nurse. I work in a large hospital. I usually get up at half past six, because I start work at eight. My job is hard, but I like it a lot. I have a brother, Arjun, who lives in Toronto. He's an engineer and he's great fun. In my free time I love cooking and reading novels. I don't like football at all. I started learning Spanish a year ago. Last summer I went to Barcelona with some friends. We visited the Sagrada Familia, ate tapas and spent two days at the beach. We had a great time! Next year I'm going to go to Mexico, because I want to practise my Spanish and get to know Mexican culture. I'm very pleased with my progress.

Bombay or Mumbai?

Spanish often keeps older or Spanish forms of place names: Bombay, Londres (London), Nueva York, Pekín (Beijing). The Spanish academies recommend some of these traditional names, but the new official names are increasingly common too.

docs.title: Your own text
docs.text:
Write ten to twelve sentences about yourself, in this order. Use Priya's text as a model, but write about your own life.

  1. Your name, nationality, where you live (me llamo, soy, vivo).
  2. Your age and job or studies (tengo … años, soy, trabajo, estudio).
  3. Your daily routine (me levanto, desayuno, voy).
  4. Your family, with a description (tengo, es, tiene).
  5. Your likes and dislikes (me gusta, me encanta, no me gusta nada).
  6. Your last holiday (fui, visité, comí, lo pasé).
  7. Your plans (voy a, quiero).

docs.title: Role-plays
docs.text:
Practise these situations with a partner, or play both parts yourself. Each one uses several lessons.

Situation Lessons Start with You arrive at a hotel, give your name and spell it, ask what time breakfast is. 1, 2, 3, 14 Buenas tardes, tengo una reserva. You order lunch in a café for yourself and a friend, then ask for the bill. 8 Para mí, el menú del día, por favor. You are lost and ask for the station; you check you have understood. 9 Perdone, ¿la estación está lejos? You buy a jumper, ask for another size and colour, and pay by card. 13 ¿Lo tiene en una talla más grande? A friend asks about your weekend; you tell what you did and what you are going to do next weekend. 14, 15 ¿Qué hiciste el fin de semana?

Table 16.9. Role-plays that combine lessons.

Say it

Speak for one minute without stopping about yourself: who you are, what you do every day, what you did last weekend and what you are going to do next weekend. Record yourself, listen back, and note one mistake to fix. Then do it again.

docs.title: 16.6 Culture: where to go from here
docs.text:
Exams and levels. The levels used in this book come from the Common European Framework of Reference for Languages (CEFR), which describes language ability in six levels, from A1 (beginner) to C2 (mastery). This course covers A1 and the beginning of A2. The official exams of Spanish as a foreign language are the DELE (Diplomas de Español como Lengua Extranjera), awarded by the Instituto Cervantes on behalf of Spain's Ministry of Education, at all six levels. A newer exam, SIELE, is taken on a computer and also promoted by the Instituto Cervantes. A1 or A2 is a good first goal after this book.

Living Spanish. The best next step is contact with the language as it is really used:

  • Listen to music from different countries, from flamenco and Mexican rancheras to salsa, tango, cumbia and pop. Look up the lyrics and listen again.
  • Watch films and series from Spain, Mexico, Argentina, Colombia and elsewhere, first with Spanish subtitles, then without.
  • Read graded readers, children's books and the news. Many newspapers and broadcasters in Spain and Latin America publish their articles and programmes freely online.
  • Talk. An intercambio (Lessons 6 and 12) gives you real conversation for free. Online, you can find exchange partners anywhere.
  • Travel, if you can, and use every chance to speak: ordering, asking the way, chatting at a market.

Which Spanish? You may wonder whether to learn the Spanish of Spain or of Latin America. The answer is: the one you will use most, and understand the other. The grammar of this book is shared by all educated speakers; the differences are mainly in a few sounds (Lesson 1), the plural "you" (Lesson 2), the use of the present perfect (Lesson 15) and everyday vocabulary (in the culture notes of every lesson). A Spanish speaker from any country will be glad that you have learnt their language, whichever accent you have.

Mistakes are normal. Native speakers are generally patient and encouraging with learners, and most will be pleased that you are trying. Do not wait until your Spanish is perfect to use it: you learn by speaking, being misunderstood and trying again.

docs.title: 16.7 Summary
docs.text:
Summary: what you can now do

Check each statement. If you are not sure, go back to the lesson in brackets.

  • I can pronounce Spanish words, spell my name and place the stress correctly (Lesson 1).
  • I can greet people, introduce myself and others, and choose tú or usted (Lesson 2).
  • I can use numbers, give dates and tell the time (Lesson 3).
  • I can use nouns with the right article and make them plural (Lesson 4).
  • I can choose between ser, estar and hay (Lesson 5).
  • I can use the present tense of regular, irregular, stem-changing and reflexive verbs (Lessons 6, 10, 11).
  • I can describe people and talk about my family (Lesson 7).
  • I can order food and drink and pay (Lesson 8).
  • I can ask for and understand directions (Lesson 9).
  • I can say what I like and dislike (Lesson 12).
  • I can buy clothes, ask about sizes, colours and prices, and compare things (Lesson 13).
  • I can talk about plans and make bookings (Lesson 14).
  • I can tell what I did in the past (Lesson 15).

docs.title: 16.8 Exercises
docs.text:
Exercise 1

Complete with ser, estar or hay: Mi oficina ___ en el centro.

Answer

está. Mi oficina está en el centro. Location takes estar.

Exercise 2

Complete with ser, estar or hay: En mi calle ___ dos supermercados.

Answer

hay. En mi calle hay dos supermercados. Existence takes hay.

Exercise 3

Give the plural: el lápiz azul.

Answer

los lápices azules. los lápices azules. z becomes c before e; azul adds -es.

Exercise 4

Translate: "We like the beaches of Mexico."

Answer

Nos gustan las playas de México. Nos gustan las playas de México. Plural thing liked, so gustan.

Exercise 5

Complete with the present: ¿A qué hora ___ (acostarse) tú?

Answer

te acuestas. ¿A qué hora te acuestas? Reflexive and o → ue.

Exercise 6

Complete with the preterite: Ayer mis amigos ___ (venir) a cenar.

Answer

vinieron. Ayer mis amigos vinieron a cenar.

Exercise 7

Say "Next week I'm going to buy a car" in Spanish.

Answer

La semana que viene voy a comprar un coche. La semana que viene voy a comprar un coche. In much of Latin America: un carro or un auto.

Exercise 8

Give the feminine plural of trabajador.

Answer

trabajadoras. trabajadoras

Exercise 9

Choose: Hoy hace / tiene / está mucho calor.

Answer

hace. Hoy hace mucho calor. Weather takes hacer.

Exercise 10

Correct the sentence: Mi hermana es veinticinco años y es muy cansada hoy.

Answer

Mi hermana tiene veinticinco años y está muy cansada hoy. Age takes tener; a temporary state takes estar.

Exercise 11

Ask a stranger politely, using usted, if they can help you.

Answer

¿Puede ayudarme, por favor? ¿Puede ayudarme, por favor? or ¿Me puede ayudar, por favor?

Exercise 12

Write three sentences about the same topic, eating, in the present, the preterite and with ir a: what you usually have for lunch, what you had yesterday, and what you are going to have tomorrow.

Answer

A possible answer: Normalmente como un bocadillo. Ayer comí una ensalada. Mañana voy a comer paella.

docs.title: 16.9 Quiz
docs.text:
Final quiz: the whole course

Exercise 13

Hola, ¿___ estás?

  1. qué
  2. cómo
  3. dónde
  4. cuál
Answer

cómo

¿Cómo estás? = How are you?

Exercise 14

Choose the correct sentence.

  1. Soy treinta años.
  2. Tengo treinta años.
  3. Estoy treinta años.
  4. Hay treinta años.
Answer

Tengo treinta años.

Age is expressed with tener.

Exercise 15

A mis padres les ___ mucho viajar.

  1. gusta
  2. gustan
  3. gustamos
  4. gusto
Answer

gusta

An infinitive (viajar) takes the singular gusta, even when the people are plural.

Exercise 16

La farmacia ___ al lado del banco.

Answer

está

Location of a known place takes estar.

Exercise 17

Ayer yo ___ a la playa y ___ un libro.

Hint: ir, leer

Answer

fui · leí

Exercise 18

Mañana ___ a llover.

Answer

va

ir a + infinitive; the subject is the weather, third person singular.

Exercise 19

Say "I get up at seven" in Spanish.

Answer

Me levanto a las siete / Yo me levanto a las siete

Exercise 20

Match the question to the answer.

AB¿De dónde eres?Diez euros.¿Qué hora es?Fui al cine.¿Cuánto cuesta?Soy de Lima.¿Qué hiciste ayer?Son las tres. Answer

¿De dónde eres? — Soy de Lima.; ¿Qué hora es? — Son las tres.; ¿Cuánto cuesta? — Diez euros.; ¿Qué hiciste ayer? — Fui al cine.

Exercise 21

Tap the wrong word.

Mi amiga Laura es muy simpático y trabaja en un hospital.

Answer

Wrong word: simpático.

Corrected: Mi amiga Laura es muy simpática y trabaja en un hospital.

The adjective agrees with Laura, so it is feminine.

Exercise 22

Tap the wrong word.

Madrid es en el centro de España.

Answer

Wrong word: es.

Corrected: Madrid está en el centro de España.

Location takes estar.

Exercise 23

Put the words in order.

Words: año / a / El / estudiar / en / voy / Chile. / que / viene

Answer

El año que viene voy a estudiar en Chile.

Exercise 24

What is the speaker going to do on Saturday?

Read this aloud or have someone read it to you:

El sábado voy a ir a la montaña con mi hermano, y el domingo voy a descansar en casa.

  1. go to the mountains
  2. rest at home
  3. stay at home with a brother
  4. go to the beach
Answer

go to the mountains

Transcript: “El sábado voy a ir a la montaña con mi hermano, y el domingo voy a descansar en casa.”

El sábado voy a ir a la montaña = On Saturday I'm going to go to the mountains.

Exercise 25

Write what you hear.

Dictation. Have someone read the sentence aloud, then write it down.

Me llamo Ana, soy de Chile y me encanta bailar.

Answer

Me llamo Ana, soy de Chile y me encanta bailar.

Exercise 26

Say it aloud.

El verano pasado fui a España y lo pasé muy bien.

Answer

Say: El verano pasado fui a España y lo pasé muy bien.

docs.title: Lesson 5: Ser and Estar
docs.text:
Ser y estar: two ways to be

English has one verb "to be". Spanish has two, ser and estar, and they are not interchangeable. "I am English" uses ser; "I am tired" uses estar; "I am in Madrid" uses estar again. The difference is one of the first things that makes Spanish feel like Spanish, and once you see the logic it is less mysterious than it looks: roughly, ser says what something is, estar says where it is and how it is at the moment. In this lesson you learn both verbs in full, the uses of each, a few adjectives that change their meaning with the verb, and how to choose between hay and está.

Learning outcomes

By the end of this lesson you will be able to:

  • conjugate ser and estar in the present tense;
  • use ser for identity, origin, jobs, characteristics, time, material and events;
  • use estar for location, feelings and temporary conditions;
  • recognise adjectives whose meaning changes with ser and estar, such as listo and aburrido;
  • choose between hay and está when you talk about places.

masculinefeminineplural

docs.title: 5.1 Dialogue: a phone call
docs.text:
Lucía phones Daniel on a Thursday afternoon.

  • Lucía: ¡Hola, Daniel! ¿Dónde estás? — Hi, Daniel! Where are you?
  • Daniel: Estoy en un café cerca de la catedral. ¿Y tú? — I'm in a café near the cathedral. And you?
  • Lucía: Estoy en casa. ¿Estás solo? — I'm at home. Are you on your own?
  • Daniel: No, estoy con Marta, una amiga. Es de Valencia. — No, I'm with Marta, a friend. She's from Valencia.
  • Lucía: ¿Es estudiante también? — Is she a student too?
  • Daniel: No, es médica. Trabaja en el hospital. — No, she's a doctor. She works at the hospital.
  • Lucía: ¿Y cómo es? — And what's she like?
  • Daniel: Es muy simpática y muy inteligente. Pero hoy está muy cansada. — She's very nice and very clever. But today she's very tired.
  • Lucía: Claro, los médicos trabajan mucho. Oye, la fiesta de Pablo es el sábado. — Of course, doctors work a lot. Listen, Pablo's party is on Saturday.
  • Daniel: ¿Dónde es la fiesta? — Where's the party?
  • Lucía: Es en su casa. La casa está en la calle Toro, número doce. — It's at his house. The house is at number twelve, Calle Toro.
  • Daniel: ¿A qué hora es? — What time is it?
  • Lucía: Es a las nueve. ¡Es una sorpresa! — It's at nine. It's a surprise!
  • Daniel: ¡Qué bien! Estoy muy contento. Hasta el sábado. — Great! I'm really pleased. See you on Saturday.

Look at every "is" and "am" in the dialogue and ask: is the speaker saying what someone or something is, or where and how they are?

  • ser: Marta es de Valencia (origin), es médica (job), es simpática (character); the party es el sábado, es en su casa, es a las nueve (an event: when and where it takes place); es una sorpresa (what it is).
  • estar: estoy en un café, la casa está en la calle Toro (location); está cansada, estoy contento (how someone feels now).

Character and appearance (usually with ser)

Spanish Sounds like English cansado, cansada [kahn-SAH-doh] tired contento, contenta [kohn-TEHN-toh] happy, pleased triste [TREES-teh] sad enfadado, enfadada [ehn-fah-DAH-doh] angry (Spain) enojado, enojada [eh-noh-HAH-doh] angry (Latin America) nervioso, nerviosa [nehr-BYOH-soh] nervous enfermo, enferma [ehn-FEHR-moh] ill, sick ocupado, ocupada [oh-koo-PAH-doh] busy preocupado, preocupada [preh-oh-koo-PAH-doh] worried abierto, abierta / cerrado, cerrada [ah-BYEHR-toh / seh-RRAH-doh] open / closed sucio, sucia / limpio, limpia [SOO-syoh / LEEM-pyoh] dirty / clean lleno, llena / vacío, vacía [YEH-noh / bah-SEE-oh] full / empty

Table 5.2. States and feelings. Like all adjectives, they agree with the person or thing: Marta está cansada, los chicos están cansados.

docs.title: Jobs
docs.text:
Masculine Feminine English médico médica doctor profesor profesora teacher enfermero enfermera nurse abogado abogada lawyer camarero camarera waiter, waitress (mesero, mesera in Mexico) ingeniero ingeniera engineer estudiante estudiante student periodista periodista journalist

Table 5.3. Some jobs.

docs.title: 5.3 Grammar: the two verbs
docs.text:
Both verbs are irregular, and both are used constantly, so learn them perfectly.

Person ser estar English yo soy estoy I am tú eres estás you are él, ella, usted es está he, she is; you are nosotros, nosotras somos estamos we are vosotros, vosotras sois estáis you are (Spain) ellos, ellas, ustedes son están they are; you are

Table 5.4. Ser and estar in the present tense. Switch on Practice and write the forms from memory.

  • Soy, eres, es, somos, sois, son. — Say the whole of ser aloud three times.
  • Estoy, estás, está, estamos, estáis, están. — Then estar.

Pay attention to the written accents of estar. está [ehs-TAH] ("is") and esta [EHS-tah] ("this", feminine) are different words: the accent marks the stress on the last syllable. All the forms of estar except estoy and estamos carry one.

docs.title: 5.4 Grammar: when to use which
docs.text: Figure 5.1 Ser, estar or hay? A decision chart. First question: are you saying that something exists, with a, some or a number? If yes, use hay. If no, second question: are you saying where a person or thing is? If yes, use estar, except for the place where an event takes place, which uses ser. If no, third question: are you saying how someone or something is now, a feeling, a condition or the result of a change? If yes, use estar. Otherwise use ser, for identity, origin, jobs, characteristics, time and dates, material and events.

docs.title: Uses of ser
docs.text:
Use Example English identity, who or what Soy Daniel. Es una sorpresa. I'm Daniel. It's a surprise. origin, nationality Marta es de Valencia. Es española. Marta is from Valencia. She's Spanish. job, religion, membership Es médica. Somos estudiantes. She's a doctor. We're students. characteristics Es alta y simpática. She's tall and nice. relationship Pablo es mi primo. Pablo is my cousin. possession (ser de) El libro es de Ana. The book is Ana's. material (ser de) La mesa es de madera. The table is (made of) wood. time, days, dates Son las tres. Hoy es lunes. It's three o'clock. Today is Monday. events: when and where La fiesta es en mi casa. The party is at my house. prices, totals ¿Cuánto es? Son diez euros. How much is it? It's ten euros.

Table 5.5. The uses of ser.

Common mistake: un or una with jobs

After ser, a job, nationality or religion takes no article: Es médica, "She's a doctor", not es una médica. The article comes back when you add an adjective: Es una médica excelente, "She's an excellent doctor".

docs.title: Uses of estar
docs.text:
Use Example English location of people and things Estoy en un café. Madrid está en el centro de España. I'm in a café. Madrid is in the centre of Spain. how you are ¿Cómo estás? — Estoy bien. How are you? — I'm well. feelings and moods Estamos contentos. Está nerviosa. We're happy. She's nervous. physical states Están cansados. Estoy enfermo. They're tired. I'm ill. conditions of things La sopa está fría. La puerta está abierta. The soup is cold. The door is open. with bien and mal Está bien. Está mal. It's fine. It's wrong.

Table 5.6. The uses of estar.

Estar is also the verb of the "-ing" form, Estoy estudiando ("I am studying"). You do not need it yet; it is mentioned here so that you recognise it.

docs.title: Permanent and temporary: a useful idea, not the whole rule
docs.text:
You will often read that ser is for permanent things and estar for temporary ones. That is a good first guide, and it explains es alta (she is tall: a lasting trait) against está cansada (she is tired: right now). But it is not the real rule, as two examples show:

  • Location always takes estar, even when it is permanent: Madrid está en España. Madrid is not going anywhere.
  • Time takes ser, even though it changes every minute: Son las tres.

So think of it this way: ser classifies and defines (what, who, what kind, from where, when an event happens); estar locates and describes a state or condition (where something is, how someone or something is now).

docs.title: The same adjective with both verbs
docs.text:
With most descriptive adjectives you can use either verb, and the verb changes the message:

  • Luis es nervioso. — Luis is a nervous person. (his character)
  • Luis está nervioso. — Luis is nervous. (now, before his exam)
  • La sopa es buena aquí. — The soup is good here. (as a rule)
  • ¡La sopa está muy buena! — The soup tastes really good! (this soup, now)
  • ¡Qué guapa eres! — How pretty you are!; ¡Qué guapa estás! — How pretty you look (today)!

A few adjectives change their meaning altogether:

Adjective with ser with estar listo es listo — he is clever está listo — he is ready aburrido es aburrido — he is boring está aburrido — he is bored malo es malo — he is bad, wicked está malo — he is ill (Spain); it has gone off (food) rico es rico — he is rich está rico — it is tasty (food) verde es verde — it is green está verde — it is unripe

Table 5.7. Adjectives that change meaning with ser and estar.

Common mistake: es bien

"It's fine", "it's OK" and "it's wrong" are está bien and está mal, never es bien. bien and mal are adverbs, and they go with estar. With ser use the adjectives: Es bueno ("It's good"), Es malo ("It's bad").

Two special cases

Death is grammatically a state, so it takes estar: El pez está muerto ("The fish is dead"). Marital status is often said with estar, Estoy casado ("I'm married"), though Soy casado is also heard, especially in Latin America. With feliz ("happy"), both verbs are common.

docs.title: Hay or está?
docs.text:
Both can translate "is" when you talk about places, and they are easy to confuse. The difference is the difference between "a" and "the":

Use Example something new, not yet mentioned: a, some, numbers, no article hay Hay un banco en la plaza. — There's a bank in the square. a particular, known thing or person: the, my, names está / están El banco está en la plaza. — The bank is in the square.

Table 5.8. Hay or está?

  • ¿Hay un baño por aquí? — Is there a toilet around here? (any toilet)
  • ¿Dónde está el baño? — Where is the toilet? (the one I know exists)
  • Hay dos farmacias en esta calle. — There are two chemists in this street.
  • Mis llaves están en la mesa. — My keys are on the table.

Worked example: choosing the verb

Translate: "My brother is a teacher. He's from Bilbao, but now he's in Mexico. He's very happy there. The school is in the centre, and there's a park near the school."

  1. My brother is a teacher: job, no article → Mi hermano es profesor.
  2. He's from Bilbao: origin → Es de Bilbao,
  3. but now he's in Mexico: location → pero ahora está en México.
  4. He's very happy there: feeling → Está muy contento allí.
  5. The school is in the centre: location of a known thing → El colegio está en el centro,
  6. and there's a park near the school: something new → y hay un parque cerca del colegio.

docs.title: Ser or estar?
docs.text:
Sentence Verb Why Ana ___ de Chile. Ana es de Chile. origin Yo ___ cansado. Yo estoy cansado. state Nosotros ___ en clase. Nosotros estamos en clase. location Mis padres ___ abogados. Mis padres son abogados. job ¿Qué hora ___? ¿Qué hora es? time La ventana ___ abierta. La ventana está abierta. condition El concierto ___ en el teatro. El concierto es en el teatro. event ¿Cómo ___ tú? ¿Cómo estás tú? how you are La casa ___ muy grande. La casa es muy grande. characteristic

Table 5.9. Practice: choose and conjugate the verb.

docs.title: Who are they, and how are they?
docs.text:
Read each pair aloud. The first sentence says what the person is like; the second says how they are today.

  • Carmen es muy alegre, pero hoy está triste. — Carmen is a very cheerful person, but today she's sad.
  • Jorge es tranquilo, pero hoy está nervioso: tiene un examen. — Jorge is calm by nature, but today he's nervous: he has an exam.
  • Mis abuelos son mayores, pero están muy bien. — My grandparents are old, but they're very well.

Say it

Describe a friend in four sentences: who they are, where they are from, what they are like, and how they are today. For example:

Mi amiga se llama Elena. Es de Lima. Es muy simpática y trabajadora. Hoy está un poco cansada.

docs.title: 5.6 Culture: "How are you?" and "What are you like?"
docs.text:
¿Cómo estás? and ¿Cómo eres? These two questions show the difference between the verbs perfectly. ¿Cómo estás? means "How are you?" (today, now); ¿Cómo eres? means "What are you like?" (as a person). In a job interview or on a language exchange you might hear ¿Cómo eres? Descríbete. ("What are you like? Describe yourself.")

Being ill in Spain and in Latin America. In Spain estoy malo is the everyday way to say "I'm ill", and estoy enfermo is a little more formal. In much of Latin America estoy enfermo is the normal phrase, and estar malo is used less for people.

Angry and annoyed. Spain says estar enfadado for "to be angry"; Latin America says estar enojado. Both are understood everywhere.

Polite descriptions. Spanish speakers often soften descriptions of people. Instead of viejo ("old"), they say mayor ("older"): Mi abuela es mayor. And nicknames based on looks, such as gordo ("fatty") or flaco ("skinny"), are used affectionately between friends and family in many Latin American countries in a way that surprises many English speakers. Listen to how they are used before trying them yourself.

¿Dónde está…? The phrase ¿Dónde está…? is one of the most useful in any trip: ¿Dónde está la estación? ¿Dónde está el museo? Add perdone (to someone you call usted) or perdona (tú) in front to stop someone politely in the street: Perdone, ¿dónde está la estación? Lesson 9 shows how to understand the answer.

docs.title: 5.7 Summary
docs.text:
Summary

  • ser: soy, eres, es, somos, sois, son. estar: estoy, estás, está, estamos, estáis, están.
  • ser classifies and defines: identity, origin, nationality, job (no article), characteristics, relationships, possession and material (ser de), time and dates, events (la fiesta es en mi casa), prices.
  • estar locates and describes a state: location of people and things (even permanent), how you are, feelings, physical states, conditions; always with bien and mal.
  • The same adjective can go with both verbs: es nervioso (by nature) / está nervioso (now). Some change meaning: listo, aburrido, malo, rico, verde.
  • hay introduces something new (a, some, numbers); está / están locates something known (the, my, names).

docs.title: 5.8 Exercises
docs.text:
Exercise 1

Complete with ser: Nosotros ___ de Irlanda.

Answer

somos. Nosotros somos de Irlanda. Origin uses ser.

Exercise 2

Complete with estar: ¿Dónde ___ mis llaves?

Answer

están. ¿Dónde están mis llaves? Location, and the subject (mis llaves) is plural.

Exercise 3

Ser or estar? Mi madre ___ enfermera.

Answer

es. Mi madre es enfermera. A job, with no article.

Exercise 4

Ser or estar? El café ___ frío. (The coffee in your cup has gone cold.)

Answer

está. El café está frío. The condition of the coffee now.

Exercise 5

Ser or estar? La reunión ___ en la sala dos. (la reunión = the meeting)

Answer

es. La reunión es en la sala dos. The place where an event takes place uses ser.

Exercise 6

Hay or está? ___ un supermercado cerca de mi casa.

Answer

Hay. Hay un supermercado cerca de mi casa. Something new, with un.

Exercise 7

How do you say "The children are bored"? (the children: los niños)

Answer

Los niños están aburridos. Los niños están aburridos. With estar, aburrido means bored; with ser, it would mean boring.

Exercise 8

Translate "I'm ready" for a woman.

Answer
