Estoy lista. Estoy lista. Estar listo means to be ready; ser listo means to be clever.

Exercise 9

Correct the mistakes: Pedro está un estudiante. Es en la biblioteca y es muy cansado.

Answer

Pedro es estudiante. Está en la biblioteca y está muy cansado. A job takes ser and no article; location and tiredness take estar.

Exercise 10

Write four sentences about yourself: your name, where you are from, what you are like, and where you are now.

Answer

Model answer: Soy Laura. Soy de Dublín. Soy alegre y un poco tímida. Ahora estoy en casa. Check that you used ser for the first three and estar for the last.

docs.title: 5.9 Quiz
docs.text:
Quiz: ser and estar

Exercise 11

Madrid ___ en el centro de España.

  1. es
  2. está
  3. hay
  4. son
Answer

está

Location takes estar, even when it is permanent.

Exercise 12

Hoy ___ martes.

  1. es
  2. está
  3. estoy
  4. hay
Answer

es

Days, dates and the time take ser.

Exercise 13

Which sentence means "He is ready"?

  1. Es listo.
  2. Está listo.
  3. Hay listo.
  4. Son listos.
Answer

Está listo.

estar listo = to be ready; ser listo = to be clever.

Exercise 14

Vosotros ___ muy simpáticos, pero hoy ___ cansados.

Answer

sois · estáis / estais

Character with ser (sois); a state now with estar (estáis).

Exercise 15

Say "She is a doctor" in Spanish.

Answer

Es médica / Ella es médica / Es médico / Ella es médico

No article before a job after ser.

Exercise 16

Match each sentence to the reason for the verb.

ABSoy de Perú.timeEstoy en el hotel.feelingSon las dos.originEstoy triste.location Answer

Soy de Perú. — origin; Estoy en el hotel. — location; Son las dos. — time; Estoy triste. — feeling

Exercise 17

Tap the wrong word.

La fiesta está en casa de Pablo.

Answer

Wrong word: está.

Corrected: La fiesta es en casa de Pablo.

Where an event takes place uses ser.

Exercise 18

Put the words in order: "There is a bank near the station."

Words: Hay / banco / estación. / de / la / un / cerca

Answer

Hay un banco cerca de la estación.

Exercise 19

Write what you hear.

Dictation. Have someone read the sentence aloud, then write it down.

Mi hermana es médica y está en el hospital.

Answer

Mi hermana es médica y está en el hospital.

docs.title: Lesson 13: Shopping and Clothes
docs.text:
De compras: la ropa

Shopping is where your Spanish meets the real world: you need to ask for a colour and a size, try something on, say that it is too big, ask the price and pay. This lesson gives you the words for clothes and colours, the phrases of a shop, prices with big numbers, and three pieces of grammar that you will use all the time: the demonstratives (this, that, that one over there), the direct object pronouns (it, them), and comparisons (cheaper than, as nice as).

Learning outcomes

By the end of this lesson you will be able to:

  • name clothes and colours, and make colours agree with what they describe;
  • ask for a size, try clothes on and say how they fit;
  • ask and understand prices, including numbers above a thousand, in euros and pesos;
  • point things out with este, ese and aquel, and use esto and eso;
  • replace a noun with lo, la, los, las: me lo llevo;
  • compare things with más … que, menos … que, tan … como, mejor and peor.

masculinefeminineplural

docs.title: 13.1 Dialogue: a jacket for the winter
docs.text:
Emma, a student from Dublin, is spending a year in Madrid. It is November and she needs a warm jacket. She goes into a clothes shop.

  • Dependienta: Buenas tardes. ¿La puedo ayudar en algo? — Good afternoon. Can I help you with anything?
  • Emma: Sí, gracias. Busco una chaqueta para el invierno. — Yes, thanks. I'm looking for a jacket for the winter.
  • Dependienta: Muy bien. ¿De qué color la quiere? — Very well. What colour do you want it in?
  • Emma: Negra o azul oscuro. Me gusta mucho esa chaqueta de ahí. ¿La tiene en azul? — Black or dark blue. I really like that jacket there. Do you have it in blue?
  • Dependienta: Sí, aquí está. ¿Qué talla tiene? — Yes, here it is. What size are you?
  • Emma: La treinta y ocho, creo. ¿Puedo probármela? — A thirty-eight, I think. Can I try it on?
  • Dependienta: Claro. Los probadores están al fondo, a la derecha. — Of course. The fitting rooms are at the back, on the right.
  • Emma: Me queda un poco grande. ¿Tiene una talla más pequeña? — It's a bit big on me. Do you have a smaller size?
  • Dependienta: Sí, tome, la treinta y seis. — Yes, here you are, the thirty-six.
  • Emma: Esta me queda perfecta. ¿Cuánto cuesta? — This one fits me perfectly. How much is it?
  • Dependienta: Ochenta y nueve euros. Está rebajada. — Eighty-nine euros. It's reduced.
  • Emma: Es más barata que la negra. Me la llevo. ¿Puedo pagar con tarjeta? — It's cheaper than the black one. I'll take it. Can I pay by card?
  • Dependienta: Por supuesto. ¿Algo más? — Of course. Anything else?
  • Emma: ¿Cuánto cuestan aquellos zapatos marrones? — How much are those brown shoes over there?
  • Dependienta: Sesenta euros. ¿Qué número tiene? — Sixty euros. What size do you take?
  • Emma: El treinta y nueve… pero hoy no, gracias. Solo la chaqueta. — Thirty-nine… but not today, thanks. Just the jacket.

Notice:

  1. Three words for "that": esa chaqueta (near the shop assistant), aquellos zapatos (further away), and esta for "this one", the one Emma is wearing.
  2. Small words replace nouns: ¿La tiene en azul? ("Do you have it?"), probármela ("try it on"), me la llevo ("I'll take it"). La stands for la chaqueta.
  3. Clothes size is la talla; shoe size is el número.
  4. Me queda grande ("it's big on me") uses quedar, a verb of the gustar type (Lesson 12): the clothes are the subject.

docs.title: 13.2 Vocabulary: clothes, colours and the shop
Clothes
docs.text:
Spanish (Spain) Also heard in Latin America English la camisa the shirt la camiseta la playera (Mexico), la remera (Argentina) the T-shirt el jersey el suéter the sweater, jumper la chaqueta la chamarra (Mexico), la campera (Argentina) the jacket el abrigo the coat los pantalones the trousers los vaqueros los jeans the jeans la falda la pollera (Argentina, Uruguay) the skirt el vestido the dress el traje the suit la corbata the tie los zapatos the shoes las zapatillas (de deporte) los tenis (Mexico) the trainers, sneakers las botas the boots los calcetines the socks el sombrero / la gorra the hat / the cap la bufanda the scarf las gafas (de sol) los lentes, los anteojos the glasses (sunglasses)

Table 13.1. Clothes. Spain's words are understood everywhere; the second column shows common regional alternatives.

Common mistake: la ropa is singular

La ropa means "clothes" but is a singular word: Esta ropa es muy bonita ("These clothes are very nice"). And los pantalones is usually plural, as in English, though el pantalón is also correct and common in shops.

docs.title: Colours
docs.text:
Spanish Forms English blanco blanco, blanca, blancos, blancas white negro negro, negra, negros, negras black rojo rojo, roja, rojos, rojas red amarillo amarillo, amarilla, amarillos, amarillas yellow morado morado, morada, morados, moradas purple verde verde, verdes green azul azul, azules blue gris gris, grises grey marrón marrón, marrones brown (Spain; café in Mexico) rosa rosa pink (rosado in much of Latin America) naranja naranja orange

Table 13.2. Colours and their forms.

Colours are adjectives, so they follow the rules of Lesson 7: they come after the noun and agree with it.

  1. Colours in -o have four forms: un vestido negro, una falda negra, unos zapatos negros, unas botas negras.
  2. Colours in -e or a consonant have two forms, singular and plural: una camisa verde, unas camisas verdes, un abrigo azul, unos abrigos azules.
  3. Colours that are also the names of things (rosa, "rose"; naranja, "orange") often do not change: una camiseta naranja, unos calcetines naranja. The plural rosas, naranjas is also accepted. To avoid the question, Latin Americans often say rosado and anaranjado, which agree normally.
  4. With claro ("light") and oscuro ("dark"), the colour does not change at all: una chaqueta azul oscuro, unos pantalones verde claro.

To ask the colour: ¿De qué color es? ("What colour is it?") or ¿De qué color la quiere? ("What colour do you want it in?").

docs.title: In the shop
docs.text:
Spanish English la tienda / la tienda de ropa the shop / the clothes shop la zapatería the shoe shop el mercado the market el centro comercial the shopping centre, mall el dependiente / la dependienta the shop assistant el probador the fitting room la caja the till, checkout la talla the size (clothes) el número the size (shoes) el precio the price barato / caro cheap / expensive las rebajas the sales (Spain) la oferta / el descuento the special offer / the discount en efectivo in cash con tarjeta by card el recibo / el tique the receipt el cambio the change (money)

Table 13.3. Words for shops and paying. In Spain the change is also la vuelta; in parts of South America it is el vuelto.

docs.title: Useful phrases
docs.text:
Spanish English Solo estoy mirando, gracias. I'm just looking, thanks. Busco unos pantalones negros. I'm looking for some black trousers. ¿Lo tiene en otro color? Do you have it in another colour? ¿Tiene una talla más grande? Do you have a bigger size? ¿Puedo probármelo? Can I try it on? Me queda bien. / Me queda grande. It fits me. / It's too big for me. ¿Cuánto cuesta? / ¿Cuánto cuestan? How much is it? / How much are they? ¿Cuánto es? How much is it (altogether)? Me lo llevo. I'll take it. ¿Se puede cambiar? Can it be exchanged?

Table 13.4. Phrases for shopping.

docs.title: Fitting: the verb quedar
docs.text:
quedar works like gustar: the clothes are the subject, and the person is me, te, le. So it is queda for one item and quedan for several, and the adjective agrees with the clothes:

  • La falda me queda corta. — The skirt is too short for me.
  • Los pantalones me quedan largos. — The trousers are too long for me.
  • Ese vestido te queda muy bien. — That dress really suits you.

Cuesta and cuestan

The verb costar ("to cost") has the o→ue change of Lesson 10, and like a price in English it agrees with the thing: ¿Cuánto cuesta la camisa? but ¿Cuánto cuestan los zapatos?

docs.title: 13.3 Grammar: this, that and that one over there
Three distances
docs.text:
English has two demonstratives, this and that. Spanish has three, and each has four forms to agree with the noun.

Figure 13.1 Three distances. Este is near the speaker, ese is near the listener or a little way off, and aquel is far from both. Masculine Feminine Masc. plural Fem. plural Place word this (near me) este jersey esta falda estos zapatos estas botas aquí (here) that (near you) ese jersey esa falda esos zapatos esas botas ahí (there) that (over there) aquel jersey aquella falda aquellos zapatos aquellas botas allí (over there)

Table 13.5. The demonstratives. Practice hides them.

Two things to watch:

  • The masculine singular has no -o: este, ese, aquel, but the plural has -os: estos, esos, aquellos.
  • In everyday speech ese is used for most things that are not right next to you. aquel is for things clearly far away, in space or in time: en aquella época, "in those days".

docs.title: This one, that one
docs.text:
The same words stand alone, without a noun, to mean "this one, that one":

  • ¿Qué camisa prefieres, esta o esa? — Which shirt do you prefer, this one or that one?
  • Me gustan más aquellos. — I like those over there better.

Éste or este?

Older books write the pronouns with an accent, éste, ésa, aquél, to show that no noun follows. The current spelling rules of the Spanish Academies no longer require it, and this book writes them without accents. You will still see the accent in older texts.

docs.title: Esto, eso, aquello: for things without a name
docs.text:
When you do not know what something is, or you mean an idea or a situation rather than a particular noun, use the neuter forms. They never change and never go before a noun.

  • ¿Qué es esto? — What is this?
  • Eso es muy caro. — That's very expensive.
  • ¿Cuánto cuesta eso? — How much is that? (pointing at something whose name you don't know)
  • Eso es. — That's it. Exactly.

docs.title: 13.4 Grammar: it and them, and comparing
The direct object pronouns
docs.text:
A direct object is the person or thing that receives the action: in "I'm buying the shirt", the shirt. To avoid repeating it, English says "I'm buying it". Spanish uses these pronouns:

Replaces Pronoun Example a masculine singular noun lo ¿El abrigo? Lo compro. — The coat? I'll buy it. a feminine singular noun la ¿La camisa? La compro. — The shirt? I'll buy it. a masculine plural noun los ¿Los zapatos? Los compro. — The shoes? I'll buy them. a feminine plural noun las ¿Las botas? Las compro. — The boots? I'll buy them.

Table 13.6. Lo, la, los, las. They agree with the noun they replace.

The other persons use pronouns you already know: me (me), te (you), nos (us), os (you all): ¿Me ayuda, por favor?, "Can you help me, please?"

The position is the same as for reflexive pronouns (Lesson 11): before the conjugated verb, or attached to an infinitive.

  • La quiero en azul. — I want it in blue.
  • No los necesito. — I don't need them.
  • Voy a comprarlo. = Lo voy a comprar. — I'm going to buy it.

Common mistake: forgetting the gender

"It" is lo or la depending on the noun, not on the thing itself. A shirt is feminine, so la; a jumper is masculine, so lo. ¿La camisa? Lo compro is a mistake English speakers often make.

docs.title: Me lo llevo and probármelo
docs.text:
Two shopping phrases combine a reflexive pronoun with lo or la. The reflexive pronoun always comes first:

  • Me lo llevo. / Me la llevo. — I'll take it. (llevarse, "to take away")
  • Me los llevo. — I'll take them.
  • ¿Puedo probármelo? / ¿Me lo puedo probar? — Can I try it on? (probarse, o→ue, "to try on")

When two pronouns are attached to an infinitive, a written accent keeps the stress where it was: probar → probármelo [proh-BAR-meh-loh]. Lesson 1 explains why: the word now ends in a vowel with the stress three syllables from the end, and such words always carry a written accent.

docs.title: Comparing things
docs.text:
Structure Meaning Example más + adjective + que more … than, -er than Esta camisa es más cara que esa. — This shirt is more expensive than that one. menos + adjective + que less … than El mercado es menos caro que la tienda. — The market is less expensive than the shop. tan + adjective + como as … as Estos zapatos son tan cómodos como aquellos. — These shoes are as comfortable as those. mejor que better than Esta tela es mejor que la otra. — This fabric is better than the other one. peor que worse than La calidad es peor que antes. — The quality is worse than before. mayor que / menor que older than / younger than Mi hermana es mayor que yo. — My sister is older than me.

Table 13.7. Comparisons. The adjective still agrees with the noun it describes.

Notes:

  • The adjective agrees as usual: Las botas son más caras que los zapatos.
  • Do not say más bueno or más malo for quality: say mejor and peor. Their plurals are mejores and peores.
  • After que and como, use yo and tú, not mí and ti: Eres más alto que yo.
  • The most: put el, la, los, las before más: Esta es la chaqueta más barata de la tienda, "This is the cheapest jacket in the shop". "In" after a superlative is de.

docs.title: Prices and big numbers
docs.text:
Lesson 3 took you to a thousand. Above that, Spanish builds numbers with mil ("thousand"), which does not take "one" and does not change in the plural, and millón ("million"), which does.

Number Spanish 1 000 mil 1 250 mil doscientos cincuenta 2 000 dos mil 15 900 quince mil novecientos 100 000 cien mil 500 000 quinientos mil 1 000 000 un millón 3 000 000 tres millones

Table 13.8. Big numbers. Spanish writes a point or a space for thousands (1.250 or 1 250) and a comma for decimals in Spain (12,50 €); Mexico and some other countries use the English system (1,250 and 12.50).

  • Never un mil: 1,000 is just mil, and 2,000 is dos mil, never dos miles.
  • millón takes de before a noun: un millón de pesos, dos millones de euros.
  • Hundreds agree with a feminine noun: doscientos euros, but doscientas libras ("two hundred pounds").

Saying prices:

  • 12,50 €: doce euros con cincuenta, or simply doce cincuenta
  • 99,99 €: noventa y nueve euros con noventa y nueve céntimos
  • $350 in Mexico: trescientos cincuenta pesos
  • $1.200 in Argentina or Chile: mil doscientos pesos

Worked example: choosing between two jackets

You compare a black jacket (120 €) and a blue one (89 €). The blue one fits better.

  1. Price, with más … que: La chaqueta negra es más cara que la azul.
  2. The other way round, with menos: La azul es menos cara que la negra.
  3. Fit, with mejor: La azul me queda mejor.
  4. Decision, with a pronoun: Me llevo la azul. Me la llevo.
  5. Price: Son ochenta y nueve euros.

docs.title: Este, ese, aquel
docs.text:
Point and say, then listen.

  • Este sombrero es muy bonito. — This hat is very pretty. (in my hand)
  • Esa bufanda es de lana. — That scarf is wool. (near you)
  • Aquellas botas son muy caras. — Those boots are very expensive. (in the window across the street)
  • ¿Cuánto cuestan estos calcetines? — How much are these socks?
  • ¿Qué es eso? — What's that?

docs.title: It and them
docs.text:
Question Answer ¿Compras el vestido? Sí, lo compro. ¿Quieres la gorra? Sí, la quiero. ¿Necesitas los calcetines? No, no los necesito. ¿Te pruebas las botas? Sí, me las pruebo. ¿Te llevas el abrigo? Sí, me lo llevo.

Table 13.9. Switch on Practice and write the pronoun.

docs.title: At the till
docs.text:
• Hola, buenas. ¿Cuánto es? — Hi. How much is it?
  • Son cuarenta y cinco euros con veinte. — That's forty-five euros twenty.
  • ¿Aceptan tarjeta? — Do you take cards?
  • Sí, claro. ¿Quiere una bolsa? — Yes, of course. Do you want a bag?
  • No, gracias. ¿Me da el tique, por favor? — No, thanks. Can I have the receipt, please?

Say it

Act out a scene in a clothes shop with a partner. The customer looks for a garment, asks for a colour and size, tries it on, says how it fits, asks the price and pays. Use at least one demonstrative, one pronoun (lo, la, los, las) and one comparison. For example:

Busco una camisa blanca. ¿Tiene esta en la talla cuarenta? Me queda un poco pequeña. ¿Tiene una más grande? Esta me queda mejor. ¿Cuánto cuesta? Me la llevo.

docs.title: 13.6 Culture: shopping in Spain and Latin America
docs.text:
Opening hours. In Spain, many small shops open from about ten to two, close for lunch, and open again from about five until eight or half past eight. Department stores and shopping centres stay open all day. Sunday opening depends on the region and the city. In large Latin American cities, shopping centres are usually open every day until late, and they are popular places to spend a weekend afternoon, especially in hot or rainy weather.

Sales. Spain has two traditional sales seasons, las rebajas: in winter, starting just after Three Kings' Day on 6 January, and in summer, starting around the beginning of July. Shop windows fill with signs saying rebajas, liquidación ("clearance") and percentages off: un treinta por ciento de descuento.

Markets. Most Spanish towns have a covered mercado municipal for fresh food, and a weekly open-air market, el mercadillo, for clothes and household goods. In Mexico the open-air street market is called el tianguis, a word from Nahuatl, the language of the Aztecs. Across Latin America, craft markets sell textiles, ceramics and jewellery.

Bargaining. In shops, prices are fixed everywhere. In some street and craft markets in Latin America, a little friendly bargaining, regatear, is normal: ¿Me lo deja más barato? ("Can you let me have it cheaper?"). In Spain bargaining is rare, except perhaps at a flea market.

Currencies. Spain uses the euro (el euro, divided into céntimos). Mexico, Argentina, Chile, Colombia and Uruguay each have their own peso; Peru has the sol; Guatemala the quetzal; Ecuador and El Salvador use the US dollar. Mexican and other pesos are written with the $ sign, so a price of $500 in Mexico City is in pesos, not dollars.

Sizes. Spain uses European sizes for clothes (36, 38, 40 …) and shoes (37, 38, 39 …). In Mexico and much of Latin America, sizes often follow the US system or are given as chica, mediana, grande (in Spain pequeña, mediana, grande). Always try clothes on: ¿Puedo probármelo?

docs.title: 13.7 Summary
docs.text:
Summary

  • Colours follow the noun and agree: una falda negra, unos abrigos azules. Rosa and naranja often stay the same; azul oscuro and verde claro never change.
  • Size: la talla for clothes, el número for shoes. Fit: me queda bien / grande / pequeño, agreeing with the clothes: me quedan largos.
  • Price: ¿Cuánto cuesta? / ¿Cuánto cuestan? / ¿Cuánto es? mil never takes un or a plural; un millón de euros.
  • Demonstratives: este, esta, estos, estas (here), ese, esa, esos, esas (there), aquel, aquella, aquellos, aquellas (over there). esto, eso, aquello for things without a name.
  • Direct object pronouns: lo, la, los, las agree with the noun they replace and go before the verb or on the end of an infinitive: lo compro, voy a comprarlo, me lo llevo.
  • Comparisons: más … que, menos … que, tan … como, mejor, peor, mayor, menor.

docs.title: 13.8 Exercises
docs.text:
Exercise 1

Give the Spanish for "the red shoes".

Answer

los zapatos rojos. los zapatos rojos. Plural masculine noun, so rojos.

Exercise 2

Give the Spanish for "a green skirt".

Answer

una falda verde. una falda verde. Verde has the same form for masculine and feminine.

Exercise 3

Complete with the right form of este: ___ camisetas son muy baratas.

Answer

Estas. Estas camisetas son muy baratas. Feminine plural.

Exercise 4

Complete with the right form of aquel: ¿Cuánto cuesta ___ abrigo?

Answer

aquel. ¿Cuánto cuesta aquel abrigo? Masculine singular, with no -o.

Exercise 5

Answer with a pronoun: ¿Compras la bufanda? — Yes, I'm buying it.

Answer

Sí, la compro. Sí, la compro. La bufanda is feminine.

Exercise 6

How do you say "I'll take them" about some boots (las botas)?

Answer

Me las llevo. Me las llevo.

Exercise 7

Write 2,500 in words.

Answer

dos mil quinientos. dos mil quinientos. Mil does not change in the plural.

Exercise 8

Ask the price of some trousers.

Answer

¿Cuánto cuestan los pantalones? ¿Cuánto cuestan los pantalones? Plural subject, so cuestan.

Exercise 9

Translate: "This shop is cheaper than that one."

Answer

Esta tienda es más barata que esa. Tienda is feminine, so esta, barata and esa.

Exercise 10

Correct the two mistakes: ¿El jersey? La compro. Es más bueno que el otro.

Answer

¿El jersey? Lo compro. Es mejor que el otro. El jersey is masculine, so lo; for quality, use mejor rather than más bueno.

docs.title: 13.9 Quiz
docs.text:
Quiz: shopping and clothes

Exercise 11

___ zapatos de aquí son muy cómodos.

  1. Este
  2. Estos
  3. Estas
  4. Esto
Answer

Estos

Zapatos is masculine plural, so estos.

Exercise 12

¿La camiseta? Sí, ___ quiero en negro.

  1. lo
  2. la
  3. los
  4. le
Answer

la

La camiseta is feminine singular, so la.

Exercise 13

Los pantalones me ___ largos.

Hint: quedar, plural

Answer

quedan

The trousers are the subject, so quedan.

Exercise 14

Esta chaqueta es ___ cara como aquella.

Answer

tan

tan … como means as … as.

Exercise 15

Write 3,000 in words.

Answer

tres mil

Exercise 16

Match the Spanish to the English.

ABla tallain cashel númerothe fitting roomen efectivothe size of clothesel probadorthe size of shoes Answer

la talla — the size of clothes; el número — the size of shoes; en efectivo — in cash; el probador — the fitting room

Exercise 17

Put the words in order: "I'm going to try it on."

Words: lo / voy / a / probar. / Me

Answer

Me lo voy a probar.

Exercise 18

Tap the wrong word.

Mi hermano compra unas camisas blancos.

Answer

Wrong word: blancos.

Corrected: Mi hermano compra unas camisas blancas.

Camisas is feminine plural, so blancas.

Exercise 19

Write what you hear.

Dictation. Have someone read the sentence aloud, then write it down.

Busco unos pantalones negros de la talla cuarenta.

Answer

Busco unos pantalones negros de la talla cuarenta.

Exercise 20

Say it aloud.

¿Cuánto cuesta esta camisa? Me la llevo.

Answer

Say: ¿Cuánto cuesta esta camisa? Me la llevo.

docs.title: Lesson 1: Sounds, Letters and Stress
docs.text:
Los sonidos, las letras y el acento

Spanish is a gift to the learner in one respect: it is written almost exactly as it is spoken. Once you know the sound of each letter and one short set of rules for stress, you can read aloud any Spanish word you meet, even one you have never seen, and spell almost any word you hear. English cannot promise that (think of though, through, tough and cough). This lesson gives you the whole system: the alphabet and the names of the letters, the five pure vowels, the consonants that behave differently from English, and the rules that tell you which syllable to stress and when to write an accent. Take it slowly and use the listen buttons a great deal: good habits formed now will make everything after this easier.

Learning outcomes

By the end of this lesson you will be able to:

  • say the names of the letters and spell your name aloud;
  • pronounce the five Spanish vowels clearly and without gliding;
  • pronounce the consonants that differ from English: b/v, c, d, g, h, j, ll, ñ, qu, r/rr, y, z;
  • find the stressed syllable of any written word, and know when a written accent is needed;
  • recognise the main differences between the pronunciation of Spain and of Latin America.

docs.title: 1.1 Dialogue: spelling your name
docs.text:
Oliver arrives at a small hotel in Granada. The receptionist needs to write his surname, which is not a Spanish name, so she asks him to spell it. Listen, then read along.

  • Recepcionista: Buenas tardes. ¿Su nombre, por favor? — Good afternoon. Your name, please?
  • Oliver: Oliver Whitfield. — Oliver Whitfield.
  • Recepcionista: Perdón, ¿cómo se escribe su apellido? — Sorry, how do you spell your surname?
  • Oliver: Uve doble, hache, i, te, efe, i, e, ele, de. — W, H, I, T, F, I, E, L, D.
  • Recepcionista: ¿Con hache después de la uve doble? — With an H after the W?
  • Oliver: Sí, con hache. — Yes, with an H.
  • Recepcionista: Muy bien. ¿Y su correo electrónico? — Very good. And your email address?
  • Oliver: Oliver, punto, uve doble, arroba, ejemplo, punto, com. — oliver.w@ejemplo.com
  • Recepcionista: Perfecto. Su habitación es la doce. ¡Bienvenido a Granada! — Perfect. Your room is number twelve. Welcome to Granada!
  • Oliver: Muchas gracias. — Thank you very much.

Useful words from the dialogue: el nombre [NOHM-breh], first name; el apellido [ah-peh-YEE-doh], surname; ¿Cómo se escribe? [KOH-moh seh ehs-KREE-beh], how is it spelt?; el punto, dot; la arroba [ah-RROH-bah], the @ sign.

How to read the sound guides

Each new word in this book has a sound guide in square brackets, written with English spelling: [ah-peh-YEE-doh]. Syllables are separated by hyphens and the stressed syllable is in capitals. Read ah as in father, eh as in bet, ee as in see, oh as in more (without the r), oo as in food. rr means a rolled r, and th means the th of thin. The guides are only an aid: the recordings are the real model.

docs.title: 1.2 Vocabulary: the alphabet
docs.text:
The Spanish alphabet has 27 letters: the 26 of English plus ñ. The names of the letters are feminine (la a, la be), and you need them for spelling names, addresses and email addresses.

Letter Name Sounds like Example a a [ah] casa house b be [beh] bueno good c ce [theh] Spain, [seh] Latin America cine cinema, casa house d de [deh] dos two e e [eh] mesa table f efe [EH-feh] foto photo g ge [heh] (throaty h) gato cat, gente people h hache [AH-cheh] hola hello (silent h) i i [ee] sí yes j jota [HOH-tah] (throaty h) jamón ham k ka [kah] kilo kilo l ele [EH-leh] libro book m eme [EH-meh] madre mother n ene [EH-neh] no no ñ eñe [EH-nyeh] España Spain o o [oh] ojo eye p pe [peh] padre father q cu [koo] queso cheese r erre [EH-rreh] pero but, perro dog s ese [EH-seh] sol sun t te [teh] tres three u u [oo] uno one v uve [OO-beh] vino wine w uve doble [OO-beh DOH-bleh] wifi wifi x equis [EH-kees] taxi taxi y ye [yeh] yo I z zeta [THEH-tah] Spain, [SEH-tah] Latin America zapato shoe

Table 1.1. The alphabet. The letters k and w appear only in words borrowed from other languages.

A few names vary from country to country. V is uve in Spain, but many Latin Americans say ve or ve corta ("short v"), and then call b be larga or be alta to tell them apart. W is uve doble in Spain and doble ve or doble u in much of Latin America. Y has the official name ye, but the older name i griega ("Greek i") is still very common.

ch, ll and rr

Older dictionaries treat ch and ll as separate letters, and you may still see them listed that way. Since 2010 the Spanish academies count them as pairs of letters (digraphs), like rr, and not as letters of the alphabet. They still have their own sounds: ch as in church (chocolate), ll as explained below, and rr always rolled.

docs.title: 1.3 The five vowels
docs.text:
English has around a dozen vowel sounds, depending on the accent, and writes them in confusing ways. Spanish has five, and each letter always has the same sound.

Vowel Sound As in English Examples a [ah] father, but shorter mamá, casa, hablar e [eh] bet mesa, tres, verde i [ee] see, but shorter sí, libro, mil o [oh] more without the r no, ocho, todo u [oo] food, but shorter uno, luna, azul

Table 1.2. The five vowels. They are short, clear and never swallowed.

Three habits from English will give you a foreign accent, so watch for them:

  1. Do not glide. English no is really "noh-oo", and say is "seh-ee". Spanish no is one pure vowel: keep your lips still until the sound ends. Say no, no, no and se, se, se and feel the difference.
  2. Do not weaken unstressed vowels. In English the unstressed vowels of banana become a vague "uh" (buh-NA-nuh). In Spanish every vowel keeps its full sound: banana is [bah-NAH-nah], three clear a's. Likewise Canadá, chocolate, animal.
  3. Do not change the vowel before r. The a of English car changes colour before the r; in carta [KAR-tah] the a stays a plain [ah].

docs.title: Two vowels together
docs.text:
The vowels a, e, o are called strong and i, u weak. A weak vowel next to another vowel joins it in the same syllable, making a diphthong:

Diphthong Example Diphthong Example ai, ay aire, hay ia familia ei, ey seis, rey ie bien oi, oy hoy io adiós au auto ua agua eu Europa ue bueno iu ciudad ui, uy muy

Table 1.3. Diphthongs. Each pair is said in one syllable: bien is one syllable, [byehn].

Two strong vowels stay in separate syllables: museo [moo-SEH-oh], idea [ee-DEH-ah], leer [leh-EHR]. A written accent on the weak vowel also splits a diphthong, so the two vowels are said separately: día [DEE-ah], país [pah-EES], río [RREE-oh]. Compare seis (one syllable) with país (two).

docs.title: 1.4 The consonants
docs.text:
Most Spanish consonants sound much as they do in English: f, k, l, m, n, p, s, t give no trouble, though p, t and k are said without the small puff of air that follows them in English pin, tin, kin. (Hold a sheet of paper in front of your mouth: it should hardly move when you say papá.) The consonants below need attention.

Letters The rule Examples b, v The same sound. At the start of a phrase and after m or n, a firm [b]; between vowels, a soft [b] with the lips barely touching. vino, bien, un vaso, uva, Cuba c before a, o, u; qu before e, i [k]. The u of qu is silent. casa, cosa, queso, quince c before e, i; z [th] in most of Spain, [s] in Latin America, the Canary Islands and parts of southern Spain. cinco, gracias, zapato, azul ch [ch] as in church. chico, noche d At the start and after n or l, [d] with the tongue against the teeth; between vowels and at the end of a word, soft, like the th of this. dos, nada, ciudad, Madrid g before a, o, u; gu before e, i Hard [g], as in go; soft between vowels. The u of gu is silent. gato, amigo, guitarra, guerra g before e, i; j A throaty [h], like ch in Scottish loch; softer, like English h, in much of Latin America. gente, girar, jamón, hijo gü [gw]: the two dots tell you to say the u. pingüino, bilingüe h Always silent. hola, hora, ahora ll, y [y] as in yes for most speakers; [sh] or [zh] in Argentina and Uruguay. Y alone, or at the end of a word, is the vowel [ee]. llamo, calle, yo, y, muy ñ [ny], like the ny of canyon. año, mañana, niño r One quick tap of the tongue, like the tt of American better. pero, caro, hablar rr, and r at the start of a word or after l, n, s A rolled r: several fast taps. perro, rojo, Enrique, alrededor x [ks] between vowels; often [s] before a consonant. In México, Oaxaca and a few other names, it is the throaty [h] of j. taxi, examen, extra, México

Table 1.4. The consonants that differ from English.

docs.title: The rolled r
docs.text:
The rolled r is the sound learners worry about most. It matters, because it can change the meaning of a word:

  • pero (but) and perro (dog)
  • caro (expensive) and carro (car, in Latin America)
  • cero (zero) and cerro (hill)

To find the single tap, say the English phrase put it on quickly, American-style: the t in the middle is almost exactly a Spanish r, so "pot-a" becomes para. For the roll, relax the tip of your tongue just behind your upper teeth and blow so that it flutters. Practising with a d in front helps: d-rrr, then ropa, rápido, arroz. If you cannot roll it yet, do not give up speaking: use a strong single tap, and keep practising a few seconds a day. Many native speakers took years as children too.

Common mistake: pronouncing the h

The h is always silent: hotel is [oh-TEHL], hospital is [ohs-pee-TAHL], hay sounds exactly like ay. The breathy h-sound of English is written j (or g before e and i) in Spanish: jardín [har-DEEN], garden.

Spelling follows sound

Because c, g and z change sound before e and i, Spanish changes the spelling to keep the sound the same when a word changes. The [k] sound is ca, que, qui, co, cu; the [g] sound is ga, gue, gui, go, gu; the [th] or [s] sound of z is za, ce, ci, zo, zu. So lápiz (pencil) becomes lápices in the plural, and chico becomes chiquito. You will see this again and again.

docs.title: 1.5 Stress and the written accent
docs.text:
Every Spanish word of more than one syllable has one stressed syllable, said a little louder and longer. Stress can change meaning: papa [PAH-pah] is a potato (in Latin America) or the Pope, but papá [pah-PAH] is dad. Fortunately, the spelling always tells you where the stress goes. There are three rules.

Figure 1.1 Finding the stress. A decision chart. First ask whether the word has a written accent; if so, stress that vowel. If not, ask whether it ends in a vowel, n or s; if so, stress the next-to-last syllable; otherwise stress the last syllable.

Rule 1. A word that ends in a vowel, -n or -s is stressed on the next-to-last syllable:

  • casa [KAH-sah], hablan [AH-blahn], lunes [LOO-nehs], amigo [ah-MEE-goh], tomate [toh-MAH-teh]

Rule 2. A word that ends in any other consonant is stressed on the last syllable:

  • hablar [ah-BLAR], ciudad [syoo-DAHD], español [ehs-pah-NYOHL], reloj [rreh-LOH]

Rule 3. A word that breaks rules 1 and 2 carries a written accent on the stressed vowel. The accent is always the acute accent (´), slanting up to the right:

  • café, sofá, canción, inglés: they end in a vowel, n or s, but are stressed on the last syllable.
  • lápiz, árbol, fácil, césped: they end in another consonant, but are stressed on the next-to-last.
  • música, teléfono, sábado, miércoles, rápido: words stressed three or more syllables from the end always have a written accent, whatever their last letter.

Read the rules in reverse and they also tell you how to spell: if you hear the stress where rules 1 and 2 put it, write no accent; if you hear it anywhere else, write an accent on that vowel.

Worked example: why inglés loses its accent in inglesa

  1. inglés is said [een-GLEHS], stressed on the last syllable. It ends in -s, so rule 1 would put the stress on in-. The real stress breaks the rule, so it needs an accent: inglés.
  2. inglesa is said [een-GLEH-sah]. The stress has not moved, but there is now an extra syllable. It ends in a vowel and is stressed on the next-to-last syllable, exactly as rule 1 expects. No accent: inglesa.
  3. The same reasoning explains canción → canciones and alemán → alemana, and, the other way round, joven → jóvenes: the plural adds a syllable, so the stress is now three from the end and needs an accent.

docs.title: Accents that tell words apart
docs.text:
A handful of short words carry an accent only to distinguish them from another word spelt the same way. The pronunciation is the same; the meaning differs.

With accent Meaning Without accent Meaning tú you tu your él he el the sí yes si if mí me (after a preposition) mi my té tea te you, yourself (object) sé I know se himself, herself más more mas but (literary) qué, cómo, dónde what? how? where? que, como, donde that, as, where (not a question)

Table 1.5. Accents that distinguish meaning.

Question words always carry the accent, in direct and indirect questions: ¿Dónde vives? (Where do you live?), No sé dónde vive. (I don't know where he lives.) Capital letters keep their accents too: Ángel, Óscar, ÁFRICA.

Common mistake: leaving accents out

An accent is part of the spelling, not an optional extra. papa and papá, esta (this) and está (is), hablo (I speak) and habló (he spoke) are different words. On a phone, hold down the vowel to get the accented letter; on a computer, set up a Spanish or "US International" keyboard.

docs.title: Punctuation: ¿ and ¡
docs.text: Questions and exclamations are marked at both ends: ¿Cómo estás?, ¡Qué bonito! The opening mark goes where the question or exclamation begins, which is not always the start of the sentence: Y tú, ¿de dónde eres? In speech, a yes/no question is shown only by the rising tune of the voice: Hablas español. (You speak Spanish.) ¿Hablas español? (Do you speak Spanish?)

docs.title: Read aloud
docs.text:
Read each word aloud before you press the listen button, then compare. Look first for the stress, using the three rules.

Word Stressed syllable Meaning ventana ven-TA-na window universidad u-ni-ver-si-DAD university examen e-XA-men exam jardín jar-DÍN garden azúcar a-ZÚ-car sugar pájaro PÁ-ja-ro bird profesor pro-fe-SOR teacher gracias GRA-cias thank you

Table 1.6. Find the stressed syllable. Switch on Practice to hide the answers.

docs.title: Tongue twisters
docs.text:
Spanish speakers use trabalenguas, "tongue-tanglers", to practise difficult sounds. Here are two traditional ones.

  • Erre con erre, cigarro; erre con erre, barril. Rápido ruedan los carros cargados de azúcar del ferrocarril. — R with r, cigar; r with r, barrel. Fast roll the wagons loaded with sugar of the railway. (The rolled r.)
  • Tres tristes tigres tragaban trigo en un trigal. — Three sad tigers were swallowing wheat in a wheat field. (The tapped r after t.)

docs.title: Spelling aloud
docs.text:
• ¿Cómo se escribe tu nombre? — How do you spell your name?
  • ¿Se escribe con be o con uve? — Is it spelt with a b or a v? (See Exercise 9.)
  • Jota, o, ese, e. José, con acento en la e. — J, O, S, E. José, with an accent on the e.
  • Ele, o, pe, e, zeta. López, con acento en la o. — L, O, P, E, Z. López, with an accent on the o.

When spelling, say con acento or con tilde for a written accent (both are used; tilde is the technical word), mayúscula for a capital letter and minúscula for a small one.

Say it

Spell your own first name and surname aloud, letter by letter, as Oliver did. Then say these five words, paying attention to the vowels and the r: pero, perro, caro, carro, ahora.

docs.title: 1.7 Culture: one language, many accents
docs.text:
Spanish is the official language of Spain, Mexico, most of Central and South America, Cuba, the Dominican Republic, Puerto Rico and Equatorial Guinea, and it is spoken by millions of people in the United States. By most counts it is the second most widely spoken native language in the world, after Mandarin Chinese. It goes by two names: español and castellano (Castilian, after Castile, the kingdom in which it grew up). Both are correct. Castellano is often preferred in Spain, where Catalan, Galician and Basque are also spoken, and in several South American countries; español is usual in Mexico and elsewhere.

Two ways to say cinco. The most noticeable difference between Spain and Latin America is the letter z, and c before e and i. Most speakers in central and northern Spain distinguish casa (house) from caza (hunting): the second has a th sound. All Latin Americans, Canary Islanders and many Andalusians say both with an [s], which is called seseo. Both pronunciations are standard and correct, so choose one and be consistent. The idea that the Spanish th comes from a king with a lisp is a popular myth; it is the result of ordinary sound changes over centuries.

Other differences you will hear.

  • ll and y. Nearly everywhere they sound the same, [y]. In Argentina and Uruguay both sound like English sh or the s of pleasure: yo me llamo sounds like "sho meh SHAH-moh".
  • s at the end of a syllable. In the Caribbean, much of the coast of Latin America, Andalusia and the Canary Islands, it is often softened to a breath, [h], or dropped: los dos may sound like "loh doh".
  • j. In Spain, the j is a strong, rasping sound; in Mexico, Colombia and the Caribbean it is often a soft [h].

None of this should worry you. Educated speakers from Madrid, Mexico City, Bogotá and Buenos Aires understand each other without difficulty, just as speakers from London, Texas and Sydney do. The sounds this book gives are understood everywhere.

The academies. Spanish has an official referee for spelling and grammar: the Real Academia Española (RAE), founded in Madrid in 1713, which today works together with the academies of the other Spanish-speaking countries in the Association of Academies of the Spanish Language (ASALE). Their dictionary and spelling rules are freely available online, and they are the source for the alphabet in this lesson.

The ñ. The letter ñ began in medieval manuscripts as a small n written above another n, to save space; the wavy line is the remains of that n. Today it is a symbol of the language itself, and Spanish speakers have defended it whenever keyboards and computer systems threatened to leave it out.

docs.title: 1.8 Summary
docs.text:
Summary

  • Spanish is written as it is spoken. The alphabet has 27 letters: the English 26 plus ñ. ch, ll, rr are pairs of letters with their own sounds.
  • There are five vowels, always short and pure: a, e, i, o, u. Never glide and never reduce an unstressed vowel to "uh".
  • b = v; h is silent; j and g before e, i are a throaty h; ll and y sound like y (sh in Argentina); ñ is ny; r is a tap and rr a roll; c before e, i and z are th in most of Spain and s in Latin America.
  • Stress: words ending in a vowel, -n or -s are stressed on the next-to-last syllable; words ending in another consonant on the last; a written accent marks every exception and every word stressed three syllables from the end.
  • Accents also distinguish words (tú / tu, sí / si, él / el) and mark question words (qué, dónde, cómo).
  • Questions and exclamations open with ¿ and ¡.

docs.title: 1.9 Exercises
docs.text:
Exercise 1

How many letters does the Spanish alphabet have?

Answer

27. The 26 letters of English plus ñ.

Exercise 2

Which letter of the Spanish alphabet is always silent?

Answer

h. hola, hotel, ahora: the h is never pronounced.

Exercise 3

Underline (or say) the stressed syllable: comer, comen, comedor.

Answer

co-MER (ends in r: last syllable), CO-men (ends in n: next-to-last), co-me-DOR (ends in r: last syllable).

Exercise 4

One of these words needs a written accent. Which one? arbol, mesa, papel.

Answer

árbol. It is stressed on ár-, the next-to-last syllable, but ends in -l, so rule 2 would put the stress on the last syllable. The accent marks the exception. mesa and papel follow the rules.

Exercise 5

The word telefono is stressed on the second syllable, -le-. Write it correctly.

Answer

teléfono. teléfono: stressed three syllables from the end, so it always has an accent.

Exercise 6

Is the g in gente hard, like English go, or throaty, like the Spanish j?

Answer

throaty. Before e and i, g sounds like the Spanish j. For a hard g before e or i, Spanish writes gu: guerra, guitarra.

Exercise 7

How many syllables are there in bueno, in día and in museo?

Answer

bueno: two (bue-no, ue is a diphthong). día: two (dí-a, the accent splits the vowels). museo: three (mu-se-o, e and o are both strong).

Exercise 8

Spell the name Gutiérrez aloud, using the names of the letters.

Answer

Ge, u, te, i, e con acento, erre, erre, e, zeta. You can also say doble erre for rr.

Exercise 9

In Spanish, vaca (cow) and baca (roof rack) sound exactly the same. Why do Spanish speakers often ask ¿con be o con uve? when spelling?

Answer

Because b and v have the same sound, a listener cannot tell from the sound which letter a word has, so the speller has to say it. The same happens with silent h: ¿con hache o sin hache?

Exercise 10

Choose the right word for each meaning: (a) Yes, I'm English: si / sí; (b) your name: tu / tú; (c) the book: el / él.

Answer

(a) sí; (b) tu; (c) el.

docs.title: 1.10 Quiz
docs.text:
Quiz: sounds, letters and stress

Exercise 11

Which word has a silent letter?

  1. hora
  2. gato
  3. mesa
  4. taxi
Answer

hora

The h is always silent in Spanish.

Exercise 12

In which word is the r rolled?

  1. pero
  2. caro
  3. perro
  4. hablar
Answer

perro

rr is always rolled; a single r between vowels is one tap.

Exercise 13

Where is the stress in ciudad?

  1. ciu-
  2. -dad
Answer

-dad

It ends in d, a consonant other than n or s, so the stress falls on the last syllable.

Exercise 14

Write correctly, with its accent: musica

Answer

música

Stressed three syllables from the end, so it always carries an accent.

Exercise 15

The name of the letter ñ is ___.

Answer

eñe

Exercise 16

Match each letter to its Spanish name.

ABhuvejzetavhachezjota Answer

h — hache; j — jota; v — uve; z — zeta

Exercise 17

Tap the word that is missing its written accent.

El cafe es para mi madre.

Answer

Wrong word: cafe.

Corrected: El café es para mi madre.

café ends in a vowel but is stressed on the last syllable, so it needs an accent. mi (my) has no accent.

Exercise 18

Put the words in order: "How do you spell your surname?" (polite)

Words: se / apellido? / su / ¿Cómo / escribe

Answer

¿Cómo se escribe su apellido?

Exercise 19

Write what you hear.

Dictation. Have someone read the sentence aloud, then write it down.

El perro de mi amigo se llama Rayo.

Answer

El perro de mi amigo se llama Rayo.

Exercise 20

Say it aloud, rolling the r of the second word.

Pero el perro es caro.

Answer

Say: Pero el perro es caro.

docs.title: Lesson 9: The City and Directions
docs.text:
La ciudad y las direcciones

Even with a phone in your pocket, you will often need to ask the way: the battery is flat, the map shows two cathedrals, or the station has three entrances. Asking a stranger is also one of the easiest ways to start a real conversation in Spanish. In this lesson you learn the names of the places in a town, how to ask where something is and whether there is one nearby, how to say where things are with prepositions of place, and how to understand the answer: straight on, turn left, take the second street, cross the square.

Learning outcomes

By the end of this lesson you will be able to:

  • name the main places and features of a town;
  • ask ¿Dónde está …? about a particular place and ¿Hay un … por aquí? about any place of a kind;
  • say where things are with cerca de, lejos de, al lado de, enfrente de, entre and other prepositions;
  • understand and give directions in the usted and tú forms;
  • use the ordinal numbers primero to quinto and say how to get somewhere by transport or on foot.

masculinefeminineplural

docs.title: 9.1 Dialogue: where is the museum?
docs.text:
Daniel has arrived in a small town for the weekend. He has just got off the bus and stops a woman in the street. The places are on the map in Figure 9.1.

  • Daniel: Perdone, señora. ¿Dónde está el museo, por favor? — Excuse me, madam. Where is the museum, please?
  • Señora: ¿El museo? Está muy cerca. Siga todo recto por la calle Mayor. — The museum? It's very close. Go straight on along Calle Mayor.
  • Daniel: ¿Todo recto? — Straight on?
  • Señora: Sí. Pase la primera calle y continúe hasta la segunda. El museo está en la esquina, a la derecha, enfrente de la iglesia. — Yes. Go past the first street and carry on to the second. The museum is on the corner, on the right, opposite the church.
  • Daniel: ¿Está lejos? — Is it far?
  • Señora: No, está a cinco minutos a pie. — No, it's five minutes on foot.
  • Daniel: Muchas gracias. Y otra pregunta: ¿hay una farmacia por aquí? — Thank you very much. And another question: is there a chemist's near here?
  • Señora: Sí, hay una aquí mismo, a la derecha, en la esquina. — Yes, there's one right here, on the right, on the corner.
  • Daniel: ¡Perfecto! ¿Y la estación de tren? — Perfect! And the railway station?
  • Señora: Para la estación, tome la segunda calle a la derecha. La estación está al final de la calle, a la izquierda. — For the station, take the second street on the right. The station is at the end of the street, on the left.
  • Daniel: Muy amable. ¡Adiós! — That's very kind of you. Goodbye!
  • Señora: De nada. ¡Que disfrute del museo! — You're welcome. Enjoy the museum!

Notice:

  1. Daniel says ¿Dónde está el museo? about a particular museum, but ¿Hay una farmacia? when any chemist's will do.
  2. The woman uses the polite usted form for directions: siga, pase, tome. Between friends you would hear sigue, pasa, toma.
  3. Location uses estar, as you learned in Lesson 5: el museo está en la esquina.
  4. al lado del hotel: de + el contracts to del (Lesson 4).

docs.title: Places
docs.text:
Spanish Sounds like English la ciudad [syoo-DAHD] town, city el centro [SEHN-troh] the centre el barrio [BAH-rryoh] neighbourhood, district la calle [KAH-yeh] street la avenida [ah-beh-NEE-dah] avenue la plaza [PLAH-sah] square el parque [PAR-keh] park el banco [BAHN-koh] bank; also bench el cajero automático [kah-HEH-roh ow-toh-MAH-tee-koh] cash machine, ATM la farmacia [far-MAH-syah] chemist's, pharmacy el hospital [ohs-pee-TAHL] hospital (the h is silent) el museo [moo-SEH-oh] museum la iglesia [ee-GLEH-syah] church la catedral [kah-teh-DRAHL] cathedral el ayuntamiento [ah-yoon-tah-MYEHN-toh] town hall el mercado [mehr-KAH-doh] market el supermercado [soo-pehr-mehr-KAH-doh] supermarket la estación de tren [ehs-tah-SYOHN deh TREHN] railway station la estación de autobuses [ow-toh-BOO-sehs] bus station la parada de autobús [pah-RAH-dah] bus stop la oficina de turismo [oh-fee-SEE-nah deh too-REES-moh] tourist office la biblioteca [bee-blyoh-TEH-kah] library el cine, el teatro [SEE-neh, teh-AH-troh] cinema, theatre el aeropuerto [ah-eh-roh-PWEHR-toh] airport

Table 9.1. Places in town.

False friend: la librería

la librería is a bookshop. A library, where you borrow books, is la biblioteca.

docs.title: Features of the street
docs.text:
Spanish English Spanish English la esquina corner el semáforo traffic lights el cruce crossroads la rotonda roundabout el puente bridge el río river el paso de peatones pedestrian crossing la acera pavement, sidewalk el final de la calle the end of the street la entrada, la salida entrance, exit

Table 9.2. Features of the street.

docs.title: Getting about
docs.text:
Spanish English en autobús by bus en metro by underground, subway en tren by train en taxi by taxi en coche (Spain), en carro, en auto (Latin America) by car en bicicleta, en bici by bicycle a pie on foot andando (Spain), caminando (everywhere) walking

Table 9.3. Transport. Spanish says "in" a vehicle (en autobús) but "to foot" (a pie).

docs.title: ¿Dónde está …? or ¿Hay …?
docs.text:
You met both estar for location (Lesson 5) and hay, "there is, there are" (Lesson 4). In the street they divide the work cleanly:

You want Ask Example a particular place you know exists ¿Dónde está + el / la …? ¿Dónde está la catedral? — Where is the cathedral? any place of a kind ¿Hay + un / una … por aquí? ¿Hay un cajero por aquí? — Is there a cash machine near here? several particular places ¿Dónde están + los / las …? ¿Dónde están los servicios? — Where are the toilets?

Table 9.4. Asking where. hay never changes: hay un banco, hay dos bancos.

The answers follow the same pattern: La catedral está en la plaza. Sí, hay uno en la esquina. Notice that un becomes uno when it stands alone without its noun: ¿Hay un banco? — Sí, hay uno allí. The feminine stays una.

Common mistake: hay el …

Do not use hay with the definite article. Not Hay el museo en la plaza, but El museo está en la plaza (a particular museum) or Hay un museo en la plaza (there is a museum there).

To be polite, start with Perdone or Disculpe ("Excuse me", to usted), or with Perdona or Disculpa to a young person you would call tú. Another useful opener is ¿Sabe dónde está …? — "Do you know where … is?"

docs.title: Prepositions of place
docs.text:
Figure 9.1 The town centre. A small street map. Calle Mayor runs straight up from the point marked "Estás aquí". The first street across it is Calle del Sol, the second is Calle de la Paz. Between the start and Calle del Sol are the bank on the left and the chemist's on the right. Between Calle del Sol and Calle de la Paz are the park and the market on the left, and the hotel on the right. Beyond Calle de la Paz are the church on the left, and the museum and, further right, the station. Spanish English Example from Figure 9.1 cerca de near El banco está cerca de la farmacia. lejos de far from La estación está lejos del banco. al lado de next to El parque está al lado del mercado. enfrente de opposite El museo está enfrente de la iglesia. delante de in front of La parada está delante del hotel. detrás de behind El aparcamiento está detrás del mercado. entre … y … between … and … El hotel está entre la farmacia y el museo. a la derecha de to the right of La estación está a la derecha del museo. a la izquierda de to the left of El parque está a la izquierda del mercado. en la esquina on the corner La farmacia está en la esquina. al final de at the end of La estación está al final de la calle. en in, on, at El hotel está en la calle Mayor.

Table 9.5. Prepositions of place. The parking and the bus stop are not drawn on the map.

Almost all of these end in de, and de + el becomes del: al lado del hotel, but al lado de la farmacia, al lado de los bancos. Without a noun after them, the de disappears: Está cerca. Está a la derecha. Está enfrente.

Aquí means "here", ahí "there" (near you), and allí "over there". Aquí mismo is "right here".

docs.title: How far is it?
docs.text:
Distance and time are introduced with a:

  • ¿Está lejos? — No, está a cinco minutos. — Is it far? — No, it's five minutes away.
  • Está a diez minutos a pie. — It's ten minutes on foot.
  • Está a dos kilómetros del centro. — It's two kilometres from the centre.
  • Está a veinte minutos en autobús. — It's twenty minutes by bus.

To ask how to get somewhere, use ¿Cómo llego a …? ("How do I get to …?"), from the regular verb llegar, "to arrive". Remember a + el = al: ¿Cómo llego al museo?, ¿Cómo llego a la estación?

docs.title: Direction phrases, usted and tú
docs.text:
Directions use a verb form called the imperative, the form for instructions. You will study it properly later; for now, learn these phrases as they are. The usted form is what a stranger will usually say to you; the tú form is what friends say to each other.

To usted To tú English siga todo recto sigue todo recto go straight on gire a la derecha gira a la derecha turn right gire a la izquierda gira a la izquierda turn left tome la primera calle toma la primera calle take the first street cruce la plaza cruza la plaza cross the square pase el semáforo pasa el semáforo go past the traffic lights continúe hasta el puente continúa hasta el puente carry on as far as the bridge suba la calle sube la calle go up the street baje la calle baja la calle go down the street

Table 9.6. Directions. Practice hides the verbs.

Notice the swap of vowels: for an -ar verb, the usted instruction ends in -e (girar → gire) and the tú instruction in -a (gira, the same as "he turns"). For seguir ("to follow, continue"), an irregular -ir verb, the forms are siga and sigue.

Derecha and derecho

a la derecha means "to the right". todo derecho or siga derecho means "straight on", and is the usual expression in Latin America; in Spain people mostly say todo recto. In Latin America you will also hear doble a la derecha ("turn right", from doblar) instead of gire. Listen for the last vowel: derecha is a side, derecho is ahead.

Many people avoid the imperative altogether and simply describe the route in the present tense, which you already know from Lesson 6:

  • Sigues todo recto, giras a la izquierda y el banco está allí. — You go straight on, you turn left and the bank is there.
  • Usted cruza la plaza y toma la segunda calle. — You cross the square and take the second street.

docs.title: Ordinal numbers
docs.text:
Number Masculine Feminine English 1.º / 1.ª primero (primer) primera first 2.º / 2.ª segundo segunda second 3.º / 3.ª tercero (tercer) tercera third 4.º / 4.ª cuarto cuarta fourth 5.º / 5.ª quinto quinta fifth

Table 9.7. Ordinal numbers. They are adjectives, so they agree with the noun.

  • Ordinals usually come before the noun and agree with it: la segunda calle, el cuarto piso, las primeras casas.
  • primero and tercero drop the -o before a masculine singular noun, like bueno (Lesson 7): el primer semáforo, el tercer piso, but la primera calle.
  • They are abbreviated with a raised o or a: 1.º, 2.ª. Above about tenth, people use ordinary numbers: el piso doce.

Worked example: from the start to the station

Use Figure 9.1. You are at "Estás aquí". Give directions to the station, first to a stranger (usted), then to a friend (tú).

  1. Start: you face up Calle Mayor. Siga todo recto por la calle Mayor.
  2. The first street is Calle del Sol; the station is on Calle de la Paz, the second. Tome la segunda calle a la derecha.
  3. Walking right along Calle de la Paz, the station is on your left, at the end: La estación está al final de la calle, a la izquierda.

To a friend: Sigue todo recto, toma la segunda calle a la derecha, y la estación está al final, a la izquierda.

docs.title: Where is it?
docs.text:
Look at Figure 9.1 and answer each question aloud. Then listen to the answer.

Question Answer ¿Dónde está la farmacia? Está en la calle Mayor, en la esquina, enfrente del banco. ¿Dónde está el hotel? Está entre la farmacia y el museo. ¿Hay un parque por aquí? Sí, hay uno al lado del mercado. ¿Dónde está la iglesia? Está enfrente del museo. ¿Está lejos la estación? No, está a cinco minutos a pie.

Table 9.8. Questions and answers about the map.

docs.title: Follow the directions
docs.text:
Start at "Estás aquí" each time. Listen and find where you end up.

  • Siga todo recto y tome la primera calle a la izquierda. Está a la derecha, en la esquina. — (the market)
  • Siga todo recto, pase la calle del Sol, y está a la derecha, antes de la calle de la Paz. — (the hotel)
  • Está aquí mismo, a la izquierda, en la esquina. — (the bank)
  • Siga todo recto hasta la calle de la Paz y cruce. Está a la izquierda. — (the church)

Say it

Choose a place near where you live or study. Explain to a visitor (usted) how to get there from your front door, in three or four instructions. For example:

Al salir, gire a la izquierda. Siga todo recto hasta el semáforo. Cruce la calle y tome la segunda calle a la derecha. El supermercado está al final, enfrente del parque.

docs.title: 9.6 Culture: towns in Spain and Latin America
docs.text:
The square at the heart. Most Spanish towns have a main square, often called la plaza mayor, with the town hall and the main church around it; the one in Salamanca, where our characters study, is among the most admired in Spain. Many Latin American cities founded during the colonial period were laid out on a grid of straight streets around a central square. In Peru, Chile and several other countries it is called la plaza de armas; in Mexico City and other Mexican cities, el zócalo. Life happens in the square: people meet there, children play there in the evening, and it is the natural landmark for any directions.

Blocks. In Latin America, distances in town are often given in blocks: está a tres cuadras, "it's three blocks away". In Spain a block of buildings is una manzana (the same word as "apple"), but people more often count streets: la tercera calle.

Addresses. A Spanish address puts the street first and the number after it, followed by the floor and the door: Calle Mayor, 12, 3.º izquierda means number 12, third floor, the flat on the left. Spaniards call the ground floor la planta baja, so their "first floor" is one floor up, as in British English. In much of Latin America the ground floor is el primer piso, as in American English.

Transport words. The bus has different names in different places:

Place Bus Underground Spain el autobús, el bus el metro Mexico el camión, el autobús el metro Argentina el colectivo el subte (Buenos Aires) Cuba, Puerto Rico, the Canary Islands la guagua —

Table 9.9. Words for the bus and the underground.

Asking a stranger. People in Spain and Latin America are generally happy to help, and sometimes they will walk with you part of the way. Speak slowly and politely, use usted with older people, and if the answer is too fast, say Más despacio, por favor ("More slowly, please") or ¿Puede repetir, por favor? ("Could you repeat, please?").

docs.title: 9.7 Summary
docs.text:
Summary

  • Asking: ¿Dónde está el museo? (a particular place); ¿Hay una farmacia por aquí? (any place of a kind). Answer with está or hay. ¿Cómo llego a …? = How do I get to …?
  • Prepositions of place: cerca de, lejos de, al lado de, enfrente de, delante de, detrás de, entre … y …, a la derecha de, a la izquierda de, en la esquina, al final de. de + el = del.
  • Distance: Está a cinco minutos a pie; está a dos kilómetros.
  • Directions (usted / tú): siga / sigue todo recto; gire / gira a la derecha; tome / toma la primera calle; cruce / cruza la plaza. Latin America also: siga derecho, doble.
  • Ordinals: primero, segundo, tercero, cuarto, quinto, agreeing with the noun; primer, tercer before a masculine singular noun.
  • Transport: en autobús, en metro, en tren, en coche, a pie.

docs.title: 9.8 Exercises
docs.text:
Exercise 1

Give the Spanish for "the railway station".

Answer

la estación de tren. la estación de tren

Exercise 2

You need any cash machine. Ask if there is one near here.

Answer

¿Hay un cajero por aquí? ¿Hay un cajero automático por aquí?

Exercise 3

Complete with está or hay: ¿Dónde ___ la catedral?

Answer

está. ¿Dónde está la catedral? A particular place takes estar.

Exercise 4

Complete: El banco está al lado ___ hotel.

Answer

del. El banco está al lado del hotel. de + el = del.

Exercise 5

A friend asks the way. Tell them "turn left" (tú).

Answer

Gira a la izquierda. Gira a la izquierda. To usted: Gire a la izquierda.

Exercise 6

Translate "the first traffic lights" (one set of lights: el semáforo).

Answer

el primer semáforo. el primer semáforo. primero loses its -o before a masculine singular noun.

Exercise 7

Say "It's ten minutes on foot."

Answer

Está a diez minutos a pie. Está a diez minutos a pie. Also andando or caminando.

Exercise 8

What is the difference between a la derecha and todo derecho?

Answer

a la derecha means "on the right, to the right"; todo derecho means "straight on" (Spain usually says todo recto).

Exercise 9

Correct the mistake: Hay el museo enfrente de la iglesia.

Answer

El museo está enfrente de la iglesia. A particular place, with el, goes with estar. Alternatively, Hay un museo enfrente de la iglesia.

Exercise 10

Using Figure 9.1, tell a stranger (usted) how to get from "Estás aquí" to the park.

Answer

Siga todo recto y tome la primera calle a la izquierda. El parque está a la derecha, después del mercado. (Walking left along Calle del Sol, you pass the market and then reach the park, both on your right; después de means "after".)

docs.title: 9.9 Quiz
docs.text:
Quiz: the city and directions

Exercise 11

You want any chemist's, not a particular one. You ask:

  1. ¿Dónde está la farmacia?
  2. ¿Hay una farmacia por aquí?
  3. ¿Está una farmacia?
  4. ¿Hay la farmacia?
Answer

¿Hay una farmacia por aquí?

Any place of a kind takes hay with un or una.

Exercise 12

"Go straight on" to a stranger (usted), in Spain:

  1. Sigue todo recto.
  2. Siga todo recto.
  3. Gire todo recto.
  4. Siga a la derecha.
Answer

Siga todo recto.

Exercise 13

La parada está enfrente ___ museo.

Answer

del

enfrente de + el museo = enfrente del museo.

Exercise 14

Tome la ___ calle a la izquierda. (second)

Answer

segunda

calle is feminine, so segunda.

Exercise 15

Say "the third floor" (piso is masculine).

Answer

el tercer piso

Exercise 16

Match the Spanish to the English.

ABal lado debehindenfrente defar fromdetrás denext tolejos deopposite Answer

al lado de — next to; enfrente de — opposite; detrás de — behind; lejos de — far from

Exercise 17

Tap the wrong word.

El hotel está en el primero piso.

Answer

Wrong word: primero.

Corrected: El hotel está en el primer piso.

Before a masculine singular noun primero becomes primer.

Exercise 18

Put the words in order.

Words: llego / estación? / la / ¿Cómo / a

Answer

¿Cómo llego a la estación?

Exercise 19

Write what you hear.

Dictation. Have someone read the sentence aloud, then write it down.

Gire a la derecha y cruce la plaza.

Answer

Gire a la derecha y cruce la plaza.

Exercise 20

Say it aloud.

Perdone, ¿dónde está la oficina de turismo?

Answer

Say: Perdone, ¿dónde está la oficina de turismo?

docs.title: Lesson 15: What Happened: The Preterite
docs.text:
El pretérito: lo que pasó

So far you have talked about the present (Lessons 6 to 13) and about plans (Lesson 14). The last big step of this course is the past: what you did yesterday, last weekend, on your holidays. Spanish has several past tenses, and the one you need first is the preterite (el pretérito indefinido or pretérito perfecto simple), the tense of finished actions: I went, we saw, she bought. In this lesson you learn its regular endings, the handful of irregular verbs that everyone uses every day, and the words that place an action in the past. By the end you will be able to tell the story of a trip.

Learning outcomes

By the end of this lesson you will be able to:

  • form the preterite of regular -ar, -er and -ir verbs, with their written accents;
  • spell the yo form of verbs ending in -car, -gar and -zar correctly;
  • use the irregular preterites fui (ser and ir), hice, tuve, estuve and recognise others such as pude, quise, vine, dije;
  • place events in the past with ayer, anoche, la semana pasada, hace dos años and similar expressions;
  • tell a short story of a holiday, and ask someone about theirs;
  • recognise the present perfect (he comido), which Spain uses for today's events.

masculinefeminineplural

docs.title: 15.1 Dialogue: back from the holidays
docs.text:
It is the first Monday of September. Diego, who planned his trip in Lesson 14, is back at work in Madrid. Laura asks him about his holiday with his sister Ana.

  • Laura: ¡Hola, Diego! ¿Qué tal las vacaciones? — Hi, Diego! How were the holidays?
  • Diego: ¡Fenomenal! Lo pasamos genial. — Fantastic! We had a great time.
  • Laura: ¿Adónde fuisteis al final? — Where did you go in the end?
  • Diego: Primero estuvimos tres días en Madrid. Mi hermana visitó el Museo del Prado y yo la llevé al Retiro. — First we spent three days in Madrid. My sister visited the Prado Museum and I took her to the Retiro park.
  • Laura: ¿Y después? — And then?
  • Diego: Después fuimos a Sevilla en tren. Hizo muchísimo calor: ¡cuarenta y dos grados! — Then we went to Seville by train. It was terribly hot: forty-two degrees!
  • Laura: Ya te lo dije. ¿Comprasteis un sombrero? — I told you so. Did you buy a hat?
  • Diego: Sí, compramos dos. Y comimos un gazpacho buenísimo. — Yes, we bought two. And we ate a wonderful gazpacho.
  • Laura: ¿Y Granada? ¿Visitasteis la Alhambra? — And Granada? Did you visit the Alhambra?
  • Diego: Sí, el último día. Tuvimos que reservar las entradas un mes antes, pero valió la pena. — Yes, on the last day. We had to book the tickets a month ahead, but it was worth it.
  • Laura: ¿Y a tu hermana le gustó España? — And did your sister like Spain?
  • Diego: Le encantó. Sacó cientos de fotos. Volvió a México el lunes pasado. ¿Y tú? ¿Qué hiciste en agosto? — She loved it. She took hundreds of photos. She went back to Mexico last Monday. And you? What did you do in August?
  • Laura: Fui al pueblo de mis abuelos, en Asturias. Descansé, leí mucho y me bañé en el mar todos los días. — I went to my grandparents' village in Asturias. I rested, read a lot and swam in the sea every day.
  • Diego: ¡Qué envidia! — I'm so jealous!

Notice:

  1. Every verb that tells what happened is in the preterite: visitó, compramos, comimos, descansé, leí.
  2. Regular forms carry a written accent on the last syllable in the yo and él forms: llevé, visitó, sacó, volvió.
  3. Some very common verbs are irregular and have no accents: fuimos, estuvimos, hizo, tuvimos, dije, hiciste.
  4. gustar and encantar (Lesson 12) work in the past too: le gustó, le encantó.

docs.title: 15.2 Vocabulary: time in the past, and holidays
When did it happen?
docs.text:
Spanish Sounds like English ayer [ah-YEHR] yesterday anteayer [ahn-teh-ah-YEHR] the day before yesterday anoche [ah-NOH-cheh] last night ayer por la mañana [ah-YEHR pohr lah mah-NYAH-nah] yesterday morning el lunes [ehl LOO-nehs] on Monday (last Monday, in a past sentence) el fin de semana pasado [ehl feen deh seh-MAH-nah pah-SAH-doh] last weekend la semana pasada [lah seh-MAH-nah pah-SAH-dah] last week el mes pasado [ehl mehs pah-SAH-doh] last month el año pasado [ehl AH-nyoh pah-SAH-doh] last year el verano pasado [ehl beh-RAH-noh pah-SAH-doh] last summer hace dos días [AH-seh dohs DEE-ahs] two days ago hace un año [AH-seh oon AH-nyoh] a year ago en 2019 [ehn dohs meel dyeh-see-NWEH-beh] in 2019 en agosto [ehn ah-GOHS-toh] in August una vez / dos veces [OO-nah behs / dohs BEH-sehs] once / twice

Table 15.1. Time expressions for the past. Pasado agrees with its noun: el mes pasado, la semana pasada. In most of Spain, hace and vez are said with a th sound: [AH-theh], [behth].

Hace means ago

To say how long ago something happened, put hace in front of the length of time: hace tres días (three days ago), hace una hora (an hour ago), hace mucho tiempo (a long time ago). It is the verb hacer (Lesson 10), which never changes in this phrase. To ask: ¿Cuándo fuiste a Perú? — Hace dos años.

docs.title: What did you do?
docs.text:
Spanish English viajar to travel visitar un museo to visit a museum conocer una ciudad to get to know a city, to see a city for the first time sacar fotos to take photos (Latin America also: tomar fotos) tomar el sol to sunbathe bañarse en el mar to swim in the sea probar la comida típica to try the local food alojarse en un hotel to stay in a hotel alquilar un coche to hire a car descansar to rest salir de noche to go out at night perder el tren to miss the train pasarlo bien / pasarlo mal to have a good time / a bad time

Table 15.2. Holiday activities.

docs.title: How was it?
docs.text:
Spanish English ¿Qué tal el viaje? How was the trip? ¿Qué tal te fue? How did it go (for you)? Fue genial. / Fue fenomenal. It was great. / It was fantastic. Fue un desastre. It was a disaster. Lo pasé muy bien. I had a very good time. Me encantó. I loved it. No me gustó nada. I didn't like it at all. Valió la pena. It was worth it.

Table 15.3. Reacting to a past event.

docs.title: 15.3 Grammar: the regular preterite
docs.text:
The preterite tells of an action that is complete and finished, usually at a time that is stated or clear: Ayer visité el museo. (Yesterday I visited the museum.) It translates the English simple past (I visited) and, in questions and negatives, did you visit?, I didn't visit.

Figure 15.1 The preterite on the time line. A time line. On the left, three completed events in the past, marked as dots: last year I went to Mexico, on Saturday I visited Toledo, yesterday I ate paella; they use the preterite. In the middle, now, which uses the present. On the right, future plans with ir a: tomorrow I am going to study, in August I am going to travel.

The endings are added to the stem (the infinitive without -ar, -er, -ir). There are two sets: one for -ar verbs, and one shared by -er and -ir verbs.

Person hablar comer vivir yo hablé comí viví tú hablaste comiste viviste él, ella, usted habló comió vivió nosotros, nosotras hablamos comimos vivimos vosotros, vosotras hablasteis comisteis vivisteis ellos, ellas, ustedes hablaron comieron vivieron

Table 15.4. The regular preterite. Switch on Practice and write the endings.

Four things to notice:

  1. The accents matter. hablo [AH-bloh] is "I speak"; habló [ah-BLOH] is "he spoke". Only the stress and the accent tell them apart. Say the preterite forms with a strong stress on the last syllable: hablé, habló, comí, comió.
  2. The nosotros forms of -ar and -ir verbs are the same as in the present. hablamos means "we speak" or "we spoke"; vivimos means "we live" or "we lived". The context, usually a time word, decides: Ayer hablamos con Ana. (Yesterday we spoke to Ana.) For -er verbs they differ: comemos (we eat), comimos (we ate).
  3. Stem-changing -ar and -er verbs do not change in the preterite. The "boot" of Lesson 10 belongs to the present only: pienso but pensé; vuelvo but volví; cuesta but costó.
  4. Reflexive verbs keep their pronouns: me levanté, te duchaste, se acostó, nos bañamos.

docs.title: Spelling changes in the yo form
docs.text:
Lesson 1 showed that Spanish changes spelling to keep a sound the same before e and i. The yo ending -é causes three such changes:

Infinitive ends in Change in yo Examples But él form -car c → qu sacar → saqué, buscar → busqué, tocar → toqué sacó -gar g → gu llegar → llegué, pagar → pagué, jugar → jugué llegó -zar z → c empezar → empecé, cruzar → crucé, almorzar → almorcé empezó

Table 15.5. Spelling changes. The sound does not change; only the letters do.

docs.title: -er and -ir verbs with a vowel before the ending
docs.text:
When the stem of an -er or -ir verb ends in a vowel, the i of the él and ellos endings becomes y, because Spanish does not allow an unstressed i between two vowels:

  • leer: leí, leíste, leyó, leímos, leísteis, leyeron
  • creer (to believe): creyó, creyeron
  • oír (to hear): oyó, oyeron

docs.title: -ir verbs that change their stem
docs.text:
The -ir verbs with a stem change in the present (Lessons 10 and 11) also change in the preterite, but only in the él and ellos forms, and only by one vowel: e → i and o → u.

Infinitive yo él, ella, usted ellos, ellas, ustedes dormir dormí durmió durmieron pedir pedí pidió pidieron preferir preferí prefirió prefirieron vestirse me vestí se vistió se vistieron

Table 15.6. -ir verbs with a change in the third person. At this level it is enough to recognise them.

Worked example: a regular day in the past

Put this present-tense routine into the past, as if it happened yesterday: Me levanto a las siete, desayuno, llego a la oficina a las nueve y trabajo hasta las seis.

  1. me levanto → me levanté (regular -ar, yo: -é)
  2. desayuno → desayuné
  3. llego → llegué (-gar: add u to keep the hard g)
  4. trabajo → trabajé

Result: Ayer me levanté a las siete, desayuné, llegué a la oficina a las nueve y trabajé hasta las seis.

docs.title: 15.4 Grammar: irregular preterites
docs.text: A small group of very common verbs is irregular in the preterite. The good news: most of them share one set of endings, and none of them has a written accent.

docs.title: Ser and ir: the same forms
docs.text:
The preterites of ser (to be) and ir (to go) are identical. The sentence always makes clear which is meant: fui a Sevilla (I went to Seville) has a destination; fue genial (it was great) has a description.

Person ser / ir yo fui tú fuiste él, ella, usted fue nosotros, nosotras fuimos vosotros, vosotras fuisteis ellos, ellas, ustedes fueron

Table 15.7. The preterite of ser and ir.

  • El sábado fuimos a la playa. — On Saturday we went to the beach. (ir)
  • La fiesta fue en casa de Pablo. — The party was at Pablo's house. (ser)
  • ¿Adónde fuiste ayer? — Where did you go yesterday? (ir)
  • El viaje fue muy largo. — The journey was very long. (ser)

docs.title: Hacer, tener, estar and their family
docs.text:
These verbs have a new stem and a special set of endings: -e, -iste, -o, -imos, -isteis, -ieron. Note that the yo form ends in unstressed -e and the él form in unstressed -o.

Person hacer tener estar yo hice tuve estuve tú hiciste tuviste estuviste él, ella, usted hizo tuvo estuvo nosotros, nosotras hicimos tuvimos estuvimos vosotros, vosotras hicisteis tuvisteis estuvisteis ellos, ellas, ustedes hicieron tuvieron estuvieron

Table 15.8. Three key irregular preterites. Hizo is spelt with z to keep the sound of hice.

The same pattern works for other verbs from this course:

Infinitive Stem yo él, ella, usted poder pud- pude pudo poner pus- puse puso querer quis- quise quiso venir vin- vine vino saber sup- supe supo decir dij- dije dijo (ellos: dijeron)

Table 15.9. More irregular preterites with the same endings. After j, -ieron becomes -eron: dijeron.

docs.title: Ver and dar
docs.text:
Two short verbs use the regular -er/-ir endings, but without accents because the forms are one syllable: ver: vi, viste, vio, vimos, visteis, vieron. dar (to give), although it is an -ar verb, takes the same endings: di, diste, dio, dimos, disteis, dieron.

  • Anoche vi una película muy buena. — Last night I saw a very good film.
  • Mis padres me dieron un regalo. — My parents gave me a present.

docs.title: Hay in the past
docs.text:
The preterite of hay is hubo, "there was, there were", for an event: Hubo un concierto en la plaza. (There was a concert in the square.) For the weather, use hacer: hizo calor, hizo buen tiempo; and llovió, nevó for rain and snow.

Common mistake: accents on irregular forms

Regular preterites have accents (hablé, comió); irregular ones do not. Write hice, tuvo, fui, fue, vio, dio, never hicé, tuvó, fuí. And do not confuse fue (he went, it was) with fui (I went, I was).

docs.title: For recognition: the present perfect, and the imperfect
docs.text:
You will hear two more past tenses, which later courses teach in full.

The present perfect (pretérito perfecto compuesto) is formed with haber + a participle in -ado or -ido: he hablado (I have spoken), has comido (you have eaten), ha vivido, hemos visto, habéis ido, han hecho.
